# Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks

- [Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks](#improving-jalapenos-compute-blocks)
- [Our collaboration with AMD](#our-collaboration-with-amd)
- [Optimizing RISC-V cores](#optimizing-risc-v-cores)
- [Designing a RISC-V core from a specification](#designing-a-risc-v-core-from-a-specification)
- [What’s next](#whats-next)

- [Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks](#improving-jalapenos-compute-blocks)
- [Our collaboration with AMD](#our-collaboration-with-amd)
- [Optimizing RISC-V cores](#optimizing-risc-v-cores)
- [Designing a RISC-V core from a specification](#designing-a-risc-v-core-from-a-specification)
- [What’s next](#whats-next)

OpenAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI. [In August,⁠](https://openai.com/index/jalapeno-first-results/) we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

## Improving Jalapeño’s compute blocks

We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:

**In the vector unit**, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

**In the matrix unit**, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during [Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up⁠](https://openai.com/index/jalapeno-first-results/).

## Our collaboration with AMD

We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

## Optimizing RISC-V cores

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

**On the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s.**

**On the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together.**

## Designing a RISC-V core from a specification

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

**Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets.**

**On Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets.**

Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design.

## What’s next

We have demonstrated that our models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed, we’re partnering with Synopsys to train [GPT‑Synopsys⁠(opens in a new window)](https://investor.synopsys.com/news/news-details/2026/OpenAI-and-Synopsys-Announce-GPT-Synopsys-Frontier-Intelligence-to-Revolutionize-Chip-Design/default.aspx), a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do.

# Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI partner to bring Le Figaro journalism to ChatGPT

The collaboration will make Le Figaro’s journalism discoverable in ChatGPT using summaries and excerpts, including links to underlying stories.

Share

Le Groupe Figaro and OpenAI [announced a strategic partnership⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.groupefigaro.com/uploads/a014d3b4-4841-4a25-bee0-82f5360c1f77.pdf) today to help more people discover and engage with Le Figaro’s journalism. The partnership covers current reporting and archive content from Le Figaro and associated publications, spanning news, business, culture and lifestyle. These articles will be discoverable using summaries and excerpts, including links to underlying stories.

> “*This partnership reflects Groupe Figaro’s ambition to build meaningful relationships with a leader in artificial intelligence research and deployment. Combining Groupe Figaro’s editorial heritage and trusted brands supported by a team of more than 600 journalists who provide a reliable source of information with OpenAI’s technological expertise and global reach will bring new opportunities for innovation and create long-term value for our readers.*”

*— Marc Feuillée, Chief Executive Officer, Groupe Figaro*

> “*Le Figaro’s reporting helps readers make sense of the stories shaping France and the wider world, and we want AI to help more people discover that work. This partnership reflects our commitment to working with publishers to support quality journalism and connect it with new audiences.*”

*— Varun Shetty, Vice President of Media Partnerships, OpenAI*

Le Figaro will retain full editorial independence and control over its journalism. The partnership builds on OpenAI’s work with news organisations around the world to improve the discovery of reliable information, create responsible applications of AI for publishers, and develop new ways for audiences to engage with original reporting.

Le Figaro also plans to introduce ChatGPT Enterprise across various teams to support their day-to-day work. It will explore additional uses of OpenAI technology in its workflows and reader services, guided by its AI charter and editorial standards.

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
body:
17th November 2026 - Link Blog
[External sandboxes for coding agents](https://blog.primeradiant.com/external-sandboxes-for-coding-agents/). I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.
I worked on this project with [Prime Radiant](https://primeradiant.com), the AI research lab behind Superpowers and [other projects](https://github.com/orgs/prime-radiant-inc/repositories).
[My post](https://blog.primeradiant.com/external-sandboxes-for-coding-agents/) on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.
To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:
[external-sandbox-v86](https://github.com/prime-radiant-inc/external-sandbox-v86)runs a Node.js server which then uses[v86](https://github.com/copy/v86)to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.[external-sandbox-container](https://github.com/prime-radiant-inc/external-sandbox-container)is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.[external-sandbox-quicksand](https://github.com/prime-radiant-inc/external-sandbox-quicksand)is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's[Quicksand](https://github.com/microsoft/quicksand)sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!
Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.
The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:
I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences
body:
Final URL: https://news.microsoft.com/source/2026/11/17/microsoft-and-salesforce-announce-copilotforce-bringing-trusted-customer-context-and-action-into-microsoft-ai-experiences/

Published Time: 2026-11-17T18:10:16+00:00

Markdown Content:
*   _New integrations connect Salesforce with Microsoft Copilot, Teams and Fabric, helping enterprises turn Salesforce customer insights into action while maintaining existing security and permissions._

*   _New two-way Zero Copy integrations between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric enable organizations to securely query and analyze data across both platforms without maintaining duplicate datasets._

*   _Accenture is serving as design and implementation partner and pilot customer, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization._

**REDMOND, Wash., and SAN FRANCISCO — Nov. 17, 2026 —** Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Salesforce Inc. (NYSE: CRM) today announced Copilotforce, a new partnership that helps employees get more done in the tools they already use by bringing Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences.

Unveiled at Microsoft Ignite, the partnership introduces new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin available in public preview with 38+ prebuilt sales skills. Together, these capabilities help businesses move faster, reduce manual work and get more value from their existing technology investments — while maintaining the security, governance and permissions they already rely on.

Bringing Salesforce workflows together with conversations, meetings and documents in Microsoft 365 means less time spent moving between systems and more time on the work that matters. Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with the work happening across the business so employees can make more informed decisions and take action without constantly switching applications.

Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides relevant context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive. Work IQ and Salesforce help sellers understand not only what’s recorded in CRM, but what’s happening across customer conversations and collaboration — and what needs to happen next.

Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can securely retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within their existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies its existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Data, context and the apps where sellers work come to life in practical workflows across the sales cycle, including:

*   **Grow Revenue****.** Use the Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills to decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a concrete path to signature. Customer priorities and deal context inform the proposals and business cases sellers develop in Word and PowerPoint, with clear owners, milestones and next steps.

*   **Manage Risk.** Connect Salesforce opportunity data with customer concerns raised in Outlook, escalations discussed in Teams and unresolved commitments. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to the customer concern in an Outlook thread, the escalation discussed in Teams or the unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal, helping sellers identify where to intervene.

*   **Move faster.** Turn customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities using the Call Follow-Up skill. Sellers can review and confirm next steps instead of manually reconstructing conversations and updating multiple systems.

With Copilot as the front door to business process, Salesforce in Copilot allows organizations to bring together Salesforce data, workflows, agents and prebuilt skills from the systems they already rely on through Copilot’s open and interoperable platform.

“AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it,” said **Judson Althoff, CEO, Microsoft Commercial Business**. “Bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with the work context delivered by Work IQ in Microsoft Copilot allows our joint customers to unlock actionable insights across their core business applications. Copilotforce will give sales teams the intelligence they need to make faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand.”

“Through Copilotforce, we’re bringing Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today, embedding trusted Salesforce context and intelligent sales workflows directly where sellers work,” said **Miguel Milano, President & Chief Operating Officer, Salesforce**. “By bringing together the #1 CRM with the #1 productivity surface, we’re transforming AI from a standalone tool into a powerful driver of productivity, smarter decisions and customer success.”

**Expanding connection in the places people work**

For many organizations, the work first starts in Microsoft Teams, where people share files, make decisions and hand work to each other. Sales Cloud in Teams, now available in pilot, brings Salesforce customer context directly into those conversations, so sellers can see pipeline and quota progress, get deal notifications and find briefing materials without leaving the place where decisions are already being made.

Across these Microsoft and Salesforce integrations, customer data remains protected at every boundary: Salesforce controls data access and governs supported business actions, while Microsoft ensures communications and documents adhere to existing enterprise compliance policies. Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules, so teams can act with confidence while customer records stay governed and auditable.

AI is only as useful as the context it can reach, and for many enterprises customer data lives in Salesforce while operational and financial data lives in Microsoft Fabric. Microsoft and Salesforce are bringing a two-way Zero Copy connection between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric, so teams can work with fuller context across both platforms without building pipelines or maintaining duplicate datasets.

With Data Federation, now generally available, joint customers can now directly query and analyze supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data within Salesforce Data 360. A service agent can see a customer’s recent purchases on their account, a marketer can build a segment from spending behavior and an AI agent can answer from current data, all without moving the source data out of Fabric. Salesforce Data 360 shortcut, now in public preview, allows organizations to securely share curated Data 360 customer intelligence into OneLake so data teams can analyze it alongside enterprise datasets for analytics, reporting and AI workloads without duplicating data.

**From design partner to pilot customer**

Accenture is working with Microsoft and Salesforce as the design and implementation partner for the new integrations, bringing deep expertise across 13 industries globally in delivering business outcomes with both partners. In addition, having scaled Copilot to more than 740,000 people and as one of the largest Salesforce users globally with 55,000 users, Accenture is also a pilot customer, deploying and validating the integrations within its own global sales organization and sharing learnings to help clients turn investments they have already made in Salesforce and Microsoft into a better way to sell, driving faster growth and lowering risk.

“As a Global Partner of the Year for both Salesforce and Microsoft and one of their top customers, we are uniquely positioned to bring our expertise to help design and implement Copilotforce so that our clients can quickly get more value from their technology investments,” said **Julie Sweet, Chair and CEO, Accenture**. “The combined strengths of our three companies will reinvent sales with AI, giving sellers more time with customers while trusted intelligence and agents work alongside them in the tools they already use. We are also excited to serve as customer zero for Copilotforce.”

**Availability***

Salesforce in Copilot is available in public preview (beta) beginning today. Data federation from Microsoft OneLake into Salesforce Data 360 is generally available, and data sharing from Data 360 into OneLake is in public preview. Sales Cloud in Teams is in pilot with enterprise customers, with open beta coming later this year.

To learn more about what’s new in Copilot at Microsoft Ignite, visit [https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/blog/](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/blog/).

Microsoft enables digital transformation for the era of an intelligent cloud and an intelligent edge. Its mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. title: Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is now generally available for fast, low-cost decision making
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/microsoft-decision-model-ga/

Published Time: 2026-11-17T18:10:02+00:00

Markdown Content:
Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is now generally available in Microsoft Foundry and through OpenRouter and Vercel. The model is powering experiences across Microsoft and has been used by more than 4,000 customers since launching in public preview last month.

By [Achint Srivastava](https://commandline.microsoft.com/author/achint-srivastava)VP of Software Engineering, Office of the CTO, Microsoft

2026.11.17

As software developers, we’ve always wanted to embed intelligence inside our software, applications, and workflows, rather than anticipate all scenarios and hardcode every decision. LLMs have shown they have the general intelligence to enable this new software architecture, but three challenges stand in the way of deploying it to software at scale: cost, latency, and control.

It’s well-known that cheaper, faster models can be integrated in more places in software. But _control_ is equally important. To integrate AI more broadly in software, especially at enterprise scale, we must be able to rely on the decisions a model makes.

Generative models are increasingly intelligent, but the way they’re trained works against the control and reliability that software needs. They’re rewarded for completing tasks, providing answers, and reaching goals, so they tend to make assumptions, sound confident, and take action, even when doing so is wrong or risky.

What the industry needs, and is excited about, is a new kind of model designed and trained from first principles to make more reliable decisions: a decision model.

We recently released [Microsoft-Decision-1](https://commandline.microsoft.com/microsoft-decision-1-model-foundry/) as our first answer to this challenge. Microsoft’s decision models are designed to make calibrated decisions in the face of uncertainty across a wide range of real-world software use cases. They choose among permitted actions, within constraints set by the developer, and provide calibrated confidence scores so applications can defer when uncertainty is high. And because they specialize in decision-making, they’re significantly faster and less expensive than general-purpose LLMs for decision-making tasks.

Today we’re **announcing the general availability of Microsoft-Decision-1.1**, with greater intelligence, better calibration, and more than twice the speed of our first model, all at a low cost. It’s designed to make structured decisions in software at scale, for tasks like routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control. And we’ve added multimodal support, so the model can now accept images, such as photos and screenshots, as part of a request. **Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is ready for enterprise production deployment and is available in [Microsoft Foundry](https://aka.ms/decision-1.1) and through [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/microsoft/microsoft-decision-1.1) and [Vercel](https://vercel.com/changelog/decision-1-1-now-available-on-ai-gateway).**

## How we built Microsoft-Decision-1.1

Making intelligence foundational to software requires a model that’s smart at making decisions, fast enough to keep applications responsive, and affordable enough to embed everywhere. Achieving all three together is the main challenge of building a decision model and requires joint innovation across modeling and infrastructure. Here’s how we approached this:

*   **Latency:** Decision models need to operate in real time, even when processing complex requests with long inputs and hundreds of questions. Unlike traditional LLM inference engines optimized for generating text token by token, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 uses a custom inference engine optimized for the computational demands of decision models.
*   **Cost:** Our custom inference engine optimizes for low cost, not just low latency, by efficiently routing requests across our fleet of GPUs. We also based on a mid-sized mixture-of-experts model, Gemma 4 26B A4B, which has enough active parameters to deliver the intelligence needed for decisions, while remaining efficient enough to run across a flexible range of hardware (A100, H100/200, GB200/300).
*   **Intelligence:** Decision models need to stay small enough to run everywhere, generalize well to new or unseen tasks, and be trained specifically to make decisions. To get there, we combined supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with hundreds of synthetic and licensed datasets spanning tens of thousands types of tasks from a wide range of industries to teach the model to make nuanced judgments rather than memorize answers, discriminate between closely related choices, recognize uncertainty, and know when to answer vs. abstain.
*   **Calibration:** We also trained the model to know what it doesn’t know: to give consistent answers across similar scenarios, accurately report its level of confidence in its answers, split confidence when more than one answer is valid, and abstain when information is incomplete. This allows developers to set their own thresholds for when to act, flag, or escalate.

## Benchmarks

On the [Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-decision-index), which scores model quality, calibration, and latency, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 scores 68, up six points from our first model and ahead of Jev 1.14, Google’s Gemini Decision 1, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna (Decisions). Microsoft-Decision-1.1 is more than twice as fast as our first model, at the same cost.

# Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

GPT-6.2

### AstraSol

## A new standard for professional work

GPT-6.2 Sol: our go-to model for everyday work

We’re introducing **GPT‑6.2 Astra**, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and **GPT‑6.2 Sol**, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

**Agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model.**

We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1Vals Science Index v1

**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 evaluates models on scientific research workflows.*[1](#user-content-fn-benchmark-implementations)*

In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1BenchCAD 2.1 CoreAutomationBench 1.0.6

**Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations across knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge.**

## GPT-6.2 Sol: our go-to model for everyday work

Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid plan. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.

In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

**FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging.**

Its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the important tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released [LifeVal ⁠](https://openai.com/index/lifeval/) evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.

**LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis.**

## Professional outputs that match industry standards

We trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.

Harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. [Astra for Law ⁠](https://openai.com/index/astra-law-6-2), our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.

**Harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations.**

Our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of [GDPval ⁠](https://openai.com/index/gdpval/) that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. title: Put Gemini to work for you
body:
Put Gemini to work for you
The best assistant knows you and helps you get things done. Today, you can now hand off even more tasks to Gemini and move on with your day. We’ve built it for anyone who has tasks piling up during all the classes, meetings, and school drop-offs that fill the day. Our goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.
Starting now, this update is rolling out free of charge for hundreds of millions of people across the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, using our new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. We’re also rolling out a set of advanced features, starting in the U.S.
How it’s changing my daily routine
If your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards are already in the Google ecosystem, Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because this sensitive data already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.
Here’s how I’m using it.
Recently, our minivan’s check-engine light came on. Ugh. I pulled out Gemini and told it, "Our minivan is overdue for a service appointment. Please call the two nearest dealerships and figure out how to get an appointment early Friday morning over the next month or so."
Because Gemini already knows we drive a 2019 Honda Odyssey and where we live through [Personal Intelligence](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/personal-intelligence/), it found the nearest shops on Google Maps and called both at once
[1](#footnote-1)
. Thankfully, I didn’t have to suffer through any hold music. Gemini did the job, found a time in my Google Calendar when I was free, and added the Friday early morning appointment in less than five minutes. Done. (On the dealership's end, Gemini disclosed right away that it's an AI. Businesses can [opt out](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7690269) whenever they want, and Gemini won’t give out my payment or private account info unless I say so.)
In the background, Gemini called both dealerships at once, sat through the hold music for me, booked an appointment at the shop that accepts appointments vs. walk-ins only, and put Friday's appointment on my calendar without me having to check it.
Last month it saved us real money after we got hit with a surprise $389 electric bill. I gave Gemini permission to access our utility portal with the new Google Password Manager integration and asked for it to analyze our past billing statements in my email. Gemini worked for a few minutes, and then nailed it. The primary culprit was our heat pump, which it turns out was kicking on around 4 p.m., right in the middle of peak pricing. My wife and I never would have caught that digging through the PDFs and emails ourselves.
I use it for smaller stuff, too. For our upcoming holiday trip back to Oklahoma, I recently asked Gemini to give me the best options for a USB-C charger. Gemini quickly compared chargers thanks to Google’s Shopping Graph, asked me follow-up questions about the wattage and color, and then helped me check out using the new Google Pay integration. The best part: it also found a discount code so I saved an extra $10. Done.
Gemini now uses the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) to make purchases like this. We’re working with American Express (coming soon), Mastercard, and Visa to keep your purchases secure with digital tokens on supported cards. And when you shop with Gemini, you still earn your card's points, cashback, or purchase protections during checkout. You can also set a hard spending cap upfront, and Gemini is designed to stay within your budget. All of your receipts and tracking info land straight in Google Wallet, which is expanding to iOS [starting today](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/google-pay/wallet-available-ios-united-states/). Up next, we’ll integrate the [Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)](https://developers.google.com/merchant/ucp) into Gemini so everyone can expect an even faster and more reliable shopping experience from discovery to checkout.
Gemini lets you set the spending limit and still earn every airline mile, cashback point, and perk on your card.
Gemini helps with weeknight dinners, too. I recently stared down a nearly empty fridge rushing out the door in the morning, and I texted Gemini with the new RCS integration
[2](#footnote-2)
: “Add lasagna, strawberries, cucumbers, and vanilla ice cream to our Instacart order.” On the walk out, I saw an empty Cheerios box in the pantry, so I snapped a photo and sent a quick follow-up: “Add this too.” Gemini added it, and then handed me off to Instacart to complete the order. Groceries were on the doorstep when we got home. Done. Today, Gemini connects with more than 60 popular apps and, as a developer, you can apply to join our [Connected Apps Platform](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/connected-apps-one-place/).
My wife and I also use Gemini to sort out medical bills, keep track of insurance renewals, and stay on top of our kids' schedules. Earlier this week, I forwarded a batch of school emails from Gmail to gemini@google.com. In less than a minute, every date was on my calendar with my wife invited. Better yet, it noticed a conflict during basketball practice and asked if I wanted to text one of the other parents to trade carpool duty.
How we protect your data
As Gemini becomes more capable, we continually advance our security defenses. When you assign Gemini a task, it uses [Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/agent-compute-engine-deep-dive) to work in a hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users. Each virtual machine is sandboxed, so Gemini works in a separate, isolated environment that’s regularly tested by our security red teams. This sandbox is just one of multiple layers of defense, including prompt-injection filters that scan search results, webpages, and more alongside Google Safe Browsing to limit which links Gemini can open.
As Gemini works on a task, you can jump in to give it more instructions at any point, and it’s also designed to pause and check with you before critical steps. For example, Gemini is designed to ask for your confirmation or pre-approval before clicking "Buy," and will ask clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous. For routine stuff you already trust, like adding those Cheerios to your grocery cart, you can set that to “Always allow” so it doesn’t pester you.
And finally, we give you access to settings and tools that help you safeguard your data and protect your privacy. You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime. For a closer look at how we’ve implemented a multi-layer defense-in-depth security strategy, read our [technical paper](https://blog.google/security/how-geminis-defense-in-depth-approach-works/).
And please participate in our bug bounty program through Google’s [AI Vulnerability Reward Program (AI VRP)](https://bughunters.google.com/about/rules/google-friends/ai-vulnerability-reward-program-rules) to advance the security of agentic systems.
How you can help us improve
While we’ve tested tasks extensively to minimize mistakes, we haven't eliminated all of them. You may encounter situations where a task fails to complete or misses the mark. When you see this, please provide feedback by giving the response a “thumbs down.”
For example, the way personal assistants navigate the web is still evolving as sites are still adapting to these new use cases. On some sites, Gemini can make it most of the way through and then hand the screen back to you to click the final button. We’re partnering directly with major websites and security providers to help the web evolve so it works well for site owners and personal assistants. For decades, bots were blocked by default because most were malicious. Personal assistants require a more nuanced approach, and we believe open, verifiable standards will benefit everyone.
How to try it
Ready to hand off your next task? Open Gemini, flip the home-screen toggle from Chat to Task, and tell Gemini what you need done. Starting in the U.S., you can also forward emails to [gemini@google.com](mailto:gemini@google.com) or text Gemini by following these instructions:
- Open Gemini on Android or iOS and tap Settings
- Tap Channels
- Tap Set up under Text with Gemini
- Verify your phone number
We can’t wait to see what Gemini crosses off your list first.

title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
body:
Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
17th November 2026
[Datasette Lite](https://lite.datasette.io/) is my port of the [Datasette](https://datasette.io/) Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/). I’ve released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it’s now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.
You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:
- Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
- Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
- Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
- Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
- Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools
The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.
As an example, consider the following URL:
Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you’ll find yourself on a page that looks like this:
That’s Datasette running the new [datasette-maplibre](https://github.com/datasette/datasette-maplibre) plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.
Let’s break down that URL to see what it’s doing:
https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
The ?install=datasette-maplibre
installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=...
as many times as you like to load more plugins.
&url=https://.../demo.db
loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have [open CORS headers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS)—I host files like this in [Gists](https://gist.github.com/), because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
loads [this metadata.yml file](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml). The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit [that homepage here](https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/) for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent
is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette—here it’s loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries
SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23
is a URL-encoded #
) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent
column in the data.
That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in [URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Feb/13/url-addressable-python/) last year.
The full set of supported URL arguments is [described in the Datasette Lite README](https://github.com/simonw/datasette-lite#load-a-different-datasette-version).
I’ve already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here’s [a recent issue](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/issues/3056#issuecomment-6902484982) describing a pagination bug—I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:
Demo of the bug:
[https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score]—click next and the second page is empty.Here’s that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43):
[https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score]
How this works, using service workers
Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version [back in 2022](https://simonwillison.net/2022/May/4/datasette-lite/), originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.
The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML
.
This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML
don’t execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.
The new version takes a completely different approach based on [Service Workers](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Service_Worker_API). These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.
Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io
domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:
/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
/app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)
Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/
prefix. What’s that about?
The /app/<session>/
prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.
Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre
plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.
The service worker for lite.datasette.io
is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.
Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.
(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)
I had Claude Fable 5.2 [generate several SVG diagrams](https://gisthost.github.io/?4192a5a24136cad4c8490ccb15e87d83) to help explain this. Here’s my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:
This system started life [back in May](https://simonwillison.net/2026/May/30/pyodide-asgi-browser/) as an [AI research spike](https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/pyodide-asgi-browser#readme) generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn’t until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!
Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite
I added this feature [last night](https://github.com/simonw/datasette-lite/commit/de661dbee42a68304811a0035b78e6b683203cd1) as an off-shoot of investigating [a potential bug in SQLite](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/16/llm/).
Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.
Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.
In the past I’ve [used various tricks](https://til.simonwillison.net/sqlite/sqlite-version-macos-python) to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process.
WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.
[datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels](https://github.com/datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels) is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for [pysqlite3](https://github.com/coleifer/pysqlite3) for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:
pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl
That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.
Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite=
URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1
, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.
Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool]([https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29)) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here’s an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:
This should work for every other Python app, too
Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.
C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can [even publish them to PyPI](https://github.com/pypi/warehouse/pull/19804) as of PEP 783 in April 2026.
One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.
I’d love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

title: Productiv-icky
body:
productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do
We have a problem.
We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them.
So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy.
But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend…
Yeses are easy. They’re quick.
But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes.
Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about.
I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate.
I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master.
Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine.
Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is.
We started measuring shovels instead of the hole.
Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff.
You feel behind. Like way behind.
So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with.
Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole.
I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom.
But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot.
Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole?
Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse.

title: Ian Buck Kicks Off NVIDIA’s Week at SC26 as Science Enters the Age of Agents
body:
NVIDIA’s Ian Buck kicked off the company’s week at SC26 in Chicago on Monday with new tools for AI agents, software that can plan experiments, run code and check results on researchers’ own systems.
In NVIDIA’s special address, Buck announced[ Nemotron for Science](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-introduces-nemotron-for-science-to-accelerate-discoveries-with-agents), the Rubin HPC GPU and an[ expanded Vera CPU platform for high-performance computing](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-expands-vera-cpu-platform-to-accelerate-scientific-discovery). He also detailed a new collaboration in quantum computing with [IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-announces-collaboration-with-ibm-and-fermi-national-accelerator-laboratory-to-launch-quantum-classical-codesign-platform-plus-error-correction-breakthrough-to-advance-practical-quantum-computing).
“The frontier of computing and the new scientific stack is going to be simulation, as always, but combined with AI and the future of quantum,” said Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA.
Buck opened the talk by looking back to his first public talk on CUDA, at an SC06 tutorial in Tampa, Florida, 20 years ago. NVIDIA now offers more than 1,000[ CUDA-X libraries](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/20-years-cuda/), he said.
Open Models for Science Agents
“[Agents] have been just a game changer in how we interface with our supercomputers, with our devices, our instruments and how we can do the research,” Buck said.
Simulation remains the foundation of scientific computing, “which will always be on the top,” Buck said, with AI, quantum and now agents working alongside it.
Nemotron for Science combines the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model with a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes for life sciences and chemistry, Buck explained. Researchers can run it locally on a DGX Spark, a workstation or their own supercomputer.
At Argonne National Laboratory, Buck said, an agent built with the toolkit took a single prompt, planned and tested hypotheses, chose which simulations to run and identified two new binding sites.
“You own your data. You own the model,” Buck said.
Buck highlighted other agents already in use:
- GROMACS: An agent from KTH Royal Institute of Technology repairs broken GROMACS setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single DGX Spark, it fixed 81% of test cases.
- SETI Institute: At the Allen Telescope Array, an agent took a one-line prompt to plot a methanol line. Buck explained that it then retuned for Doppler shift on its own [NGC 869 vs. 896, check slide].
- Nsight AI Porting Agent: NVIDIA’s new agent ported a routine from the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to GPUs, Buck said, speeding it up more than 5x using about 150 million tokens.
CPUs for the Agent Loop
Agents lean on CPUs to run tool calls between model steps, Buck explained.
“That’s exactly what agents need,” he said. “They need a CPU that can run, evaluate, run the tool, perform the operations, gather the results.”
DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, expected in early 2028. Buck said it joins Vera systems already announced at Texas Advanced Computing Center.
A New GPU for Science
Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the Vera Rubin platform, built for science, engineering, analytics and AI, Buck said.
It supports precisions from FP64 to FP4, adds sparse-data acceleration and connects over seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink. With more than 50,000 CUDA cores, it has about three times as many as Hopper, Buck said. It is expected in 2028.
Quantum Error Correction
Buck said a simulation on Jülich’s JUPITER supercomputer showed that a technique called magic state cultivation can cut the operations needed for one logical step tenfold. The work is being added to CUDA-Q.
NVIDIA, IBM and Fermilab announced plans today for a quantum computing co-design platform to support error-correction and applications research. NVIDIA and IBM are pairing NVIDIA DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk.
Buck also introduced a new breakthrough for quantum decoding. The goal, Buck explained, is to cut decoding latency from about 300 microseconds to 10. A new CUDA-Q decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, cuts error-correction research computation from 12 weeks to 45 minutes, he said.
Networking
Buck also showed one of the first deployments of [NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics switches, at Lambda](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/lambda-photonics/). He said they are 15x more reliable on bit errors and link flaps.
See[ notice](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/about-nvidia/terms-of-service/) regarding software product information.

title: Introducing ChatGPT for Sales
body:
Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-for-sales/

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing ChatGPT for Sales to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork, and close more deals. It includes our new Sales plugin with dedicated skills for sellers, and more than 30 new and enhanced partner plugins in ChatGPT, so you can use information from the tools your team already relies on to prepare for calls, tailor proposals, and follow up faster.

## A starting point for every seller

The new Sales plugin from OpenAI gives you ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Sales teams work best when everyone has a shared understanding of the customer. Which accounts are worth pursuing? What does a buyer need to move forward? Which deals need attention, and why? The answers often sit across teammates, prospecting tools, customer calls, and the CRM. Bringing that information together gives teams more time to make informed decisions and follow through on customer commitments. That starts with the work you do every day.

ChatGPT for Sales launch demo.

## Connect your sales process to ChatGPT

ChatGPT for Sales brings your tools, customer context, and sales workflows into one place. It also gives your team access to partner plugins, so ChatGPT can use customer context from your existing tools to help move opportunities forward. Choose the partner plugins that fit your sales process.

![Image 1: Sales tools grouped by workflow: content and enablement, accounts and deals, prospecting, customer conversations, performance and risk, and quotes and agreements.](https://images.ctfassets.net/kftzwdyauwt9/48BvXASnmKpi0EzXrUaWyG/5dc54e82256fe60ad4fe6431d3a6412e/introducing-chatgpt-for-sales-connected-tools.png?w=3840&q=90&fm=webp)

*   **Create content and equip sellers**. Learn your sales process and the latest product updates with Confluence, Guru, and Seismic. Rehearse pitches and practice handling objections with ChatGPT Voice. Build tailored presentations with ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma, or Canva, or create an interactive demo or ROI calculator with ChatGPT Sites.

*   **Manage accounts and advance deals**. Bring together account context from Salesforce, HubSpot, Close CRM, or monday CRM to prepare for calls, review customer commitments, and plan next steps.

*   **Find and engage buyers**. Combine account signals from Apollo, Clay, and Common Room with ChatGPT’s web research to understand what’s changing at an account and identify reasons to reach out. Use Outreach or Salesloft to plan your outreach.

*   **Turn customer conversations into action**. Use call notes from the Meetings plugin in ChatGPT, Gong, Otter.ai, or Granola to understand buyer priorities, capture agreed next steps, and draft follow-ups.

*   **Track performance and spot deal risk**. Use signals from Backstory to identify deals that need attention. Analyze connected sales data with the Data plugin in ChatGPT or Hex to explain what changed in the pipeline and where to focus next.

*   **Prepare quotes and agreements**. Bring in Docusign, Ironclad, PandaDoc, or ServiceNow CPQ to help prepare quotes and agreements when a buyer is ready to move forward.

You can also keep work moving between conversations by delegating to your [dot](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/)—an always-on agent in ChatGPT. Your dot can use these same plugins and customer context to prepare meeting briefs, track deal updates, and proactively bring you relevant changes and proposed next steps for review.

## Use cases for every sales team

### Build pipeline in the right accounts

Use ChatGPT to build a prioritized account list from your CRM information and prospect research from tools like ZoomInfo and Clay. Ask why each account fits, identify missing information, and refine the list around your team’s priorities. Then turn that research into outreach with a specific reason to engage—all in the same conversation.

### Make a stronger case to each buyer

Before a meeting, ask for a briefing that brings together account history, previous calls, and the buyer’s priorities. Explore what still needs an answer, then turn that preparation into a customer-specific pitch with Gamma or Canva. Refine the story in the conversation before your meeting.

### Keep deals moving with clear next steps

After a call, have ChatGPT draft the follow-up, capture agreed next steps, and prepare updates to the customer record. Refine the message in the conversation and review the proposed changes. With connected tools like Attio, you can save the next step to your CRM from ChatGPT.

### See where your pipeline is at risk

Ask ChatGPT to help you understand what is holding up a deal, using CRM history and customer conversations. With Rox, you can also ask a dot to check the deal each morning, flag changes that need attention, and prepare a meeting brief or follow-up sequence for your review.

**See a few examples from across the sales ecosystem showing how these tools work in ChatGPT:**

HubSpot partner demo for ChatGPT for Sales.

**Turn context into followups**

## How sales teams are winning with ChatGPT

From account research to deal follow-through, hear how sales teams are putting ChatGPT for Sales to work.

1 of 5

## Get started

[Install the Sales plugin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/sales?openaicom-did=60b04e91-10e4-4794-aba9-cc73a0c24018&openaicom_referred=true) to get started, and [learn more about ChatGPT for Sales](https://openai.com/business/solutions/sales/) and the partner plugins. Availability of partner plugins and features varies by plan, region, and workspace settings.

ChatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales for your team by opening the[Admin Console⁠(opens in a new window)](https://admin.openai.com/), selecting your workspace, and selecting Plugins. Make the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install, or [install them⁠(opens in a new window)](https://help.openai.com/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-for-plugins-and-apps) by default for your team. Review access to the required apps and the actions they can use. Workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted.

We’re continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. Our goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through.
