title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
body:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available[here]and[here].
Introduction
Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.
One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.
The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.
[The first problem](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1) Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.
In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists [set out the calculation that would settle the question](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0310285), but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.
[The second problem](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00174v1) concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.
Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.
Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.
Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.
In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.
A note about Claude’s methods
In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.
The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.
The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result [recently proved by an OpenAI model](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/ten-proofs-oai.pdf). Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.
The Hawking-Page transition
To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.
Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.
This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.
To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.
This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.
Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.
Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.
At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.
It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.
This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.
In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a

title: Linked billing on the Claude Platform
body:
Linked billing on the Claude Platform
Today we're introducing linked billing on the Claude Platform in beta. Third-party platforms, such as coding agents and workflow automation tools, can let their end customers pay for Claude API usage without sharing an API key. End customers keep their existing Anthropic billing and set their own spend limits, and platforms get a simpler, more secure way to offer Claude.
A more secure alternative to sharing API keys
Paying for Claude API usage on a third-party platform usually means sharing an API key, which works like a password: anyone who has the key can make requests billed to the customer, so the platform has to keep it safe.
With linked billing, customers link their Claude Platform organization instead, and usage is billed directly to it. No API key changes hands, so platforms have no customer keys to store, encrypt or rotate, and customers’ API keys never leave their organization.
Platforms can see usage for each linked customer. Customers approve each linked platform, set a spend limit, and can unlink at any time.
Platforms can offer Claude to customers without building the billing
Linked billing gives platforms a new way to offer Claude to their customers. Platforms send requests, and Anthropic bills the end customers directly. With linked billing, platforms can:
- Launch faster. Anthropic hosts the approval flow and the billing, so there’s no metering or invoicing to build.
- Understand usage by customer. Get each linked customer’s request count, token usage and models used in Console, or programmatically with the
[Usage and Cost Analytics API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/usage-cost-analytics-api)(beta). - Choose who pays. Decide on each request whether the platform or the end customer pays, so platforms can pass Claude API costs to customers or cover some features themselves by product or instance.
Customers get more visibility and control
Customers can easily link to platforms using Anthropic’s hosted flow. They can then draw down from their existing Anthropic commitment, or pay as they go. With linked billing, customers can also:
- Link once for the whole organization. A Console user with an Owner, Admin, or Billing role approves the link, so it works the same for individual developers and large teams.
- Set limits for each platform. Customers can set a monthly spend limit for each platform, or a default that applies to each one.
- See where API spend goes. Console shows spend for each linked platform.
- Unlink at any time. Customers can unlink directly from Console.
Requests run in the platform’s organization, so settings in the customer’s organization, such as IP allowlists, encryption keys, and data retention, don’t apply.
Platforms that support linked billing today include Asana, ClickHouse, Factory, Gumloop, Harness, Higgsfield AI, Kilo Code, Linear, Major, Mintlify, Omni, OpenArt, Niteshift, Railway, Ramp, Runlayer, Tessera, Tines, and Warp.
Getting started
Linked billing is available today in beta on the Claude Platform. Third-party platforms can add support by creating an app in [Console](https://platform.claude.com/settings/oauth-apps) and following the steps in the [docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/oauth-apps/organization-billing-connections). Claude Platform customers can link their organization from any supported platform, and find platforms that offer linked billing on [Claude Marketplace](https://claude.com/marketplace/agents-products?howYouPay=linkedBilling).

Linked billing lets them use their existing Claude commitment to power Agentic Work Management in Asana, including AI Studio and AI Teammates, with less setup and spending limits they control as adoption grows.”

“Linked billing simplifies the onboarding process for our enterprise customers. Instead of creating an Anthropic API key and sharing it with us, an admin links their Claude Platform organization once. We don’t need to hold their key, furthering the security of the integration.”

Using linked billing, they can link their Claude Platform organization to Cosmos by Harness, and Claude API usage in Cosmos is billed to that organization. We’re excited to be supporting linked billing for the Claude Platform.”

Linked billing allows them to set a monthly spend limit and keep their billing relationship with Anthropic, without sharing long-lived API keys.”
“Linked billing with Claude Platform lets customers link their Claude organization to Omni without sharing an API key. Alongside Omni’s own usage tracking, they can trace Claude token usage back to Omni for better auditability.”

Linked billing gives customers a simpler way to bring Claude and Tines together through their existing Claude Platform organization, without sharing API keys, making it easier to control spend and expand AI adoption across the business.”

Linked billing makes that easier and more secure, making it seamless for customers to link their own Claude Platform organizations to Warp without having to manage API keys or complex billing arrangements. title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
body:
EngineeringUsing a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
Claude Docs is a doc editor that you, your teammates, and Claude all work in together. The interesting part is that a Claude session anywhere, from chat to Claude Code, can open the same doc and read, write, and comment in it live, right next to you. We released Docs on September 16, 2026. This post is about the service that runs underneath it.
Three weeks before Claude Docs opened to the public, it was running as a proof of concept on a single node, used by a few thousand people inside Anthropic. We were racing toward an ambitious launch date, and our own estimate said we'd see millions of docs within the first few days.
We launched on September 16. By September 22, people had created over 4.6 million docs. Across 2 billion requests we saw only 60 server errors, and we never had to roll back. The whole Docs service ran on about 50 memory-optimized pods.
Two decisions got us there:
- A chaos loop at launch scale. We set up a test harness on our staging environment where Claude ran constantly for two weeks to try and break the service. It load tested every part of our infrastructure and fixed whatever fell over.
- Improving legibility to Claude. Claude could only close the loop effectively on fixes if our system produced accurate telemetry every iteration. We made a call early to avoid any runtime that uses memory or CPU in ways our code can't easily control (e.g. runtimes with garbage collection). When a telemetry signal looked concerning, Claude could easily trace it to a bug or a specific design decision.
But honestly, this only worked because our frontier models have gotten much better recently (I used an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.2). In our experience, they can now stick with one goal through a run like this for weeks, which is what helped us hit launch scale in a tight timeline.
A few thousand internal users on one machine told us nothing about whether the service would survive launch, and we obviously didn't have launch traffic to test with.
We wanted real evidence to decide how fast we could roll out. So on September 4, about two weeks before launch, I had Claude drive a staging cluster that mirrored production at over a million synthetic docs a day and break core components on purpose. And then... I just left it running (I've included the full cost at the end of this article).
My setup was pretty simple. The loop was a session in Claude Code that I left running: pick a scenario, run the harness, read the telemetry, propose a fix, ship it to staging, repeat. That session acted as a coordinator and handed most of the work to sub-agents. In the busiest week, that usually meant about 11 sub-agents running at a time, and 30 at the peak. The coordinator also talked to our internal variant of Claude Tag (beta) via the Slack MCP to learn from other infrastructure teams at Anthropic who had scaled similar services. Their agents checked our scaling approach for pitfalls theyâd already hit.
The fun part was picking scenarios I thought were paranoid:
- 10M new docs created in a single day
- 22,000 live connections reconnecting at once
- One hot doc with hundreds of viewers, a server killed while it was still loading a doc, and the database stalling
Each iteration looked the same. Our testing harness selected a feature like document creation and pushed creation to saturation. Claude then read telemetry using the Datadog MCP and came back with a short menu of options and a recommendation.
If the recommendation was easy to undo, Claude wrote and deployed the change to staging and reran the test. We had telemetry on every operation the service ran. Every database query, for example, reported its name and how many rows it scanned versus how many it returned, so Claude could spot a bad query and rewrite it.
Before the loop started, I told Claude which decisions needed my approval; basically anything hard to undo, like changing the database schema or key layout, or changing how a doc is stored and materialized.
When Claude ran into one of those, it stopped and asked me, usually with a recommendation that I ended up approving. Schema changes were the classic case where I wanted to be consulted: there are usually a few reasonable answers, and changing directions is often painful.
And during the whole testing process, Claude had to conform to two invariants:
- Docs had to open almost instantly (even ones with a long history)
- Once the server acknowledged an edit, tests had to show the edit was still there
My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote [a tutorial on being more ambitious with models](https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutorial-for-humans-with-models/). His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task.
So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix.
For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could:
- A diagnostic loop. Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing.
- Legible technology choices. We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote.
Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes.
Memory is the best example.
Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claudeâs first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change.
From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy.
After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what weâd need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50.
We were picky about the serviceâs runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote.
This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collectorâs schedule.
Two choices helped the most.
- We wrote the service in Rust. With no garbage collector, all of a docâs memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didnât bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it.
- We also kept dependencies to a minimum. Every library brings data structures we didnât write and canât easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves.
Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now.
The service held at launch scale. The first million docs showed up in about 30 hours, and we were past 4.6 million by September 22. We rolled prod 629 times in September and never once rolled back.
Launch week felt weirdly familiar. Claude is great at imagining ways a service can fail and had planned for most of them well before launch. Seven of the ten scenarios weâd rehearsed on staging actually happened in prod. By then the harness had already put staging through most of it, and Claude had shipped the fixes behind runtime flags. When part of the infra ran into pressure, we usually just flipped a flag.
A few months ago this probably wouldnât have worked. Older models were fine at reading telemetry through an MCP server, but ten or twenty iterations into a long loop, theyâd start forgetting what we were optimizing for, and Iâd end up restating the goal. Other Anthropic employees have called this [goal drift](https://claude.dev/blog/a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code/#why-dynamic-workflows).
Our newer frontier models are built for long-running work. Claude held all of our invariants across many compactions, and I never had to repeat them.
We're not the only ones doing this, either. Vercel [made Turborepo up to 96% faster](https://vercel.com/blog/making-turborepo-ninety-six-percent-faster-with-agents-sandboxes-and-humans) with a supervised agent loop a lot like ours.
At Claude Fable 5.2's API list price (as of November 2026), I used roughly $125,000 of inference from the end of August to launch day. A couple of years ago, work on this scale I'd guess would have taken a team of engineers about six months.
Most of that went to reading telemetry, writing proposals, generating fixes, and reviewing code.
A couple of things about the cost:
- Our launch was particularly massive. A good chunk of the money went into infrastructure that only makes sense at that scale, and that infrastructure took more inference to reason about. Claude had to think a lot harder about how a growing set of services fit together and all the ways they could fail.
- I also burned a lot of tokens figuring out the process. The loop ran nonstop while I was experimenting with the setup. Knowing what I know now, I think we could have spent about half as much.
This works for much smaller services too, and it should cost a lot less.
To get a rough number, I priced out a classic small team stack: a couple of reasonably sized Kubernetes nodes and a Postgres instance. Then I went through the changes I landed between the end of August and launch day and removed the work that setup wouldnât need:
- Fitting in with our other internal services
- Client and product work that was intermixed with the scale work
- Running across many pods
- Fine-grained rate limiting
About a third of the changes were left.
Scaling our spend down to that third and taking out the mistakes I made while I was still figuring out the setup, Iâd put a two week push like this one at $3,000 to $10,000 at the same list price (I havenât actually run this, so itâs only a rough sense).
The steps below assume one engineer with Claude Code, a staging environment, and an observability provider. The coordinator and sub-agents helped speed up the process, but if you find theyâre burning too many tokens per hour, going back to a single agent should also work quite well. If you want to try it:
- Give Claude access to your telemetry. Most observability providers have an MCP server that Claude can use.
- Have Claude write a load script that throws ten times your real traffic at the staging copy of the service and breaks things on purpose. Killing an instance, stalling the database, and deploying in the middle of a spike are good places to start. Then let Claude keep fixing whatever falls over.
- When youâre picking your stack, lean toward whatever Claude can measure most easily. For us that was Rust and as few dependencies as possible.

title: Crunchbase in North: Private market signals for growth-stage companies
body:
We’re excited to announce the launch of the Crunchbase Connector in [North by Cohere](https://cohere.com/north), bringing data across seven million companies to the AI agents and automations that your enterprise relies on.
This connector is especially valuable for enterprises researching the venture capital and startup ecosystem, with access to [Crunchbase’s predictive market models](https://data.crunchbase.com/docs/predictions-data). Simply bring your Crunchbase license, authenticate, and start equipping agents and automations with Crunchbase data.
For a full list of available Crunchbase data, check out [North documentation](https://cohere-preview-01a1d1e1-a5a1-7688-a071-f074212423b4.docs.buildwithfern.com/docs/get-started/tools/crunchbase/home).
Using Crunchbase and North
Ask questions, run analyses, and generate documents that combine Crunchbase data with your organization's internal knowledge.
Crunchbase brings more than seven million company profiles, funding round histories, and predictive intelligence on funding, growth, risk, and acquisition likelihood. [North](https://cohere.com/blog/introducing-north-2) brings that data together with your internal systems, so teams can move from research to a finished document, a flagged risk, or a running automation in one place.
Investors and M&A
Spot early opportunities and risk across your pipeline with Crunchbase predictions on funding, growth, acquisitions, and potential IPOs. Then, use North to turn those signals into documents — like memos, target lists, or risk analyses — for companies you hold and set up [automations](https://cohere.com/blog/introducing-north-automations-ai-workflows) to keep them up to date.
GTM strategy and market research
Reach deal close before your competitors do with private markets data that identifies the right companies and the right people to sell to, with your expertise on when to reach out. Combined with North, automate this work forward across the tools your team uses, whether that be checking a record in Salesforce, automating outreach, or building documents via natural language to support a potential deal.
Analysts
Use Crunchbase data to map markets and deliver insights faster, with less manual research, and predictions that help you appear ahead of the game. Combined with North, build workflows to surface new entrants as they move out of stealth and connect them to the channels where your work happens with North’s other default connectors, like Slack and Gmail.
Built for enterprise control
Crunchbase in North is bring-your-own-license, and the connector respects the entitlements and permissions that your organization already has in place across Crunchbase and North.
Every figure North pulls from Crunchbase comes with citations for quick human-in-the-loop verification. Predictive outputs are clearly identified as forecasts, and estimated valuations are distinguished from reported ones, so reviewers always know which numbers are observed and which are modeled.
Availability
The Crunchbase connector is available starting November 17, 2026 for North customers with an active Crunchbase license and single sign-on (SSO) enabled. Admins can enable it from their organization's connector settings.
To learn more, contact your Cohere account team, or [talk to sales](https://cohere.com/contact-sales) if you're new to North. Don't have a Crunchbase license? [Learn more about Crunchbase Pro](https://www.crunchbase.com/buy/cb-pro).

title: Astra for Law leads in legal intelligence
body:
Final URL: https://openai.com/index/astra-law-6-2/

Markdown Content:
Today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench. We are also enabling all ChatGPT Enterprise customers to request access through the Trusted Access Program, including through the API.

Astra for Law is a model configuration of [GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol/), our latest, most powerful frontier model. It pairs GPT‑6.2 Astra with an expanded legal search index and instructions for researching a question, weighing the authorities, and writing the answer. Today’s configuration earned full credit on the LAB-AA tests nearly 40% more often than did the runner-up, GPT‑6.2 Astra.

Since we [introduced Astra for Law in September⁠](https://openai.com/index/astra-for-law/) to a small group of firms, including [Cooley⁠](https://openai.com/index/cooley-gopublic/), [Ropes & Gray⁠](https://openai.com/index/ropes-gray-ai-diligence/), and [Sullivan & Cromwell⁠](https://openai.com/index/sullivan-cromwell/), our research team has made rapid innovations to improve its legal reasoning and expand its legal search index by over a third. On [Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research), the share of research answers that passed every check rose from about 46% to 53.8% in less than two months.

As the world grows more complex, lawyers occupy an increasingly important role. They shape nearly every system we rely on: they negotiate the agreements that move commerce, defend people’s rights in courts, and draft the laws we all live by. That’s why we’ve made law a research priority at OpenAI: to put the best intelligence in the hands of the best lawyers.

## First in the Harvey LAB-AA

Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) tests whether a model can take a legal assignment from start to finish. [LAB-AA⁠(opens in a new window)](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/harvey-lab-aa) is Artificial Analysis’s version of that test. It tests the models on 120 assignments developed by Harvey across 24 areas of law – everything from drafting deposition outlines to reviewing commercial leases to strategizing ownership changes in acquisitions. To earn full credit, an answer must meet every requirement of an assignment without hallucinating, i.e., making a material claim that is not supported by the source documents.

Astra for Law ranked first, earning full credit on 20.8% of assignments, ahead of GPT‑6.2 Astra at 15.0% and Muse Wonder Full at 13.1%.

Astra for Law ranked first at 20.8%, earning full credit about **59% more often than Muse Wonder Full**, the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model.

Astra for Law also earned that top score with **54% less output per assignment** than the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model in the evaluation, averaging about 64,000 output tokens per assignment, compared with 139,000 for Muse Wonder Full. For legal teams paying by usage, this can mean the difference between staying within budget and blowing through it.

Each dot is a model configuration. Higher means more assignments earned full credit; farther left means fewer output tokens, which include the text a model generates as it reasons and writes. Astra for Law averaged about 64,000 output tokens per assignment and earned full credit on 20.8%, compared with 139,000 and 13.1% for Muse Wonder Full. No configuration shown matched Astra for Law’s score using fewer output tokens.

### 95% fewer hallucinations per assignment than Claude Opus 5.5

Hallucinations are unacceptable in legal work. A single invented citation can cost a lawyer a client’s trust, credibility in court, and a reputation built over years. That’s why reducing hallucinations has been a priority for Astra for Law. In Artificial Analysis’s latest LAB-AA comparison, Astra for Law tied (with GPT‑6) for the **lowest rate of material hallucinations:**0.03 per assignment, compared with 0.59 for Claude Opus 5.5 (the next lowest non-OpenAI model). Notably, Astra for Law's performance on this eval included **zero material hallucinations for tasks that met the all-pass criteria**.

Astra for Law averaged 0.03 material and 0.06 minor hallucinations per assignment. Claude Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material and 0.51 minor hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many material hallucinations and 8.5 times as many minor ones.

Across the same 120 assignments, Artificial Analysis counted hallucinated claims that could mislead a reader on a substantive point. Astra for Law averaged 0.03 such errors per assignment, tied for the lowest rate in the comparison and roughly half the rate for regular GPT‑6.2 Astra (0.06).

Every OpenAI configuration tested had fewer hallucinations than Claude Opus 5.5, the best non-OpenAI result on this measure. Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many as Astra for Law.

## A top performer on the Vals AI Legal Research Bench

We've made law a research priority at OpenAI, dedicating a team of researchers to accelerate innovation for frontier legal intelligence. One early measure of their progress comes from [Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research), where practicing lawyers set questions about U.S. federal and state law. An answer has to cover every required point and pass the source checks. In September, Astra for Law earned full credit on about 46% of questions. In Vals AI’s November 16 evaluation, it earned full credit on 112 of 208 questions (53.8%), **a gain of about eight percentage points in under two months**. Across all questions, it earned **90.9% of the available points**, including partial credit.

In less than two months, the share of legal research questions on which Astra for Law earned full credit rose from about 46% to 53.8%, a gain of about eight percentage points.

Astra for Law (green) sits in the small cluster of top performers on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench.

Building Astra for Law as a model configuration lets us stay on the bleeding edge of the frontier, in this case[GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-2-astra-sol/). On top of this foundation, we iteratively refine Astra for Law’s specific settings and instructions in response to practitioner feedback, teaching it how to reason and write like a seasoned lawyer. We also continuously hone its tools, such as the legal search index. Since September, we’ve grown the index by 34%, adding over 80 million new URLs, including across international jurisdictions such as the **UK, Australia, and Canada**. Today, the updated index spans over 310 million URLs and covers [more than 99.9% of published U.S. precedential case law⁠(opens in a new window)](https://wiki.free.law/c/courtlistener/help/data-coverage/case-law).

The chart below shows how the model configuration takes advantage of both the speed of frontier innovation and builds on top of that the specific requirements that make it powerful for lawyers. On Harvey’s own Legal Agent Benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra met every requirement on **4.6%** of assignments. GPT‑6.2 Astra **tripled performance,**completing **14.6%** under the same conditions. With the legal configuration, that rose to **16.2%**, completing 11% more questions than GPT‑6.2 Astra.

This chart shows both the rate of development in frontier intelligence, as well as the impact of the model configuration. The full-credit rate more than tripled from GPT‑6 Astra to GPT‑6.2 Astra, then rose another 11% with the legal configuration. This test comes from Harvey’s own LAB (separate from the previously discussed LAB-AA).

## How lawyers are using Astra for Law

The most interesting possibilities for Astra for Law are being shaped by the lawyers who are using it for their day-to-day work. Across law firm customers and OpenAI’s own legal team, early users are building references around their practice, inviting tougher challenges to their arguments, and finding new ways to respond to changing legislation.

For example, early users at OpenAI are using Astra for Law to:

*   **Give your argument its strongest opponent.** A common use for Astra for Law is as a sparring partner. A competition lawyer gives it a reading of a statute and asks it to argue the other side, drawing on legislative history, court decisions, and versions of the law in other languages.

*   **Find the line between a recommendation and a requirement.** A policy lawyer looking at a proposed oversight bill wanted to know how much power an independent reviewer would have. If the reviewer called for a fix, would the developer have to make it? For questions like these, the lawyer puts a plain-English account of each obligation beside the bill’s exact words, so she can make fast judgment calls about which reading the text supports.

*   **Start the first call with outside counsel on the hardest question.** When the business is considering entering an unfamiliar industry, a product lawyer uses Astra for Law to map which rules would apply to the proposed activity. Instead of spending the first call asking for high-level advice, the lawyer can bring outside counsel what’s actually at issue.

*   **Turn a stack of policies into a workflow.** A legal program manager used Astra for Law to turn regulatory procedures and company policy into a workflow for colleagues handling incoming cases, enabling them to automate when to ask for more information, when to close the case, and when to escalate it to a lawyer.

*   **Build the guide you wish came with the statute.** A competition lawyer paired Astra for Law with ChatGPT’s site-building tools to annotate legislation the team uses regularly. A colleague reading a provision can hover over a term for its definition, follow a link to the materials that explain it, and see what the team advised the last time that provision came up.

## Bring Astra for Law to your practice

Starting today, every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can request Astra for Law through the Trusted Access Program in the admin console. If your team already has access, select `gpt-6.2-astra-law`in ChatGPT. Customers can also request API access to build Astra for Law into their own tools [using this form⁠](https://openai.com/business/contact-sales-legal/).

The legal profession is at an inflection point. As technology changes what businesses can do and the world becomes increasingly complex and interconnected, lawyers have an unprecedented opportunity to shape how we make sense of the moment, not just for the businesses they advise but for all of us who live by the rules they help write.

We believe the best lawyers, equipped with the best intelligence, can meet that moment. We’re only at the beginning. We can’t wait to see where you take the profession.

title: Introducing OpenAI for Chile
body:
Final URL: https://openai.com/index/introducing-openai-for-chile/

Markdown Content:
Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s [National AI Policy and action plan⁠(opens in a new window)](https://minciencia.gob.cl/areas/inteligencia-artificial/Inteligencia-Artificial/), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

The partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s [American SI Exports Program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://siexports.gov/), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

> “_Artificial Intelligence is going to be one of the most important ways we make people’s lives better—from accelerating scientific discovery to helping people build things we haven’t imagined yet. I’m excited to work with Chile to help public servants use these tools, improve public services, and support entrepreneurs building new companies. I am excited to see Chilean startups solve some of the most important problems in the world and build things that benefit people everywhere._”

—Sam Altman, CEO, OpenAI

> “_We are incredibly excited about this collaboration and the extraordinary opportunities it will open for scientific discovery, entrepreneurship, and innovation across Chile. This is about empowering Chileans to push the boundaries of what is possible, create new technologies, and develop solutions that improve people's lives._”

—Ximena Lincolao, Minister of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation of Chile

## Putting AI to work in Chile

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting new models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

For civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

To support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

Specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

## About OpenAI for Countries

OpenAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

# Strengthening NATO and allied cyber defenses with AI

Share

Strengthening NATO’s cyber defenses

- [Strengthening NATO’s cyber defenses](#strengthening-natos-cyber-defenses)
- [Supporting allied governments](#supporting-allied-governments)

- [Strengthening NATO’s cyber defenses](#strengthening-natos-cyber-defenses)
- [Supporting allied governments](#supporting-allied-governments)

Governments and national cyber agencies protect the systems that people, public services and economies depend on. Through Daybreak, we’re putting advanced AI into the hands of trusted defenders for authorized security work, from reviewing software and investigating suspicious activity to validating vulnerabilities, and developing and testing fixes.

## Strengthening NATO’s cyber defenses

OpenAI works with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to provide NATO’s core institutions with access to advanced cybersecurity models, helping protect Allied networks. NATO has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens per month as part of this work.

NATO’s early use of OpenAI tools shows how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work, supporting NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. It also helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks around the clock, and creates lessons that can benefit defenders across Europe and the broader Alliance.

OpenAI also [supported⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ccdcoe.org/news/2026/exercise-crossed-swords-tests-cyber-operations-and-multi-domain-coordination/) the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise. Organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE), the exercise included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed, and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations, using OpenAI Daybreak in the technical environment. The training put participants alongside AI agents as operators, with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight.

OpenAI remains fully committed to NATO’s principles for responsible AI adoption and to delivering solutions that are safe and secure.

> “AI-powered cyber defence models represent a generational leap in cyber security. They accelerate vulnerability discovery, detect emerging threats at machine speed and enable defenders to stay ahead of adversaries. For NATO, these technologies strengthen our cyber resilience, enhance our operational advantage and reinforce our ability to protect critical digital infrastructure at unprecedented scale and speed. As we scale adoption, we will build a deeper understanding of token consumption, usage patterns and the underlying economics of AI models. This insight will help us optimise costs, evaluate competing solutions and make informed procurement decisions.”

*—Dr Dylan Browne, NCIA General Manager*

> “The people defending our democracies should have the most advanced technology on their side. NATO’s cyber defenders protect networks that are essential to the security of the Alliance. Through Daybreak, we’re putting more capable tools in their hands to help them find and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. We look forward to deepening this work with NATO and our allies, helping turn advances in AI into stronger cyber defenses.”

*—Sasha Baker, Head of National Security Policy, OpenAI*

## Supporting allied governments

Beyond NATO, we have already provided access to our cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU’s ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany and Poland.

- **The Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine** is [using⁠](https://openai.com/index/openai-extends-cyber-access-to-ukraine-for-civilian-defense/) OpenAI’s Daybreak tool to strengthen the cyber defence of civilian infrastructure. The initiative is designed to help Ukrainian teams identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly, supporting defenders who protect essential services amid persistent cyber attacks.
- **The EU’s cyber agency, ENISA,** used our models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four ([1⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73432), [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73431) [2⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73431), [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73405) [3⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73405), [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73374) [4⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-73374)). A November [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-11/ENISA_CERTEU_JOINTREPORT_Final.pdf) [joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-11/ENISA_CERTEU_JOINTREPORT_Final.pdf) also describes a review of 27 software projects using frontier models including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak, and tools including the Codex security plug-in. Across the models tested, 95% of the 88 potential issues assessed by software maintainers were confirmed as genuine, demonstrating the value of combining AI with human expertise.
- **CERT Polska** used OpenAI models to help identify [six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cert.pl/en/posts/2026/09/vulnerabilities-in-mikrotik-routeros-actively-exploited/#Research-supported-by-LLMs) and coordinated their disclosure with the vendor. Researchers directed the work, tested findings on real systems and verified their impact, with AI accelerating analysis and the exploration of potential vulnerabilities. MikroTik released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it had observed, giving network operators a concrete way to protect affected devices.

We will continue working with governments, national cyber agencies and international partners to turn frontier AI capability into stronger, safer, more resilient systems, helping defenders find weaknesses, fix them faster and protect the services people rely on every day.

title: llm 0.37.3
body:
16th November 2026
A bug fix release for [LLM](https://llm.datasette.io), mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.
Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, [3.54.1](https://www.sqlite.org/releaselog/3_54_1.html), which includes [a fix](https://sqlite.org/bugs/info/2026-10-12T13:52:22Z) that [broke LLM's logging code](https://github.com/simonw/llm/issues/1879).
Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:
select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))
Returns this:
{"a":[1]}
But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:
{"a":"[1]"}
According [to D. Richard Hipp](https://sqlite.org/forum/forumpost/dff1a343157e422f):
That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.
The workaround looks like this:
select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

title: NVIDIA DGX Spark Developer Kit Turns a Desk Into a Supercomputing Lab
body:
At SC26, an annual supercomputing conference taking place this week in Chicago, NVIDIA is introducing the DGX Spark HPC Developer Kit for researchers, academics and developers.
The kit is a four-node cluster of [NVIDIA DGX Spark systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/), each connected directly to its two neighbors in a ring, with an NVIDIA HPC SDK installation playbook coming soon. Researchers get a place at their desk to run multi-node scientific workloads, AI models and agents, instead of waiting for time on a shared GPU cluster. The kit puts the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip on researchers’ desks.
A Supercomputing Lab on Any Desk
The DGX Spark Developer Kit changes how researchers work.
It scales from one system, or node, to four — linked directly to one another over NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking, with no network switch to buy or set up.
At four nodes, it provides 512GB of combined memory and 20TB of NVMe storage that provides researchers more capacity to distribute models and scientific workloads across the cluster. With NVFP4, researchers can deploy models with up to 700B parameters locally across the four DGX Spark clusters, such as DeepSeek V4.1.
With that much power at the desk, researchers with a fixed compute and server allocation no longer have to wait in a queue for every job. Teams can develop and debug on their own, saving server hours for production runs and keeping unpublished results, and proprietary datasets on premises.
The playbook for NVIDIA HPC SDK is coming soon, bringing GPU-accelerated C, C++ and Fortran compilers, libraries and message passing interface tools to the DGX Spark cluster — the same development tools used on NVIDIA-powered supercomputers. Teams can build and test scientific applications across four nodes, check how computation and data are distributed, and debug communication issues before scaling to larger systems.
The kit brings scientific simulation and AI models and agents to the desktop, with demonstrated four-system workloads including LAMMPS with Kokkos for materials simulation and NAMD for molecular dynamics. The broader DGX Spark community has validated GROMACS for molecular dynamics, OpenFOAM for fluid dynamics, WRF for weather modeling and NVIDIA NIM microservices such as OpenFold3 and Boltz-2 for predicting biomolecular structures.
Running on DGX Spark, new open dataset and post-training recipes for [Nemotron 3.5 Super VL](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-introduces-nemotron-for-science-to-accelerate-discoveries-with-agents) help researchers adapt the model for life sciences and chemistry, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control.
What Researchers Can Do With It
The kit opens up new possibilities for researchers.
Researchers can explore agent-assisted workflows that prepare simulation inputs, launch runs and summarize results, while the scientists validate the setup and conclusions.
Researchers can also train AI models that approximate slow simulations, then use them to refine wing designs toward minimum drag.
Before committing supercomputer time, a team can narrow a 10-million-cell simulation to the 50-500 dimensions that matter.
[Kvantify](https://www.kvantify.com/blog/nvidia-dgx-spark)is using NVIDIA cuQuantum, and reports running tensor-network simulations of quantum-chemistry circuits with up to 70 qubits and 975 gates on a single DGX Spark, benchmarking circuits generated for penicillin ground-state energy calculations.[CYRAN AI](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/case-studies/cyran-iit-delhi/), an IIT Delhi spin-out, uses DGX Spark and its PixelFlux library to accelerate JPEG 2000 decoding for large satellite images, supporting local geospatial analysis.[OpenFold](https://openfold.io/blog-finetuning-openfold3.html)shows how researchers can fine-tune OpenFold3 on NVIDIA DGX Spark to improve protein-ligand structure predictions for drug discovery.- The
[Rubin Lab at IGI](https://www.therubinlab.org/research)at University of California, Berkeley is using a DGX Spark and NVIDIA Evo 2 model to predict bacterial traits directly from genome sequences by comparing embeddings from genomic and protein language models against the classical baselines. With no 11-hour cluster queue times, results arrived 15x sooner on DGX Spark. - The
[Hartwig Group at UC Berkeley](https://hartwig.cchem.berkeley.edu/publications/?topic=10)is using a DGX Spark to perform LoRA fine-tuning on the Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B model for chemistry machine learning, training a prediction head on experimental values. By running locally on the Spark using NVFP4 quantization, the lab successfully fit a 120B-class model on a single device and bypassed multi-day cluster queue times, allowing them to run continuous eight- to 24-hour training fits back-to-back.
Where to Find the Kit
The developer kit is on display at SC26 and available for sale. DGX Spark products and cables can be purchased from top OEM partners and are also available through [NVIDIA Marketplace](https://marketplace.nvidia.com/en-us/enterprise/personal-ai-supercomputers/?manufacturer=NVIDIA&superchip=GB10&page=1&limit=15).
Partners include Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, H3C, HP, Lenovo, MSI and xFusion.
An NVIDIA playbook for building and running the NVIDIA HPC SDK, a software development kit for scientific computing, is coming soon. Once available, it will give scientists and researchers a local platform to develop multi-node GPU applications, explore FP32 and mixed-precision algorithms and run molecular dynamics and materials simulations using LAMMPS with Kokkos before scaling to data center systems.
Learn more about[ NVIDIA DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/).
Subscribe to the[ NVIDIA Local AI newsletter](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-on-rtx/?modal=subscribe-ai). Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on[ X](https://x.com/NVIDIARTXSpark),[ Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nvidiartxspark/),[ TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@nvidiartxspark) and[ Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/NVIDIARTXSpark).

title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
body:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades.
Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round.
Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.
For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it.
Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow.
Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors.
Recently, she paused her travels to accept the [2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award](https://designthesolution.org/lisa-su-woi-award/) — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before.
Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA?
A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain.
A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before.
If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner.
Q: What’s an example of that in practice ?
A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity.
In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication.
Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today.
Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms?
A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned.
As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing.
For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with [Coherent](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-coherent-announce-strategic-partnership-to-develop-optics-technology-to-scale-next-generation-data-center-architecture) and [Lumentum](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-announces-strategic-partnership-with-lumentum-to-develop-state-of-the-art-optics-technology).
Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly.
Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else?
A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing.
If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.”
That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them.
Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen?
A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable.
And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful.
Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain?
A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip.
Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week.
We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it.
Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting.
Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward?
A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of [NVIDIA](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-gb200/)[ GB200](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-gb200/). The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan.
The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production.
As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly.
That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit.
This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.”
Q: What makes this work so exciting for you?
A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.

title: Broadening access to AI for scientists
body:
ChatGPT for Academic ResearchersChatGPT for Academic ResearchersChatGPT for Academic ResearchersWe’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

The program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

*Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.*

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for new drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing *Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT*, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

- Through ChatGPT Edu, universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.
- For researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Plan helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.
Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

As these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program.

We’re also publishing *Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT*, new research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

The program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

The pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for new grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot launched in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

- Through ChatGPT Edu, universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.
- For researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Plan helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

As these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.
