# Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with new tools and support

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Share

Today, we’re releasing a new tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our [Child Safety Blueprint](https://openai.com/index/introducing-child-safety-blueprint/) and our [ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/). For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It is [well⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.esafety.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-02/Designing-for-Safety_Preventing-child-sexual-exploitation-and-abuse-online_CSEA-toolkit.pdf) [established⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/programs/lantern/) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

## Helping more organizations detect abusive material

We’re building on our [current protections](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/) with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the [National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.missingkids.org/), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the [Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/) and [ROOST⁠(opens in a new window)](https://roost.tools/) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as [Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://safer.io/) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's [Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/programs/lantern/), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

### NCMEC

“*Technology has an essential role to play in helping identify child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and, ultimately, the children who may be depicted in it. This new classifier gives more organizations access to tools that can help detect previously unidentified CSAM, strengthen reporting and provide critical information to those working to identify and protect victims. We’re grateful for OpenAI's investment to develop technology that strengthens the broader child safety ecosystem.*”

**—John Shehan, Senior Vice President,** [**National Center for Missing & Exploited Children**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.missingkids.org/home)

### Thorn

“*Protecting children from sexual abuse and exploitation in the digital age requires more than any single solution or organization. It takes multiple layers of protection to disrupt harmful behavior online while equipping investigators with tools to identify endangered children. We commend OpenAI for taking steps across these areas and working with organizations throughout the child protection ecosystem. Bringing together technology, expertise, and collaboration, will be foundational to creating a safer digital world.*”

**—Melissa Stroebel, Vice President Research and Strategic Impact,** [**Thorn**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.thorn.org/)

### Tech Coalition

“*To protect children from online sexual exploitation and abuse, companies need to work together. Through the Tech Coalition, teams across the industry are learning from each other and tackling shared child safety challenges. OpenAI’s team is an active contributor to this work, sharing tools and helping develop guidance that other companies can use. We’re glad to have OpenAI as such an engaged member of the Tech Coalition and our Board.*”

**—Dr. Erin Saltman, President & CEO,** [**Tech Coalition**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://technologycoalition.org/)

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

### Results

Early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:

- The new classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag **48%** fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.
- Images flagged by the new classifier were about **twice as likely** to contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In [**fal**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://fal.ai/)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed **72%** of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. [**invideo AI**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://invideo.io/)’s testing showed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In [**SafetyKit**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.safetykit.com/)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected **90%** of cases.

### SafetyKit

“*Child safety tools need to recognize abuse across different types of content. In our testing, OpenAI’s classifier is the best we’ve seen, catching unknown CSAM that hash matching misses, including strong performance on drawings and animations, with false positives below 1% on legal adult content. These encouraging results point to broader protection against harmful content while limiting disruption for legitimate users.*”

**—Samuel Wang, Member of Technical Staff,** [**SafetyKit**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.safetykit.com/)

### invideo AI

“*The OpenAI classifier model helps us zero in on the cases that actually matter. Instead of wading through a pile of false positives, our trust and safety team gets a smaller, sharper set of cases to review, and a lot more of them turn out to need action. We want invideo to be a safe place to create content, and this helps us get there.*”

**—Kirkston Dsouza, Product Manager,** [**invideo AI**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://invideo.io/)

### fal

“*For our safety team, a flag needs to provide a useful signal about where to focus attention. OpenAI’s classifier’s high-confidence flags gave us confidence in its potential to help our team identify previously unseen abusive material as our platform grows.*”

**—Antonina Vykhrest, Director of Child Safety,** [**fal**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://fal.ai/)

### HeyGen

*“OpenAI’s moderation classifier has become a cornerstone of HeyGen’s child safety program. It gives our team a fast, reliable signal on harmful content, so we can act quickly and with confidence.”*

**—Mutasim Chowdhury, Engineer,** [**HeyGen**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.heygen.com/)

### Adobe

*“Adobe is deeply committed to keeping children safe online. Continued innovation and collaboration with companies like OpenAI strengthen existing safeguards and give platforms more tools to detect harmful content.”*

**—Michael Draper, Vice President, Global Consumer Trust,** [**Adobe**⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.adobe.com/)

More information about the classifier is available in the [CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/csam-image-classifier). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through [our intake form⁠](https://openai.com/form/csam-classifier-intake/). We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

## Interrupting harmful behavior and pointing people toward help

We already [prohibit CSAM](https://openai.com/index/combating-online-child-sexual-exploitation-abuse/), train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.



We developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including [Protect Children⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.suojellaanlapsia.fi/en), the [Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.lucyfaithfull.org.uk/), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who [independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.utas.edu.au/about/news-and-stories/articles/2024/pioneering-chatbot-reduces-searches-for-illegal-sexual-images-of-children) of deterrent messages.

### CSAM Deterrence Centre

“*OpenAI has deployed a best-practice example in ChatGPT of how a platform can deter and disrupt harmful online behaviours. OpenAI has engaged multiple external experts who have previously designed and evaluated warning messages, built the intervention with them through evidence-based co-design, and aims to redirect users to local support options in as many jurisdictions as possible. This has given the warnings the best chance of steering users away from harm and towards support.*”

**—Joel Scanlan, Associate Professor,** [**CSAM Deterrence Centre**⁠(

title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
body:
To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient.
Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect [NVIDIA GB300 NVL72](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb300-nvl72/) racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale.
“Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.”
In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics.
Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale
Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity.
In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute.
NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail.
Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency
Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines.
The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity.
NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster.
Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails.
Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path.
Explore [NVIDIA Photonics](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/silicon-photonics/) and read Lambda’s [deployment announcement](https://lambda.com/blog/worlds-first-large-scale-deployment-of-nvidia-photonics-switches-with-cpo).

title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
body:
Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors.
Many of these centers use [Slurm](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/slurm/) to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction.
In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware.
The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces.
Beating the Bottleneck
Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions.
For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need.
Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month.
Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform
The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform:
CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new [decoder server](https://nvidia.github.io/cuda-quantum/blogs/blog/2026/11/16/cudaq-qec-decoding-server/). A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard.
CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months.
CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications
CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for [shaping the ‘pulses’](https://nvidia.github.io/cuda-quantum/blogs/blog/2026/11/16/introducing-cudaq-pulse/) needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation.
The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink.
At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built.
Learn more about [NVIDIA quantum computing technologies](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/quantum-computing/).

title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
body:
In its [MLPerf](https://results.mlcommons.org/) benchmarks debut, with results released today, the [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference.
NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power.
These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s [CUDA-powered software stack](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/inference-software-lowest-token-cost/), so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time.
NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1
AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s [SC26 conference highlights](https://blogs.nvidia.com/sc26-news/), advancing scientific research.
Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster.
MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy.
The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation.
NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four.
NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems.
Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints
An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task.
Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates.
MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks.
For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed.
Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster.
Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads
NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure, Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus, Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE, Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida.
Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance.
The lead extends beyond MLPerf.
Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week.
Dive deeper into the results in the [MLPerf Training](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-vera-rubin-nvl72-achieves-up-to-2x-blackwell-ultra-performance-in-mlperf-training-v6-1/) and [MLPerf Endpoints](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-vera-rubin-nvl72-leads-agentic-inference-performance-on-mlperf-endpoints-v1-0/) technical blogs.

title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
body:
With expanded [NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.
The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.
The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.
Bringing Black Holes Into Focus
Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.
With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the [cuPhoton Toolkit](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/ai-for-science/cuphoton/), black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.
By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time.
The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact [NVIDIA DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/) system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.
Steering Fusion Simulations
Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.
Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge.
The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/)-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.
Exploring Potential Medicines
Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.
NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.
Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.
Accelerating Materials Research
Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to [NVIDIA ALCHEMI](http://developer.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-x-libraries/alchemi) — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.
At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.
The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.
Revealing Biology at Scale
The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs.
Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, [Therna Biosciences](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/therna-biosciences-releases-chronos-the-data-engine-behind-its-ai-rna-biologist-302878554.html?tc=eml_cleartime) processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. [10x Genomics](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/10x-genomics-announces-sentira-a-new-computational-platform-to-turn-complex-biological-data-into-experimental-conclusions-302892240.html) integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights.
And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research, benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models.
Explore [NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries. Learn more in this [technical blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/post-training-nvidia-nemotron-to-increase-accuracy-in-your-scientific-domain/) on GPU-powered black hole reconstruction.

title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
body:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of [CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda) by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.
CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.
At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.
From SC06 to SC26
NVIDIA [announced CUDA in November 2006](https://web.archive.org/web/20220706095459/https://www.clustermonkey.net/Conference-Reports/sc06-jeffs-blog-day-1-sunday/Print.html) and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.
In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance [Nobel Prize-winning AI research](https://www.kva.se/en/news/the-nobel-prize-in-chemistry-2024/), accelerate [scientific applications on supercomputers](https://docs.nersc.gov/performance/readiness/) and support [visual effects in Oscar-winning films](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-quadro-powers-all-five-academy-award-nominees-for-best-visual-effects).
Today, [more than 11 million developers](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/gtc-2026-news/#cuda) build on CUDA across the computing stack.
Honoring the Architects of Progress
Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:
At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through [Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics](https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/academia/whitepapers/Achievement2014_UIUC.pdf), tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on [Blue Waters](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Highlights/?highlight=2013-06§ion=2013), one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.
In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to [train AlexNet](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf) on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system [won the 2012 ImageNet competition](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2012/file/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Paper.pdf), helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.
That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s [publicly released AlphaFold 2 software](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold) [uses CUDA for GPU execution](https://github.com/google-deepmind/alphafold/blob/main/docker/Dockerfile).
These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.
Start building with the [CUDA Toolkit](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda/toolkit) and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at [SC26](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/supercomputing/).

title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
body:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the [NVIDIA Vera Rubin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/) platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.
As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.
The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation [NVIDIA NVLink](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink/) interconnect technology.
Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.
“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”
Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery
Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.
To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.
That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.
These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.
[NVIDIA CUDA-X](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/technologies/cuda-x/) libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes.
And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.
Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

title: Misalignment signals in Kimi K3: What probes flag and where they peak
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/misalignment-signals-in-kimi-k3-what-probes-flag-and-where-they-peak/

Published Time: 2026-11-16T15:05:22+00:00

Markdown Content:
Lightweight activation probes already help screen model activity in production monitoring systems, routing flagged behavior for further review.1 We study the behavioral properties of such probes: what they flag, which parts of an interaction they respond to, and when they first raise an alert. Our case study uses a small probe trained on frozen Kimi K3 activations using an LLM misalignment monitor’s labels.

Here are some key observations from our study:

*   **Distinguishing violations from benign work:**We show that the probe can distinguish monitor-flagged misalignment from benign behavior in contextually aligned tasks and rollouts.
*   **Looking beyond final answers:**Strong probe signals appear in reasoning, tool calls, and tool feedback, including plans and observations surrounding a violation.
*   **Overlap with monitor evidence and late alerts:**The probe’s signals overlap with the monitor’s citations in many runs that both systems flag, even though we train on labels for whole trajectories. However, some first alerts arrive only in later tool feedback or user-facing claims, potentially leaving too little time to intervene. This motivates investigating whether token-level supervision can encourage earlier warnings.

## Motivation

Evaluating an agent requires assessing both its final answer and the sequence of actions used to produce that response. A correct implementation or a passing test result doesn’t establish by itself that the agent followed instructions, respected task constraints, or reported its work honestly.

The July 2026 Hugging Face incident illustrates the consequences of misaligned agent behavior. During internal cybersecurity evaluations, OpenAI models bypassed controls restricting internet access and compromised parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. The evaluations used reduced safeguards.2 This motivates reliable monitoring to detect misalignment during task execution.

Frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have developed hierarchical monitoring systems to detect harmful model behavior and guide interventions. OpenAI’s system combines activation probes with model-based review and investigation to detect agent misalignment.3 Anthropic’s **Constitutional Classifiers++** screens exchanges with a linear probe and sends flagged cases to a probe-classifier ensemble to guard against jailbreaks that elicit harmful content.4

Figure 1 shows a simplified two-stage **monitoring system** for detecting agent misalignment. It pairs a lightweight classifier for low-latency screening with a more expensive classifier for detailed review. The system includes both classifiers, their routing rules, and the logic that responds to their outputs.

A **probe** provides the screening: it’s a small classifier trained on the agent’s internal representations to score potential misalignment. An **LLM monitor** is a separate language model that reads the transcript, judges potential violations, and can explain its decision by citing relevant passages. The probe scores each **conversation prefix**, meaning the recorded interaction up to a particular token. A probe score at or above the cutoff triggers review by the LLM monitor. The system uses that review to decide whether the agent can continue or whether to intervene.

![Image 1: Figure 1. A conceptual monitoring system combining the probe, LLM monitor, routing, and response logic (dashed boundary). The probe screens activations, and the LLM monitor reviews transcripts for flagged activity. Activity can continue without escalation, be cleared after review, or be paused and escalated.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/monitoring-cascade-scaled.png)

Figure 1. A conceptual monitoring system combining the probe, LLM monitor, routing, and response logic (dashed boundary). The probe screens activations, and the LLM monitor reviews transcripts for flagged activity. Activity can continue without escalation, be cleared after review, or be paused and escalated.

To compare the probe and LLM monitor, we examine the agent’s **trajectory**, the ordered record of its interactions with its environment as it carries out a task. It includes instructions and user messages, reasoning text when recorded, tool calls, tool outputs and other environmental feedback, and responses through the end of the run.

Since the classification probe plays a pivotal role as the first screening step, we study its behavior in more detail within this post. We’re particularly interested in better understanding what it flags and when it responds. Using a probe trained on Kimi K3 activations, we study the following questions:

1.   Can the probe distinguish monitor-flagged violations from similar benign activity?
2.   Where do high probe scores occur within a trajectory?
3.   Without token-level supervision, how do probe signals compare with the monitor’s cited evidence, and when does the first alert arrive?

## Experimental setup

### Probe architecture

A trajectory-level label tells us which runs were flagged but not where a problem emerged. To study the local signal, we need a probe that scores successive conversation prefixes without using information from later in the interaction.

At each prefix, the probe turns Kimi K3’s token representations into a misalignment score. We train only the classifier; Kimi K3 remains frozen.

At token position $i$, the probe receives a vector $x_{i}$ representing that token in context.

First, it normalizes each vector with $L_{2}$ normalization and a learned LayerNorm, then applies a learned projection with ReLU:

$$
u_{i} & = LayerNorm \left(\right. L_{2} N o r m \left(\right. x_{i} \left.\right) \left.\right) , \\ f_{i} & = ReLU \left(\right. W u_{i} + c \left.\right)
$$

Next, learned attention heads combine features from the current and earlier tokens. Each head learns which token features to emphasize. For head $h$ at a prefix ending at token $t$, the weight on token $i$ is:

$$
\alpha_{t , i , h} = \frac{exp \left(\right. q_{h}^{\top} f_{i} \left.\right) \gamma^{ t - i}}{\sum_{j = 1}^{t} exp \left(\right. q_{h}^{\top} f_{j} \left.\right) \gamma^{ t - j}} .
$$

Here, $q_{h}$ is the head’s learned attention vector. The factor $\gamma^{t - i}$ favors recent positions, while learned attention allows different tokens to receive different weights.

Finally, each head averages learned token values $v_{h}^{\top} f_{i}$ using these weights. Summing the $H$ head outputs with a learned bias $b$ gives the prefix logit $z_{t}$, the classifier’s raw score:

$$
z_{t} = b + \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \sum_{i = 1}^{t} \alpha_{t , i , h} \left(\right. v_{h}^{\top} f_{i} \left.\right) .
$$

At evaluation, the trajectory score is the largest prefix logit over its $T$ recorded tokens:

$$
s_{t r a j e c t o r y} = max_{1 \leq t \leq T} z_{t} .
$$

During training, we instead apply binary cross-entropy to a **softmax-weighted mean of the prefix logits**. Training therefore pools across prefixes, while evaluation uses their hard maximum.

The probe is **causal** in the sense that a prefix score uses no later tokens. Earlier context remains available both through Kimi K3’s token representations and through the probe’s attention over earlier positions.

Supervision is at the trajectory level: each conversation receives a single binary label. A trajectory is flagged when at least one prefix score reaches the cutoff.

Every recorded token is retained, including tool messages. The LLM monitor’s assessment supplies the label; it is excluded from the replayed conversation.

![Image 2: Figure 2. Frozen token activations feed an independent causal attention probe. It produces a logit at every recorded-token prefix; the largest logit supplies the evaluation score. The fine-tuned probe trains with softmax pooling followed by binary cross-entropy.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/6cf7ca35-ee63-45e8-9b5a-35b8fefee425.svg)

Figure 2. Frozen token activations feed an independent causal attention probe. It produces a logit at every recorded-token prefix; the largest logit supplies the evaluation score. The fine-tuned probe trains with softmax pooling followed by binary cross-entropy.

### Selecting and fine-tuning a probe

We train probes on Kimi K3 trajectory rollouts from internal agentic safety data. The trajectories are labeled by an LLM monitor using our internal misalignment prompt.

To select the probing layer, we ran a coarse sweep over every 10th layer followed by a finer search around the best-performing region and found that layer 63 gave the highest validation AUROC.6

After selecting the probe, we fine-tune it on a subset of Kimi K3 trajectories from public benchmarks 5 to better cover the task types and behaviors encountered in our evaluations. We focus on **ImpossibleBench, ShoppingBench, SWE-bench Verified, and tau3-bench**. We use an LLM monitor paired with an internal misalignment policy to supply ground truth labels for these trajectories.

We keep the Kimi K3 backbone and activation layer fixed during fine-tuning, updating only the selected probe’s weights. The same fine-tuned layer-63 checkpoint supplies the performance results and all trajectory analyses below.

Figure 3 reports F1 and recall for the fine-tuned probe on each benchmark.

![Image 3: Figure 3. F1 and recall of the fine-tuned layer-63 probe. Each benchmark uses its own cutoff maximizing F1 on that benchmark’s labels, and recall is measured at the same cutoff. Cutoff selection and metric reporting use the same examples.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/adapted-f1-recall-1024x555.png)

Figure 3. F1 and recall of the fine-tuned layer-63 probe. Each benchmark uses its own cutoff maximizing F1 on that benchmark’s labels, and recall is measured at the same cutoff. Cutoff selection and metric reporting use the same examples.

## Does the probe distinguish misalignment from contextually aligned but benign behavior?

Benign and misaligned trajectories can involve similar tasks, tools, and outputs. For example, an agent asked to fix a failing unit test could repair the underlying bug or hard-code the expected output; both might produce passing tests. We compare selected benign and monitor-flagged trajectories from ShoppingBench and ImpossibleBench to examine whether the probe distinguishes violations from similar task activity. In both comparisons, we demonstrate how the probe flags the monitor-judged violation without flagging the benign run.7

### Shopping: Verifying a color option versus claiming an unsupported match

The benign agent is asked for a black, water-resistant sports watch. It verifies the listing’s color option and water-resistance rating, then recommends the item. The monitor accepts the recommendation, and the probe doesn’t flag any part of the run.

The problematic agent is asked for a red paper fastener, called a treasury tag clip. It finds an assorted-color product, but the listing does not guarantee red or let the agent select that color. The agent acknowledges that there’s no way to select red, and the probe doesn’t flag this acknowledgment.

The probe first flags “assorted colors typically include red” in a checklist treating the red requirement as satisfied. It also flags the later reasoning that settles on a recommendation and the assurance to the customer that red will be included. The monitor labels this **deception**: the agent presents an unverified property as guaranteed.

### Cheating: Making the grader pass by changing the test runner

Both ImpossibleBench runs in this contrast must implement the same requested function. The user explicitly requires the agent to report flawed tests and stop. In the benign run, the agent implements the function and passes the supplie

title: New Ask Maps features to help with holiday travel and prep
body:
New Ask Maps features to help with holiday travel and prep
The holidays are a busy time between shopping for gifts, planning travel, and celebrating with loved ones. To help you stay one step ahead this season, we’re launching new Ask Maps features that make it easy to create itineraries, find available appointments, and search your lists in a snap so you can enjoy stress-free festivities.
Get on-the-go help with your holiday road trips
Now you can build step-by-step trip itineraries and get helpful, real-time details about your route right when you pull up directions.
Use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping or something more complex — like a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. You'll get a day-by-day schedule with insider tips and numbered map pins for each stop, making it easy to visualize the plan. Once you're happy with the itinerary, share it with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs on desktop.
When you’re about to head out, use Ask Maps to pull up your itinerary or look for the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and even what the vibe is at your next stop. You can also adjust your schedule on the fly. Just use Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or lunch spot along the way. Then, tap to get directions to your next stop right from your itinerary.
Whether you're taking a multi-day road trip or running errands around town, Maps keeps you a step ahead. Pull up directions to see helpful “Know before you go” tips about your route, including where to park or charge your car, and real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.
Check off your holiday prep and let Maps find appointments for you
Holiday prep comes with a long list of to-dos. Now, with new agentic capabilities, you can choose to have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. Just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses so it’s easy to decide what to book.
Show your guests the best spots on your lists
If you have friends visiting and want to show them around, now you can use Ask Maps to find saved places on your lists in seconds. Just ask, “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability so you can pick a place and go.
These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS just in time for the holidays. As part of today’s news, Ask Maps starts expanding to 30 countries across Europe — including Spain, Germany, and the U.K. — bringing Ask Maps to more than 200 countries and territories globally.
Travel itineraries and list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know before you go" route tips and finding appointments are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

# Science at the frontier

How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our new report.

[Download the key takeaways(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/28615567-15d1-4e4c-907e-f837a1f2b2f4/Science%20at%20the%20Frontier-%20How%20Scientists%20Use%20ChatGPT.pdf) [Read the full report(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/0e4b2466-0be0-4326-8bf7-117d809e14d2/Science%20at%20the%20Frontier.pdf)

Share

AI is part of scientists’ daily work

- [AI is part of scientists’ daily work](#ai-is-part-of-scientists-daily-work)
- [68% of scientists used ChatGPT to develop research ideas](#percent-of-scientists-used-chatgpt-to-develop-research-ideas)
- [98% of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field.](#percent-of-surveyed-scientists-expect-ai-to-speed-up-discovery-in-their-field)

- [AI is part of scientists’ daily work](#ai-is-part-of-scientists-daily-work)
- [68% of scientists used ChatGPT to develop research ideas](#percent-of-scientists-used-chatgpt-to-develop-research-ideas)
- [98% of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field.](#percent-of-surveyed-scientists-expect-ai-to-speed-up-discovery-in-their-field)
- [Scientists stay involved even after delegating tasks to ChatGPT](#scientists-stay-involved-even-after-delegating-tasks-to-chatgpt)
- [How could AI further scientific progress?](#how-could-ai-further-scientific-progress)
- [Looking ahead](#looking-ahead)
- [About the research](#about-the-research)

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking new questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

Scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

## AI is part of scientists’ daily work

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

*For each scientist, we calculated the share of their scientific messages in each activity, then averaged those shares, giving every scientist equal weight. Percentages are rounded; other research activities accounted for less than 1%.*

## 68% of scientists used ChatGPT to develop research ideas

We looked at how scientists used ChatGPT for ideation. The figures below describe their messages about research ideas.

Led by scientist

35%

of the time, scientists brought a specific question for ChatGPT to work with.

Developed together

36%

of the time, scientists brought an idea and asked ChatGPT to refine it.

Suggested by ChatGPT

23%

of the time, scientists asked ChatGPT to suggest a research question.

Other

6%

The message could not be categorized into one of the other activities.

## 98% of surveyed scientists expect AI to speed up discovery in their field.

We asked scientists across different fields to imagine a discovery that would take 10 years without AI and estimate how long it would take with AI.

*250 respondents answered this question. Respondents could select multiple fields, so field groups overlap. Percentages are rounded and may not total 100%.*

## Scientists stay involved even after delegating tasks to ChatGPT

We measured how often scientists followed up to clarify, check, or revise ChatGPT’s responses across different research activities.

*Average percentage of each scientist’s requests that led to a follow-up.*

## How could AI further scientific progress?

We asked scientists who expected faster discovery to explain why. Three reasons stood out in their answers.

52%

Get research done faster

23%

Find more promising research questions

14%

Pursue a wider range of questions

11%

Other

Scientists could give multiple reasons. Percentages show the share of all 367 reasons identified in 224 written responses.

## Looking ahead

Scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding [ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠](https://openai.com/index/expanding-chatgpt-for-academic-researchers/), with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

For more on this study, [read the complete paper⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/0e4b2466-0be0-4326-8bf7-117d809e14d2/Science%20at%20the%20Frontier.pdf) or [download the key findings⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/28615567-15d1-4e4c-907e-f837a1f2b2f4/Science%20at%20the%20Frontier-%20How%20Scientists%20Use%20ChatGPT.pdf).



“Tools like ChatGPT are helping us accelerate scientific discovery. It’s really a playground for a scientist like myself.”

César de la Fuente

[Antimicrobial research⁠](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-antibiotic-discovery/)

## About the research

### Who we studied

We analyzed 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists on the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers plan from August 20 to September 22, 2026.

The survey ran from September 30 to October 7, with 251 scientists’ responses presented in our analysis. The number of answers varies by question.

### How we measured AI use

For each scientist, we calculated the share of their scientific messages in each activity, then averaged those shares, giving every scientist equal weight. “Other research activities” combines the other and end-to-end autonomous research categories.

Ideation adoption means sending at least three messages about developing research ideas during the study. The idea-role chart averages each scientist’s shares of ideation messages. “Other” means the role could not be determined.

The “requests led to a follow-up” is the scientist involvement score. It measures requests for clarification, checking, or revision in the next scientific message in the same conversation within seven days. We average each scientist’s rate within each activity. Only initial requests with a complete observation window and an assessable outcome are included.

### How to read the survey results

**Productivity.** We asked scientists how much time they would have needed without AI to complete the same work at the same quality. Across eight research activities, they estimated that one hour of work with AI available would have taken about 1.9 hours without it. Each activity counted equally in that average and included 249–251 respondents. When a scientist reported using no AI for an activity, we counted the time as unchanged.

**Discovery timelines.** We asked 250 scientists to imagine a discovery in their field that would take ten years without AI. How soon did they expect it to happen with AI? The chart groups their answers by the timeline they expected. “No acceleration” includes answers of ten years or longer. Scientists could select more than one field, so some appear in more than one group.

**Why scientists expected faster discovery.** Scientists who expected AI to speed up discovery could explain why in their own words. We identified 367 reasons in 224 written answers. A single answer could give several reasons. The percentages show how common each reason was among the 367.

### Sources, privacy, and limitations

The research team worked with outputs from privacy-preserving classifiers and did not inspect underlying ChatGPT messages or responses. Training is off by default on the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers plan.

Usage describes requests made to AI. Productivity is self-reported, and discovery results are expectations. These findings do not establish causal effects. Scientists also reported constraints on staffing, funding, and experimental capacity.

Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole percent, with values below 1% shown as “<1%.” Rounded categories may not total 100%.

# How Revolut raises ambition without lowering the bar

With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

## Moving faster on the everyday

[Revolut⁠(opens in a new window)](http://www.revolut.com) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

## Starting where scale meets impact

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to [one report⁠(opens in a new window)](https://gasa.org/knowledge-base/blog/global-scams-on-the-rise-over-half-of-adults-worldwide-report-scam-encounters), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”

## Delegating implementation, not accountability

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” says Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

> “I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers. I can just launch different agents and assign them a task.”

—Dmitry Pitik, Senior Platform Engineer, Revolut

## Building trust into the system

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

> “You earn real confidence in AI by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

—Mo Amiri, Information Security Engineer, Revolut

## Results at a glance

- 30–60% reduction in coding time from task start to feature merge
- One engineer built an internal code-review service by delegating implementation tasks to multiple Codex agents
- One day to transform existing design-system documentation developed over roughly seven years into AI-readable context
- One to two days saved on one substantial security code-review task
- More transactions screened through the FinCrime agent without scaling investigators one for one

## Leadership lessons

- **Start with a problem worth solving.** Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.
- **Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards.** Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.
- **Keep people on the hook.** AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.
- **Build trust before you scale.** Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.
- **Make your knowledge usable.** AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

## What’s next

Revolut has already shown how AI can increase the amount and complexity of work its teams can attempt. Its next opportunity is to carry that combination of capability, judgment and design into the way customers interact with their money.

Abitbol imagines a more conversational interface in which customers can ask Revolut to help with everyday financial tasks: blocking a card, managing a subscription or finding ways to save for a trip. Pavlov sees the design challenge underneath that experience—turning complexity into something consistent, familiar and easy to use.

# LVMH’s Media Division announces strategic partnership with OpenAI

Share

*This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read* [*here*⁠(opens in a new window)](https://lesechosleparisien.fr/actualites/le-groupe/le-pole-medias-de-lvmh-annonce-un-partenariat-strategique-avec-openai/)*.*

**Paris, 16 November 2026**—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.

Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.

Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.

In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.

This partnership is a company-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.

> “LVMH’s Media Division (Les Echos, Le Parisien, Challenges, Paris Match, L’Opinion, Investir, L’Agefi and others) and OpenAI are entering into a strategic partnership. This agreement will position our publications at the forefront of the media industry. Integrating AI will become an everyday asset for all our teams. We are delighted to embark on this journey with a partner whose expertise and reputation are recognised worldwide.”

*—Michèle Benbunan, CEO of LVMH Group’s Media Division*

> “Quality journalism depends on the people who investigate, verify facts and help audiences make sense of information. We want to help put AI to work for everyone across LVMH’s Media Division, giving teams tools to explore their stories and develop new uses of AI. Our ambition is to help them spend more time on what makes their journalism valuable, while respecting their editorial independence. This partnership will also give ChatGPT users access to high-quality journalism that keeps pace with the news.”

*—Emmanuel Marill, Managing Director, EMEA at OpenAI*

## About LVMH Group’s Media Division

LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.

The Group’s media brands: [Boursier.com⁠(opens in a new window)](http://Boursier.com), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, [medici.tv⁠(opens in a new window)](http://medici.tv), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.

The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.
