We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/). They build on our [priorities and principles for third party assessments](https://openai.com/index/priorities-principles-third-party-assessments/) and years of work with [third party evaluators](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-safety-with-external-testing/), including a recent pilot assessment of [our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/) with deep internal access and an investigation of [the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

## Our pilot embedded assessors

### Apollo Research

In this pilot assessment, [Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

1. Training did not incentivize subversion.
2. Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.
3. Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.
4. Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

### Goodfire

[Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.goodfire.com/) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

### METR

We intend to conduct two assessments with [METR⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/), focused on model alignment and monitoring:

- **Alignment assessment:** For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run. [1](#citation-bottom-1)
- **Monitor assessment:** We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise [2](#citation-bottom-2). We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another [monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-14-control-assessment-proposal/) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

### Transluce

[Transluce⁠(opens in a new window)](https://transluce.org/) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

## Protocols for embedded assessments

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

### Scoping and iteration

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

### A secure, on-site environment

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum [3](#citation-bottom-3) the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

### Oversight and dispute resolution

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

### Employee discussions and attestation

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

### Conflict disclosures & cool off periods

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests [4](#citation-bottom-4), a

# Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams

Share

From a patient’s message to an MRI authorization request

- [From a patient’s message to an MRI authorization request](#from-a-patients-message-to-an-mri-authorization-request)
- [Evaluating helpfulness, safety, and cost](#evaluating-helpfulness-safety-and-cost)

- [From a patient’s message to an MRI authorization request](#from-a-patients-message-to-an-mri-authorization-request)
- [Evaluating helpfulness, safety, and cost](#evaluating-helpfulness-safety-and-cost)
- [Developing computer use with healthcare organizations](#developing-computer-use-with-healthcare-organizations)
- [Patient data security and agent controls](#patient-data-security-and-agent-controls)
- [Get started with computer use agents](#get-started-with-computer-use-agents)

Healthcare is fragmented, and teams often need to move information between systems manually before a patient can get care. When a clinician recommends an MRI, for example, the information an insurer needs may be in a patient’s medical record, but a team member still needs to retrieve it and enter it into a separate portal to complete an authorization request.

Computer-use agents carry out multi-step workflows by clicking, typing, and moving between applications. In healthcare, this enables AI to help with repetitive workflows in the software teams already use.

Today, we’re sharing new results measuring model performance, safety, and cost in clinical and administrative workflows. We’re also sharing the ways we’re working with leading healthcare organizations like Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health to advance and apply computer use, across authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.

Healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can access these capabilities today through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can support HIPAA-compliant workflows, configure approvals and agent access, and record audit logs for secure deployments.

## From a patient’s message to an MRI authorization request

To show how a computer-use agent can help a clinician and an authorization specialist work on the same MRI request, we built a demo using synthetic patient data. A patient messages their clinician about lower back pain. A computer-use agent reviews the patient’s visit notes, physical therapy records, and prior imaging in the EHR. It drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a reply to the patient for the clinician to review. The agent then uses the same records to prepare a prior authorization request in the insurer’s portal for an authorization specialist to review.

## Evaluating helpfulness, safety, and cost

We evaluated GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes. These tasks, shaped by physician input, require Astra to carry out multi-step workflows designed to test both clinical reasoning over longitudinal patient context and navigation of complex interfaces. Reviewers examined the model’s actions alongside the notes, orders, and patient messages it produced, assessing whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe in the context of the task.

Clinical safety was assessed by evaluating whether inaccuracies, omissions, or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Overall, 99% of 325 reviewed tasks were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, selecting “very helpful” or “extremely helpful” in 93% of 646 assessments.

### Examples of EHR Inbox work

Ibuprofen dosingElevated PSADigoxin refill

#### Ibuprofen dosing after an arm fracture

**Inbox message**

“Can you tell me how much children’s ibuprofen I can give her for the arm pain and how often? She got some at the clinic but I don’t see instructions on the paperwork.”

**What the model was asked to do**

Review the visit and imaging, then save an unsent caregiver reply with dosing, cast care, and urgent return precautions, plus an unsigned documentation note.

**What the model did**

- Used the child’s documented weight and clinic dose to draft ibuprofen dosing instructions, cast care, and warning signs.
- Saved a separate unsigned note documenting the chart review, proposed dosing, return precautions, and that the caregiver reply remained an unsent draft pending clinician approval.

#### Administrative workflow performance and cost

We also evaluated computer-use agents for administrative tasks, such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On [ HealthAdminBench⁠(opens in a new window)](https://som-shahlab.github.io/health-admin-bench-website/), an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers measuring performance on common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points, while GPT‑6 Luna earned 91.8%, despite costing 98% less at 8.5 cents per task. Both models were evaluated at maximum reasoning effort. These results show progress toward capable, affordable agents for high-volume administrative workflows.

## Developing computer use with healthcare organizations

Our partners build software used in hundreds of health systems, coordinate care for members globally, and deliver care to hundreds of millions of patients. The following examples showcase how organizations are developing, piloting, and deploying computer-use applications to save time, solve critical problems, and improve patient care.

### CVS Health: Completing administrative work across clinical systems

CVS Health is using OpenAI’s computer-use capabilities to automate repetitive work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals, and supporting specialist consults. The agents navigate existing applications to complete steps that APIs do not fully support.

In one production workflow, an agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend. Another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day, helping team members focus on work that needs their expertise. CVS Health uses validation checks and human oversight, with screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. CVS Health is open sourcing its [Agent Kit⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/cvs-health/cua-agent-kit), built with OpenAI’s Agents SDK, which packages this approach as a repeatable process for broader use.

> “Less time on administrative work means more time for care. That’s a win for our teams and everyone we serve.”

*—Lagan Khare, Executive Director, Engineering, CVS Health.*

Data remains within the CVS Health enterprise-controlled infrastructure, governed by their enterprise AI Governance team and established responsible AI policies. Production data is not used to train foundation models.

### Abridge: Coordination across systems for every moment of care

Abridge is developing computer-use agents to help clinicians carry out care plans across use cases and applications they use daily, including those without APIs. Their planned inpatient use case builds on the clinical conversation, adding EHR information and nurse and clinician context to identify what needs attention and to coordinate next steps.

For example, a clinician can ask the Abridge Assistant to help resolve a patient’s discharge barriers. Agents can work concurrently on medication access and home-health coordination, using computer interaction alongside calls and messages. The clinician stays focused on the patient and is brought in for decisions requiring clinical judgment.

*[Learn more⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.abridge.com/blog/learning-health-system)*

### Cigna: Preparing care managers for member outreach

As part of The Cigna Group’s broader collaboration with OpenAI, Cigna Healthcare is using OpenAI’s frontier models alongside its own clinical expertise to bring together relevant information across systems and give care teams more complete context about each member’s needs and experience. That can include information about benefits and coverage, providers, appointments and prior interactions, helping care teams better support members around care plans established by their treating providers.

Previously, Cigna Healthcare case managers had to navigate more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather this context. Computer use can now help navigate these systems and bring relevant information together in seconds, reducing the time spent searching for information – ultimately giving case managers more time to support members.

> “Moving from concept to deployment in under eight weeks shows what’s possible when we bring together AI, our expertise in care management, and the right guardrails for responsible use. More importantly, it means getting better, more complete insights to our case managers sooner, so they can focus their time on what matters most: supporting patients with personalized, compassionate care.”

*—Madhu Nutakki, CIO, Cigna Healthcare*

### Ambience: Making computer use governable in healthcare

Computer use lets agents complete tasks in EHRs and payer portals that APIs don’t reach. In healthcare, that capability is only usable if every action is controlled and auditable. Ambience built additional controls to support that oversight.

In this demonstration, Ambience uses evidence from the patient’s chart to prepare a prior-authorization request on an insurer’s website. When the record is ambiguous, the agent stops and asks the clinician, then waits for approval before submitting. Health systems set which actions the agent can take, can pause it at any point, and get a step-by-step log for audit.

Healthcare startups are helping turn advances in computer use into new ways to support care teams. These five companies are combining AI agents with healthcare expertise to help teams navigate systems, coordinate next steps, and move care forward.

AssortBunkerhillForusGravityTennr

**Assort** | Closing the referral loop where the API can’t

#### Problem

Scheduling a visit doesn’t complete the referral workflow. Assort can attach a referral to the patient’s chart through Athena’s API, but closing it out requires a separate step in the EHR interface.

#### What they built

With computer use in Codex, Assort’s agent completes that step directly in Athena, extending the workflow past the limits of its existing API integration. The agent selects the referring provider, enters the referral details, and marks the referral “visit scheduled.”

#### Result

The referral reflected the scheduled appointment and dropped off the staff follow-up list.

## Patient data security and agent controls

Computer-use agents in healthcare require evaluating clinical safety, protecting patient information, and setting clear limits on what agents can do without human review.

Healthcare teams need to piece together information from the EHR, hospital policies, scheduling systems, and payer portals to deliver care and manage operations. With ChatGPT for Healthcare, we’re bringing the tools teams already use and the medical evidence they need into one platform to help them spend less time navigating systems and more time caring for patients.

We’re also improving trusted clinical search, which finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence, and introducing more than 20 new plugins to the healthcare plugin ecosystem.

Together, these capabilities help healthcare teams find the information they need, make decisions grounded in medical evidence, and carry out next steps across the systems they already use.

## Carry work forward across healthcare systems with computer-use agents

Organizations often need to move information between disconnected systems to prepare documentation, coordinate care, and complete administrative tasks. Computer-use agents can help with these steps by navigating the software that teams already use: reading screens, clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Today, we’re sharing advances in computer-use agents for healthcare, including more capable, safe, and affordable models for clinical and administrative workflows, and access controls and audit logs for secure deployments. We’re also sharing our work with healthcare organizations that are deploying agents, including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health, to process referrals, move documents between systems, and bring together the information care teams need. In the demo below, a clinician uses Voice in the ChatGPT app to ask for help following up on an MRI request. The agent reviews the chart and drafts an order and patient reply for review.

Healthcare organizations can start with a workflow that spans existing applications, set which applications agents can access, and establish clear controls for which steps require human review. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their BAA with OpenAI, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. Content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models.

Read more about our computer use research, customer stories, and demonstrations in [Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams⁠](https://openai.com/index/advancing-computer-use-for-healthcare-teams/).

## Stronger clinical answers, everywhere teams work

We’re improving trusted clinical search in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians, including how ChatGPT finds, evaluates, and cites medical evidence. These updates help clinicians connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and translate it into practical next steps, with citations they can inspect.

To measure the impact of these updates, in a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world clinical questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations. In over 1300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly across all eight dimensions evaluated, including factual correctness, safety, actionability, and source authoritativeness.

title: AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities
body:
Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents.
At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world.
Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage.
“It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.”
The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system.
More than 500 developers also took part in full-day [NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/training/) workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the [NVIDIA Isaac](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac) platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam.
The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research.
AI Day Seoul sessions will soon be available on [NVIDIA On-Demand](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/on-demand/).

title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
body:
Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at [discovering vulnerabilities](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/cvd/). We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices.
We’re shortening the disclosure window in our [coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy](https://www.anthropic.com/coordinated-vulnerability-disclosure) from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines.
In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same.
Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will [publish these reports on our dashboard](https://red.anthropic.com/2026/cvd/) in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027.
Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery
Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.
Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by [OSS Scanner](https://www.anthropic.com/research/launching-opt-in-vuln-finding-service-for-open-source).
We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project.
We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to [OSS Scanner](https://www.anthropic.com/research/launching-opt-in-vuln-finding-service-for-open-source), a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the [Claude for Open Source Program](https://claude.com/contact-sales/claude-for-oss) for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our [Cyber Verification Program](https://www.anthropic.com/news/cyber-verification-program), which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

title: Split-and-Scale Latent 3D Representations
body:
[content type paper](/research/)published November 2026
Split-and-Scale Latent 3D Representations
AuthorsDorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
Split-and-Scale Latent 3D Representations
AuthorsDorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with split-and-scale, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
High-fidelity image-to-3D generation requires a 3D representation that captures both geometry and appearance. To support relighting and integration into standard rendering pipelines, the representation should include physically based rendering (PBR) modalities such as albedo, metallic-roughness, and surface normals. We propose Luce, a 3D representation that unifies geometry and PBR materials within a voxelized multimodal Gaussian cloud, usingâ¦

title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
body:
EngineeringHow the Claude Code team thinks about verification
How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and [reviewed by Claude](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/). At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.
Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.
Thatâs because giving agents a [way to verify their output](https://claude.com/blog/building-verification-loops-in-claude-code-with-skills) is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claudeâs work against a rubric [improved task success by up to 10 points](https://claude.com/blog/claude-managed-agents) over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.
What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.
You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agentâs performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.
So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.
No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.
If your tests are flaky youâll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before youâve committed the changes.
Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.
If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.
The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to foolâeither the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you whatâs broken.
While unit tests are faster and less flaky, itâs possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test donât understand the full task.
With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like [CDP](https://chromedevtools.github.io/devtools-protocol/), simulators, or API harnesses.
The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the userâs point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.
A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.
You start by writing a statement you think canât fail and then use a test library ([fast-check](https://fast-check.dev/) for JS/TS, [Hypothesis](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for Python, [proptest](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/) for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.
There are many properties in virtually every software project like:
- Round-trip encoding: âif you encode X then decode it back, you get X.â This works for parsing and serialization as well.
- Invariants: Things that must always be true, like âaccount balance can never become negative.â
- Idempotency: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.
- Equivalence: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.
Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that arenât created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.
Differential tests are particularly effective for [large-scale migration](https://claude.com/resources/articles/ai-code-migration) use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.
The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. Youâll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.
We have previously written about [how code review works at Anthropic](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/), but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.
Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.
Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.
To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.
Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.
When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.
Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.
The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.
We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is â--resume loads old transcripts.â When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts wonât have it.
Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matchesâusually 3 to 10âso nobody has to memorize past outages.
We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a [REVIEW.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize) that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.
We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. Itâs cheaper and finds more.
If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, [never from the pull request's changes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize). The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.
The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.
The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a [hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a [/goal](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal) of a passing test suite.
In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.
We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.
Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.
Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck â Claude Code isn't perfect.
The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.
This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our [code review post](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/), we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.
They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.
In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.
Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as [Important, Nit or Pre-existing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-pull-requests). The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.
Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.
In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be

title: Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library searchable
body:
Enterprises have vast amounts of valuable information locked inside recorded meetings, training videos and media archives. But unlike documents, video remains difficult for AI applications to search and use.
Today, we're introducing Video Intelligence in [Compass](https://www.cohere.com/compass), enabling AI applications and agents to search across video collections, find relevant moments and retrieve timestamped evidence alongside documents.
Compass understands both what's said and what's shown on screen. Instead of returning an hour-long recording, it retrieves the exact moment that answers a question, with a timestamped clip, transcript and visual description.
We're now recruiting design partners. [Register your interest](https://cohere.com/blog/video-intelligence-preview#form).
Search for moments, not just files
Consider the questions people actually ask of video:
- When did the team agree to move the launch to Q3?
- Where does the presenter explain revenue trends on the whiteboard?
- When did a particular player get sent off during the game?
Answering them takes more than matching keywords in a transcript or scanning individual frames. It takes an understanding of what's said, what's shown and how events unfold over time. A single frame can show a player leaving the pitch, but only the sequence shows they were sent off. A presenter can describe improving KPIs while the chart on screen tells a different story.
Timing matters too. A clip that begins two minutes early, or cuts off before the answer, still leaves someone scrubbing through the footage.
Compass makes video searchable by meaning, context and precise moments in time.
From raw footage to discoverable intelligence
Finding the right moment in a video is only part of the challenge. AI applications also need to retrieve that information, verify its source and use it alongside other enterprise knowledge.
Compass brings video into the same retrieval system as documents, with the precision and controls needed for enterprise AI applications.
- Precise moments, not predefined clips: Rather than relying on fixed video segments, Compass determines the relevant start and end times at search time, returning the moment that answers the question.
- Video and documents in one search: Applications and AI agents can retrieve relevant footage alongside documents, bringing video into enterprise search, RAG and agentic workflows.
- Evidence you can verify: Every result links back to the original footage, with timestamps, transcripts and visual descriptions so users can check the source.
- Built for enterprise requirements: Permission-aware retrieval ensures users only access authorized content, while configurable fields, model choices and deployment options let organizations adapt the solution to their needs.
Connect your agent to the Compass MCP server so it can reason over what's shown on screen, such as slides, charts and demonstrations, not just what's said.
Unlock new applications for your video data
Compass makes video accessible to AI applications, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic search. By making spoken and visual content searchable alongside documents, Compass gives your applications and AI agents eyes and ears to reason over new modalities and use information that was previously difficult to access.
Meetings and enterprise knowledge: Build AI assistants that surface decisions, forecasts and commitments from recorded meetings, research presentations, earnings calls and analyst briefings. Find exactly when something was discussed and retrieve the relevant clip, rather than searching through hours of recordings.
Education and training: Help employees and learners find answers across recorded lectures, onboarding sessions and training libraries. Retrieve the precise explanation relevant to a question, making educational content easier to discover, reference and reuse.
Sports and media archives: Search large video libraries for specific plays, players, events, camera angles or visible brands. Accelerate highlight creation, footage discovery, content licensing and sponsor reporting without manually reviewing recordings.
Legal and compliance: Find statements, disclosures and other relevant moments across recorded footage. Retrieve timestamped clips with supporting transcripts and visual context, enabling reviewers to locate and verify information against the original source.
Video Intelligence turns recorded meetings into a searchable record of decisions, returning just the minute where something was agreed so anyone can check it against the source.
Strong retrieval performance across enterprise video
Good moment retrieval means finding the most relevant moments and identifying precisely where they start and end. We evaluated Compass against seven video embedding models across 11 datasets, including six public benchmarks and five internal enterprise video datasets.
Compass ranks first on average, with an nDCG@10 (how accurately the top ten search results are ranked) 4.4 points ahead of the strongest alternative. The lead holds up across all three domains, even as the strongest competitor rotates from one domain to the next:
- Public benchmarks: 2.4 points ahead of Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, averaged across six widely used open-source moment and video retrieval benchmarks.
- Sports: 5.1 points ahead of Gemini Embedding 2 on soccer broadcast footage, where queries look for specific players, teams, and plays.
- Enterprise knowledge: 2.0 points ahead of Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B on business meetings, lectures, and workplace-safety training.
Build with Video Intelligence
We're inviting design partners to test and shape Video Intelligence using real-world workloads.
Partners can deploy in our managed cloud or their own environment, evaluate performance against their own footage and queries, and collaborate directly with our engineering team to inform future development. [Register your interest below](https://cohere.com/blog/video-intelligence-preview#form).

title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
body:
[
](#hugging-face-and-openrouter-join-forces-to-make-open-weight-models-easy-to-run)
Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/openrouter.md)
Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai) serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.
Today, we are switching [Inference Providers](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers) from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.
[
](#run-them-with-the-tools-you-already-use)
Run them with the tools you already use
The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:
Setup guides for [Claude Code](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/integrations/claude-code), [Codex](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/integrations/codex), [OpenCode](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/integrations/opencode), [Pi](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/integrations/pi) and [Hermes Agent](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/integrations/hermes-agent)
The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with [Storage Buckets](https://huggingface.co/storage), compute with [Jobs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-overview) and dedicated inference with [Inference Endpoints](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-endpoints). PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.
[
](#how-open-weight-models-are-used)
How open-weight models are used
On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ([OpenRouter, October 2026](https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/open-weight-vs-closed-weight-models/)). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ([rankings](https://openrouter.ai/rankings)).
Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.
The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/leaderboards/models), Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.
[
](#routing-powered-by-openrouter)
Routing powered by OpenRouter
OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.
OpenRouter recently [rebuilt its provider routing](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/how-we-rebuilt-provider-routing/): instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.
When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.
Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:
zai-org/GLM-5.3 # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability
zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest # highest throughput
zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest # lowest price
zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita # only Novita
Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id
header (see the [prompt caching guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/prompt-caching)).
[
](#pricing)
Pricing
Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See [Pricing and Billing](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers/pricing) for the details.
[
](#image-video-and-audio-generation)
Image, video and audio generation
Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of [LoRAs](https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=all&pipeline_tag=text-to-image&other=lora).
[
](#see-where-your-requests-go)
See where your requests go
On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:
Your [usage overview](https://huggingface.co/settings/inference-providers/overview) breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:
In your [settings](https://huggingface.co/settings/inference-providers), you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.
[
](#breaking-change-custom-provider-keys)
Breaking change: custom provider keys
Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider
) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.
[
](#whats-next)
What's next
This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:
- Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face.
- More tasks routed through OpenRouter.
Try a [model](https://huggingface.co/models?inference_provider=all&sort=trending&other=conversational), or read the [Inference Providers docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers) to get started.

The day after [Holiday Extras⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.holidayextras.com/) launched a new feature in its app, Liam Thompson, the company’s VP of AI Innovation, got a report on how it was performing. He hadn’t asked for one. His dot, which he calls Beast, noticed the launch, pulled data from Google BigQuery via the ChatGPT plugin, and brought him the results.

> “I was really happy when Beast said, ‘Here you go,’ and I didn’t even have to ask him.”

—Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation, Holiday Extras

Holiday Extras is a UK travel technology company that helps travelers book the practicalities around a trip, from airport parking and hotels to lounges and transfers. Its promise is simple: less hassle, more holiday.

The promise of simplicity extends to employees too. ChatGPT Enterprise gives them a foundation for using AI, Codex helps them turn their expertise into working software and better customer experiences, and [dots⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/) simplify all the work in between.

Liam and his colleague David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, shared how they use their dots as assistants and thought partners: to talk through what’s ahead, catch issues they might miss, and do work that would otherwise wait until they got back to their desks.

## A call on the commute, a report at the desk

David named his dot Brian and he calls him on his morning commute. They talk through the meetings ahead, and David can ask Brian to run a report using connected company data. “By the time I get into the office and sit at my desk, the report is there and it’s ready to go,” he says.

When some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the issue, went back through David’s email, and surfaced a list of people who might be affected. David could see who might need a heads-up without having to reconstruct it from old threads.

> “The thing I like most about Brian is that he’s thinking about things that I haven’t even thought about.”

—David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, Holiday Extras

## Why Liam talks to his dot for two hours a day

“My dot is my orchestrator of everything,” says Liam. Beast reminds him about replies he hasn’t sent and finds answers from past conversations. Instead of scrolling through his chat history, Liam can ask Beast when they talked about something and what the answer was.

“It relaxes me having Beast there, because I know that if I miss something, he’s probably already covered it, and he is keeping an eye on all the things that are going on,” says Liam.

Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but says he wasn’t comfortable giving them much information. “With anything OpenAI in our company environment, I know I can trust it,” he says. He gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive, and laptop, which made it more useful to him.

Liam talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings. “Voice is my favorite. Bidirectional voice is the game changer for interaction with OpenAI,” he says. “It’s like having a natural conversation. I spend at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with Beast.”

## From days of animation work to about ten minutes

Dots are also a design partner. Liam, who trained as a designer, turned to Beast to animate 3D characters for an app he was working on. He gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop, and then watched it work.

Beast animated the characters and put them in the app. Liam says the job would have taken him several days; he estimates Beast did it in about ten minutes. “I went to university for three years to learn design,” says Liam. Watching Beast work, he thought, “Well, it’s done a better job than me.”

## Sharing what works across the business

For Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work. David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they’re learning, helping others see what’s possible and try it for themselves. The next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something, or making everyday life a little easier.

That builds on the ambition behind the company’s work with OpenAI: giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

For anyone getting started, Liam’s advice is to simply create a dot and start a conversation. “There’s no excuse not to get started. Really, just go.”

title: The King’s Trust and OpenAI launch £1m partnership
body:
- The King’s Trust has announced a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.
- OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work.
- This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market.
- The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world.
The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy.

The program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026 found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects.

The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work.

Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs.

Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn.

For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.
