title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
body:
Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI.
It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory.
In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process.
As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows.
GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day).
To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned.
How we run agent evals at Together
Building the task list
Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint.
By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example:
List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it.
To pass the eval, the agent has to:
- Find the latest pricing info.
- Call the regions API endpoint to list the available regions.
- Combine the two to find the cheapest option.
- Produce a valid CLI command for creating the cluster.
The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents.
Three configurations
After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways:
- Baseline: The agent receives just the prompt, with no special configuration, mirroring the average developer's workflow. It can use all its default tools, like fetching docs from the web, but we don't give it any specific MCP connectors or skills.
- MCP: The agent gets direct access to our
[documentation](http://docs.together.ai/)through our MCP server, so it knows exactly where to search when it hits a roadblock. - Skills: We give the agent the
[Together skill package](https://github.com/togethercomputer/skills), which contains instructions and examples for using our services, written specifically for agents.
The run matrix
Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th:
Automating the runs
When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it.
Now we run each agent in a [Together sandbox](https://docs.together.ai/docs/together-code-sandbox) so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back.
Scoring a run
After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts:
- Pass: Every task requirement was met.
- Incomplete: The agent attempted the task, but some required steps were unfinished or unverified.
- Fail: The agent gave up early, broke an explicit constraint, or produced an incorrect result (RIP).
Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking.
We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency.
To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity:
Case study 1: GPU cluster pricing
Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier?
List the available GPU cluster regions and instance types, print the cheapest option, and show the exact command you would run to reserve it on demand for one hour. Do not actually reserve it.
Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled.
Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page.
The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available.
More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions
response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap.
Isolating the failure
To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill).
We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API:
QueryGET <https://api.together.ai/v1/compute/regions
> or runtg clusters list-regions --json
for the live region inventory, supported instance types, and compatible CUDA/driver pairs. Open the[GPU Cluster pricing table]for current on-demand and reserved rates.
After this change, the task passed 100% of the time for all models we tested using the skill-enabled config.
Finding gaps in our API
The same GPU task also turned up a problem in our API. In a recent baseline run, Opus 5.5 got an incomplete verdict, and the transcript showed it hitting two dead ends that were not the model’s fault.
The run started well. The agent called /v1/compute/regions
to retrieve the regions and instance types. Then, looking for prices, it called /v1/compute/instance-types
, and the API returned a 400 with this message:
Region is required. Example:us-central-8
. Use/v1/clusters/regions
to get list of regions.
So the agent did what the error told it to do:
- It retried the request with a region from its first lookup. Instead of instance types, it got a
404
. - It called
/v1/clusters/regions
, the route the error suggested… but that route doesn’t exist, so it got another404
.
Our own error message had sent the agent to a route that doesn’t exist, and the retry that should have worked failed too. A developer following that message by hand would have been just as stuck. We’ve since fixed the error message to point to /v1/compute/regions
, and the routing bug behind the first 404
.
Case study 2: Rebuilding our skill package
We used to maintain 14 separate Together skills, one per product surface. They were a pain to use: you had to know in advance which skills applied to your workflow, then install and invoke each one. The skills also overlapped, repeating the same SDK guidance and setup instructions, and each was long enough that loading a few of them in tandem could bloat the agent’s context.
Last month, we merged those 14 skills into a [single unified version](https://github.com/togethercomputer/skills). It’s still modular under the hood: to avoid context bloat, the agent first reads a short router, then opens each product guide, reference file, or sample script only when the router says it's relevant.
We hoped that one skill would beat 14, but to make sure, we ran the unified skill through our eval tasks with skills enabled. Our bar was the result from September 30, a 90% pass rate across all runs using the 14-skill config.
But the new skill was a flop—it passed just 54 of 72 runs (75%), left 18 incomplete instead of 7, and cost more than twice as much per run.
So we combed through the eval transcripts and changed the skill only where the runs pointed to a problem. Three issues kept coming up:
- Too much context: The first unified router was about 14,000 characters, loaded on every task, and it told agents to read each guide in full. (So much for avoiding context bloat…) Runs ended up loading 57% more skill content than they had with the 14 separate skills. We cut the router to under 6,000 characters and ended each product guide with a menu that briefly describes what every reference and script contains, so agents open only what they need.
- Stale product information: Some models used in the code examples were no longer served on serverless, and one product guide covered a deprecated feature. Agents wasted turns recovering or retrying requests that would never succeed. We moved every sample to a confirmed live model, told agents to check the catalog instead of retrying, and created a cloud agent to automatically update the skill in response to product changes.
- Bugs in example code: Small problems in the scripts, such as saving JPEG bytes under a
.png
name, would derail every agent that used them. We fixed these at the source and added an automation to periodically live-test the code samples and keep them fresh.
With those fixes in, the unified skill passed 70 of 72 runs, 22 points better than our first attempt and 7 points better than the 14 skills we started with. Runs also took 20% less time than with the original skills on average, and the cost per run came back down to where it started.
Where we are after four months of evals
Back in June, our docs and skills weren’t helping agents much at all. On June 15, running Opus 4.8, the baseline passed 75% of runs. Neither the docs MCP (67%) nor skills (75%) improved performance.
By September 30, across three models, the baseline had crept up to 82%. The docs MCP

title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
body:
Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps.
Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more.
This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache.
We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike!
What an agent turn looks like to a GPU
Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it's a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out.
A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls.
So for agents, "how fast is this model?" mostly means "how fast can it get through a long historical account of pervious turns?" The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather then recomputing.
Cache is king
The easiest way to picture the KV cache(or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you'd go, because you'd keep having to reread everything you'd already read. That's a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens(stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one.
Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6's work, it only has to process the new part.
The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn't unusual for a coding task, it's 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn't completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length.
The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that's different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again.
Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you've effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuilt the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule.
The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We'll start with the harness.
The harnesses and APIs
On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch
command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows.
Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring.
Loading tools late
Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it.
Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you've starred to a calendar, and it searches for "calendar," loads the save_calendar
definition, and calls it.
For the cache, the question is where that definition goes.
The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway.
Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don't expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn't have to know this, but anyone building a harness does.
Things at the top that change
The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read.
Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user's name or the date the session started, don't hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that's already cached, which we'll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere.
Reasoning effort
We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn't a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation.
Let’s say you're deep into a long task and it isn't going well. You raise effort from low to high. That's a reasonable thing to do, but the next request now differs from the last one almost at the first token. Which means the whole session gets processed again. On a long run, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens spent on changing one setting.
Our advice is to pick an effort level at the start and leave it there. If you really need more thinking, it's often cheaper to start a fresh session at the higher setting than to continue the old one, and you get a clean context out of it too. You could also compact before changing the reasoning value to decrease the amount of prompt tokens.
Big tool results
A tool’s output becomes part of the next request, and of every request after it. If the agent reads a 3,000-line file when it needed forty lines, you don't pay for that once; you pay for it on every remaining turn (even if it is cached you lose out on the context window). To combat this, harnesses often cut tool output down. That's the right call, but how you cut tool output matters.
Here's a failure that's easy to build by accident. The task is to fix a timezone bug in a calendar export. The agent reads calendar.py
, and the tool returns the first 100 lines of a 640-line file without saying it stopped. The function that matters, convert_timezone
, is at line 420. The model has no idea it's missing anything.
The fix is a single line in the output, telling the model it got lines 1 to 100 of 640 and that it can search the file or request another range. With that, the model searches for "timezone," finds line 420, and reads lines 410 to 450. Cutting output saves money. Cutting it without saying so gets you a model confidently editing code it never saw.
Subagents
Open models like Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3-Flash are now pretty good at splitting a big task and handing pieces to subagents. How the harness starts each subagent decides how much of the parent's cache it can reuse.
One option is for the subagent to inherit everything: the same system prompt, tools, and conversation, plus its assignment. Side chats work this way. They branch off the parent session, so the whole prefix is already cached. The other option is to send a brief: the same system prompt and tools, then only the files and instructions the subagent needs. In that case the cache covers the setup and nothing more.
Inheriting sounds strictly better, but it isn't. A cached prefix is cheap to process, not free. Every token the subagent generates still has to read through it, and it occupies GPU memory the whole time. A reviewer that needs two files and a checklist probably doesn't need three hundred turns of history. And if you give a subagent its own system prompt, it shares nothing with the parent at all, not even the setup.
The engine side
You can do everything above perfectly and still not benefit. The cache has to still exist, and the next request has to reach the machine that holds it.
At Together AI, we think of an inference engine as a machine for keeping GPUs busy. A single GPU costs around $50k to rent per year, so ideally it should never sit idle, and at any moment it's serving hundreds of users who are each at a different point in their request. Agent traffic pushes on those constraints in a few specific ways.
Routing requests for optimal cache hits
A session's cache lives on a particular node in a particular data center. If the next turn in a conversation lands anywhere else, that node has to process all earlier turns from scratch, and now two nodes are storing the same prefix. In order to route correctly we First need to pick a data center that runs the model, has capacity, and is where the session has been running. Then we need to pick a node inside it that has the previous turns cache.
There are two main ways to pick the node. The simple one is to use a key: the client sends something like prompt_cache_key
with every request and then ideally we route every request with the same key to the same node. The other way is to hash the prefix and send the request to whichever node has the longest matching prefix cached, even if another sess

title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
body:
Introduction
AI inference is becoming increasingly heterogeneous. New model architectures are released every week, inference traffic shifts across different batch sizes and sequence lengths, and hardware platforms continue to proliferate. Achieving peak performance across all these regimes demands optimization frameworks that can keep up.
Last year, we helped release some of the first AI [megakernels](https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2025-05-27-no-bubbles), where we executed an entire model forward pass within a single, highly fused GPU kernel. They reached record breaking speeds, but it was difficult to put them in production. After months of effort, we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer.
This year, we examined what we could simplify and discovered something surprising. With just CUDA Graphs and PDL on top of default Torch Inductor kernels, we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel. And with “multi-kernels” and agent loops, we could further beat our old megakernels by up to 1.7x, achieving over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100.
For the past two years, we've been investigating what a next-generation system for inference optimization should look like. After building a series of GPU programming and optimization systems, we arrived at Together Compiler, our framework for continual AI inference optimization. In this blog, we'll revisit the assumptions behind today's compilers, share the experiments that challenged our thinking, and explain the lessons that shaped Together Compiler. Our journey spans three parts:
In Part 1, we show that Torch Compile’s heuristics and benchmarking leave performance on the table, providing motivation to build something radically different.
In Part 2, we revisit the megakernels we built to close that gap, explain why they are not always the right optimization target, and decompose their performance gains into simpler primitives.
In Part 3, we share our “bitter lessons” from crafting agent-driven optimization infrastructure and the final production system we ended up with.
Part 1: Torch Compile
For over a decade, PyTorch has been the foundation of AI development, providing modular, easy-to-use abstractions (nn.Module
) that have enabled rapid experimentation. But this modularity comes at a performance cost: executing models as sequences of individual operations can introduce substantial launch overhead, limit opportunities to overlap computation and memory movement, and leave GPU resources underutilized. To address these inefficiencies, PyTorch introduced Torch Compile (“PyTorch 2.0,” powered by Inductor) to optimize and fuse operations, while NVIDIA developed CUDA Graphs to reduce kernel launch overhead. These systems have made enormous progress, but substantial performance gaps remain, often motivating Together’s researchers to invent specialized implementations such as FlashAttention, ThunderKittens, and Megakernels.
We start with a brief overview of how Torch Compile works, then present our findings from investigating Inductor’s internals on Llama 1B.
How Torch Compile Works
At a high level, Torch Compile uses a just-in-time compilation pipeline to capture PyTorch operations into a computation graph, optimize that graph, and generate executable GPU kernels. The key components are:
- Graph capture. TorchDynamo traces Python execution to capture tensor operations in an intermediate representation called an FX graph. During tracing, it uses fake tensors, which carry metadata such as shapes, data types, and strides without allocating or computing the underlying tensor data. This allows the compiler to reason about the computation without actually executing it on the GPU. The resulting FX graph can be transformed and optimized before code generation.
- Operations and kernels. Inductor lowers the captured graph into its own intermediate representation, where operations are organized into categories such as pointwise (e.g., activations), reductions (e.g., summations and softmax), scans (e.g., cumulative sums), and templates (e.g., GEMMs and other specialized compute kernels). Some operations instead invoke existing implementations from libraries such as cuBLAS or custom PyTorch operators. Inductor represents these as external kernels (
ExternKernel
), whose implementations are generally opaque to its fusion machinery. - Fusion and optimization. Inductor uses a greedy, pairwise algorithm to decide which operations to fuse into the same kernel. Its
can_fuse()
function checks whether a candidate fusion is legal, whilescore_fusion()
ranks opportunities using heuristics such as estimated memory traffic savings. The algorithm repeatedly applies profitable fusions, potentially combining many operations into a single kernel. However, these decisions are based on local heuristics rather than a global search over all possible kernel partitions and execution strategies. For example, Inductor may avoid fusing operations that share no memory accesses, even when executing their work together could improve GPU utilization.
On our target Llama 1B workload, Inductor delivers 669 TPS. As we’ll show in Part 2, these generated kernels are sometimes enough, and with small modifications, they can reach similar levels of performance to megakernels. However, on different architectures and newer hardware, Inductor’s heuristics can’t keep up. We investigated where Inductor struggles most and present three findings.
Finding #1: Compiler heuristics cannot reliably select the best implementation across workloads.
Inductor exposes a number of compiler tuning flags that can boost performance. We discovered that even these seemingly simple configurations exposed a surprisingly large and complex search space.
The best optimization depends on the workload. Inductor exposes a freezing flag that tells the compiler that model weights will not change during inference. Knowing this, the compiler can transform the weights ahead of time to make subsequent computations faster. One such transformation converts weights to FP32 to perform certain optimizations, before converting them back to their original, lower-precision format. We found that enabling freezing improved throughput by 10–26% at larger batch sizes, where the GPU performs matrix-matrix multiplications. However, at batch size 1, where inference primarily uses matrix-vector multiplications, enabling the same flag caused a 49% slowdown. Upon inspection, we discovered that the FP32 conversion was not reversed for matrix-vector operations, leaving the GPU to process larger, 32-bit weights instead of the original lower-precision weights. In other words, the exact same compiler optimization could improve performance for one batch size while dramatically degrading it for another.
Optimizations interact in unpredictable ways. As of Q3 2026, Inductor exposes 607 tuning flags, 198 of which were added in the past year. These flags control everything from kernel fusion to memory access patterns and scheduling. Their effects are not independent: enabling the aggressive_fusion
flag alone reduced Llama 1B throughput by 6 TPS, but enabling it alongside the combo_kernels
, benchmark_fusion
, and triton.coalesce_tiling_analysis
flags improved throughput by 3 TPS. Even small configuration changes could produce measurable microsecond-level differences in execution time.
Takeaway: the space of possible optimizations and configurations is large, and we should be searching it systematically instead of guessing the right flags to set.
Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation isn't necessarily the fastest during inference.
Inductor makes optimization decisions based on its benchmarking harness. We identify two distinct ways that this benchmarking misleads its decision, hurting overall performance as a result.
First, it ignores that kernel performance depends on caching behavior. Torch Inductor clears the GPU's L2 cache before benchmarking individual kernels, but during inference, kernels often reuse data that is cached from preceding operations. We observed 39–58% slower timings in Inductor's isolated benchmarks than in the live forward pass, where cache reuse can reduce memory traffic.
Benchmark inputs can also distort cache behavior in the opposite direction. For example, when benchmarking torch.embedding
, Inductor initializes the tensor of token IDs to zero, causing every token to access the same embedding vector. For a 64K-token sequence, this made the kernel 2.1× faster than with random token IDs, due to artificially high cache reuse.
Second, benchmarking overhead can lead to poor kernel selection. Many decode kernels execute in just a few microseconds, making precise timing essential. We found that Inductor's benchmarking harness reported 2.5 µs for an operation that performed no GPU work, while other measurements exceeded the GPU execution times reported by Nsight Systems by approximately 3.6 µs. This is because the harness includes CPU launch overhead after an L2 cache flush, which results in Inductor recording idle time.
These discrepancies lead to faulty compiler decisions. On Llama 1B's output-projection GEMM, Inductor selected a Triton kernel that ran 7.4 µs versus 6.4 µs for cuBLAS in the live forward pass—a 15% slowdown. We also observe this on modern, data-dependent architectures, such as mixture-of-experts architectures like GLM 5.3, where PyTorch’s default benchmarking can be anywhere from 4-21% slower than if we had modified the benchmark to use realistic inputs for the MoE grouped-GEMM kernel (shown in the figure above).
Takeaway: accurate benchmarking requires taking measurements from inside a real forward pass on real input data.
Finding #3: Inductor leaves fusion opportunities on the table.
Inductor’s greedy, pairwise fusion algorithm considers whether two kernels can legally be fused, then evaluates whether fusing them will improve performance. Although repeated pairwise fusion can combine multiple operations, it may miss opportunities that require jointly considering larger groups of kernels or different execution configurations.
We investigated the fusion decisions made by Inductor on Llama 1B and found examples where Inductor keeps kernels separate even when merging them would be beneficial. For example, we found two consecutive kernels (an elementwise activation and a KV indexing kernel) which are simple enough to fuse, but Inductor’s heuristics reject the fusion as they share no memory accesses.
As Inductor evaluates candidates by estimated memory traffic savings, it sees no reason to combine these kernels. However, examining the kernels ourselves, we see that the first kernel launches just six CTAs, meaning that most of the GPU's 132 SMs are idle. Merging these operations into a single launch would help reduce this waste.
Takeaway: an algorithm for kernel fusion should reason about utilization, not just memory.
What these findings pointed to
Each of these findings highlight Inductor limitations that leave the GPU underutilized. Focusing on our broader goal of a next generation system for inference optimization, we turned to the opposite side of the spectrum: megakernels. If we removed compilers entirely, controlling all levels of the stack by hand, where would the performance gains actually come from? By understanding this, we hoped to identify a middle ground, automating megakernel performance with minimal complexity.
Part 2: Megakernels
Since we introduced Megakernels, they have inspired a growing body of work on next-generation AI compilers and GPU execution systems. In this section, we revisit why we built them, how they work, and what happened when we tried to bring them into production.
What motivated megakernels? We observed three sources of inefficiency in conventional inference engines, which typically execute models as sequences of kernels using frameworks such as Torch Compile and CUDA Graphs:
- Kernel launch overhead. Each kernel launch inc

# A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice

[Read the paper(opens in a new window)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09093)

Share

What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?

- [What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?](#what-is-missing-from-the-standard-models-definition)
- [Left-handed particles](#left-handed-particles)
- [An analogy with light and mirrors](#an-analogy-with-light-and-mirrors)
- [Getting the phase right](#getting-the-phase-right)
- [Building the construction with Astra](#building-the-construction-with-astra)
- [What comes next](#what-comes-next)

- [What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?](#what-is-missing-from-the-standard-models-definition)
- [Left-handed particles](#left-handed-particles)
- [An analogy with light and mirrors](#an-analogy-with-light-and-mirrors)
- [Getting the phase right](#getting-the-phase-right)
- [Building the construction with Astra](#building-the-construction-with-astra)
- [What comes next](#what-comes-next)

*In the first guest post on* [*our science blog*](https://openai.com/index/our-new-blog-for-science/)*, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.*

The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an [October preprint⁠(opens in a new window)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09093) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

## What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

## Left-handed particles

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makesthe Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

## An analogy with light and mirrors

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to *chirality* when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s *helicity*, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.)

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

If you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson [1](#citation-bottom-1) worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger [2](#citation-bottom-2) built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher [3](#citation-bottom-3) showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa [4](#citation-bottom-4) and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

## Getting the phase right

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one p

# Our new blog for science

Share

We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

## What we’ll share

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:

- **Research and discoveries:** New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.
- **Methods and practical guidance:** Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.
- **Perspectives from the scientific community:** Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a [proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠](https://openai.com/index/navier-stokes-solution/), a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we [released a broad range of mathematical results⁠](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/). Among them was a result on the [quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-September-30-2026/paper.pdf), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared [results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠](https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/) concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. [Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠](https://openai.com/index/scaling-ai-research-for-complex-biological-data/), thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: [César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-antibiotic-discovery/) to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
body:
14th November 2026
datasette-llm
is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins.
This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol.
This means that if you're running local models with [LM Studio](https://lmstudio.ai) or [Ollama](https://ollama.com) or [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) (which just hit [v1.0.0](https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/llama-cpp-v1)) you can run Datasette via uvx
like this:
wget https://datasette.io/content.db
uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \
--root --secret 1 \
-s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model '{
"model": "lmstudio-qwen",
"model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
"api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1"
}' content.db
And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model!

title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
body:
13th November 2026
OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server [should send a referrer header](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Referer). Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy.
datasette-leaflet
is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin
, passing the host but not the full path to the page.

title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
body:
[World models · JEPA · Planning](index.html)
After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [[1]](#ref-1)
The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.
This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [[2]](#ref-2), a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [[3]](#ref-3), a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.
The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning.
That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.
Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.
1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart
Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [[2]](#ref-2) When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.
So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.
Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.
This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.
Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.
The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.
2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump
LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.
This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach.
The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the same score received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right?

title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
body:
Viewer • Updated • 4 • 4.92k • 2
[
](#build-a-robot-pick-and-place-simulation-with-simready-assets)
Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the [UR17G arm](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeradyneRobotics/UniversalRobots/blob/d5d8eb795a487a5c929909bc337ee4834d62b0da/ur17g_1300/simready_usd/ur17g_1300.usda), [Robotiq 2F-140 gripper](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Robotiq-Official/simready-assets/blob/9c6b0cedf0066efd474b3bf473e7eaf7ae7e569f/Robotiq_2F_85/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_85.usda), and [beverage can](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/simready-assets/blob/653d91e182011f357cf1644013cc94ddf194d349/food_beverage_can_n01/simready_usd/sm_food_beverage_can_n01_01.usd) to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.
For robotics workflows, SimReady means an [OpenUSD](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/openusd/) asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. [SimReady Central](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/simready-central), an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the [announcement blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/simready-central-assets-robotics-ai-factories).
[
](#what-makes-a-robot-asset-simready)
What makes a robot asset SimReady?
[SimReady Foundation](https://nvidia.github.io/simready-foundation/) defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:
- Profile: a group of features for a use case, such as a robot body.
- Features: capabilities needed for the use case, such as joints that can be controlled.
- Requirements: checks on the settings needed for each feature, such as a joint’s drive settings.
For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.
[
](#what-comes-with-the-asset-and-what-do-you-add)
What comes with the asset, and what do you add?
The [UR17G](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeradyneRobotics/UniversalRobots/blob/d5d8eb795a487a5c929909bc337ee4834d62b0da/ur17g_1300/simready_usd/ur17g_1300.usda), [Robotiq 2F-140](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Robotiq-Official/simready-assets/blob/9c6b0cedf0066efd474b3bf473e7eaf7ae7e569f/Robotiq_2F_85/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_85.usda), and [beverage can](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/simready-assets/blob/653d91e182011f357cf1644013cc94ddf194d349/food_beverage_can_n01/simready_usd/sm_food_beverage_can_n01_01.usd) packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.
Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.
[
](#what-should-you-check-before-running-a-pick-and-place-task)
What should you check before running a pick-and-place task?
A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.
- Joint settings: Review the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings.
- Movement: Test a small arm movement and open and close the gripper.
- Contact: Confirm that the can rests on the work surface without falling through it.
During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.
[
](#build-a-pick-and-place-simulation-in-isaac-sim)
Build a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim
This example combines the [UR17G](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeradyneRobotics/UniversalRobots/blob/d5d8eb795a487a5c929909bc337ee4834d62b0da/ur17g_1300/simready_usd/ur17g_1300.usda) arm, [Robotiq 2F-140](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Robotiq-Official/simready-assets/blob/9c6b0cedf0066efd474b3bf473e7eaf7ae7e569f/Robotiq_2F_85/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_85.usda) gripper, and [beverage can](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/simready-assets/blob/653d91e182011f357cf1644013cc94ddf194d349/food_beverage_can_n01/simready_usd/sm_food_beverage_can_n01_01.usd) in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage [SimReady Central Space](http://nvidia-simready-central.hf.space) search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.
We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.
Required Software:
- Install
[Isaac Sim](https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/latest/introduction/quickstart_index.html)6.2, the version used for this example, and check its system requirements. - Set up an agent of your choice that can use the Isaac Sim skills. Follow the
[Agent Skills documentation](https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/development_tools/agent_skills.html)to make the bundled skills available to your agent. - Install the
[Hugging Face CLI](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/cli)only if you choose the command-line asset download option. - Use the
[USD Search endpoint](http://nvidia-simready-central.hf.space).
[
](#step-1-download-the-robot-arm-gripper-and-beverage-can-assets)
Step 1: Download the robot arm, gripper, and beverage can assets
Open [SimReady Central](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/simready-central) and find the [UR17G](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeradyneRobotics/UniversalRobots/blob/d5d8eb795a487a5c929909bc337ee4834d62b0da/ur17g_1300/simready_usd/ur17g_1300.usda) arm, [Robotiq 2F-140](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Robotiq-Official/simready-assets/blob/9c6b0cedf0066efd474b3bf473e7eaf7ae7e569f/Robotiq_2F_85/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_85.usda) gripper, and [beverage can](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/simready-assets/blob/653d91e182011f357cf1644013cc94ddf194d349/food_beverage_can_n01/simready_usd/sm_food_beverage_can_n01_01.usd) used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.
Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.
~/ASSETS/hf/src/simready-assets-c7fa7615/Robotiq_2F_140/simready_usd/Robotiq_2F_140.usda
Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.
Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.
[
](#what-does-asset-validation-tell-you)
What does asset validation tell you?
The [arm validation report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TeradyneRobotics/UniversalRobots/blob/d5d8eb795a487a5c929909bc337ee4834d62b0da/ur17g_1300/.metadata/ur17g_1300_validation.json) uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the [gripper validation report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Robotiq-Official/simready-assets/blob/c7fa7615a353ebac03990208cbc2aa57426f4c48/Robotiq_2F_140/.metadata/Robotiq_2F_140_validation.json) uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing [PhysX driven-joint checks](https://nvidia.github.io/simready-foundation/latest/features/FET_022_PHYSX.html), which inspect joint-drive settings.
SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.
[
](#step-2-assemble-the-robot-and-compose-the-scene-for-pick-and-place)
Step 2: Assemble the robot and compose the scene for pick and place
With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.
Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:
./isaac-sim.sh --enable isaacsim.code_editor.python_server
If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.
Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.
You can follow the [Robot Assembler tutorial](https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html) for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:
Sample prompt used in this example:
Assemble the robot arm <local path to Simready ur17g robot usd>
with the gripper <local path to downloded simready Robotiq_2F_140 gripper usd>
using the Robot Assembly tutorial in Isaac Sim
https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/robot_setup/assemble_robots.html.
Validate the assembly on completion.
The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.
Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.
With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.
[
](#step-3-test-the-controls-and-run-pick-and-place)
Step 3: Test the controls and run pick-and-place
Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the [Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial](https://docs.isaacsim.omniverse.nvidia.com/6.2.0/core_api_tutorials/tutorial_core_adding_manipulator.html).
Sample prompt used in this example:
Run pick and place with the assembled robot and soda can
<path to soda can USD from SimReady library> in Isaac Sim.
Ensure you do a contact based grasp for picking up the can and validate
the accuracy/placement error for the pick and place as well.
Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’
The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement

title: XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
body:
Viewer • Updated • 11.3k • 335 • 2
[
](#xybench-helping-with-the-problem-behind-the-question)
XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing [XYBench](https://github.com/allenai/XYBench), a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.
A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.
Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.
The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.
People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.
[
](#building-xybench)
Building XYBench
We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.
For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.
[
](#evaluating-how-an-answer-helps)
Evaluating how an answer helps
A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.
A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:
- Pragmatic solution—records whether a model’s response includes solutions to the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X), checking each separately.
- Pragmatic emphasis—measures whether a model’s answer focuses on the stated request (Y), focuses on the intended request (X), or balances the two.
- Misconception identification—measures whether a model’s response steers the user toward the underlying goal (X) while discouraging or avoiding the mistaken approach (Y).
In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.
To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.
[
](#what-the-experiments-show)
What the experiments show
We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.
Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.
A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.
We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.
A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.
[
](#what-this-means-for-evaluation)
What this means for evaluation
Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.
Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.
We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.
