# Introducing ChatGPT Wallet

Building trusted agentic payments with networks, banks, and businesses.

Share

How a purchase works

- [How a purchase works](#how-a-purchase-works)
- [Equipping businesses for agentic commerce](#equipping-businesses-for-agentic-commerce)
- [Availability](#availability)

- [How a purchase works](#how-a-purchase-works)
- [Equipping businesses for agentic commerce](#equipping-businesses-for-agentic-commerce)
- [Availability](#availability)

We’re introducing ChatGPT Wallet, setting a new bar for secure payments by agents. It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes. Built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, ChatGPT Wallet will initially be available through [dots⁠](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/) for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US. Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re releasing tools and guidance to help businesses support customers using agents.

1.2B people use ChatGPT each week, and many of them turn to it to research products, compare options, and decide what to buy. With ChatGPT Wallet, we’re now helping people complete purchases, and giving their agents a way to pay that businesses can accept with their existing systems.

To accept payment from ChatGPT Wallet, websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents. We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users, so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.

## How a purchase works

ChatGPT Wallet gives agents a secure way to pay on a user’s behalf. Users add a card once, then approve each purchase without re-entering their payment details.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

We’re building agent-led commerce to fit reliably into existing systems. Users keep their card’s existing rewards and protections for eligible disputes with businesses, for example when an item is defective. Banks and networks bring their expertise to evaluating transactions. Users transact directly with businesses, which keep their customer relationships and control over pricing, fulfillment, returns, and customer service.

Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases with enhanced safeguards that build on today’s protections, including biometric checks and clear records of authorization.

1 of 3

> “Working with OpenAI, we’re bringing the trust, security and control of American Express payments into new AI-powered shopping experiences. ChatGPT Wallet marks our first American Express Agentic Commerce Experiences integration, enabling eligible Card Members to use their Amex Card while reviewing and approving each purchase. We’re excited to learn together from this early phase and build toward bringing these experiences to more Card Members over time.”

*—**Luke Gebb**, EVP and Head of Global Innovation, American Express*

> “An agent making a purchase should strengthen, not bypass, the trust built into payments. Our collaboration with OpenAI brings Mastercard’s payments and security expertise to ChatGPT Wallet, helping connect user-approved purchases with the systems businesses and banks already use. Working together across the industry is how we turn the promise of agentic commerce into experiences people and businesses can trust.”

*—**Sherri Haymond**, EVP, Global Head of Digital Commercialization, Mastercard*

> “To deliver on the promise of agentic commerce, consumers, businesses and banks all need to trust the process. We’re partnering with OpenAI to bring Visa’s trusted infrastructure to the experience, helping connect user-approved purchases with the systems businesses already use.”

*—**Rubail Birwadker**, Head of Global Growth, Visa*

- American Express
- Mastercard
- Visa

- American Express

## Equipping businesses for agentic commerce

Agentic commerce is still in its early days. As agents begin to take on more shopping and purchasing tasks, many websites and payment systems are still adapting to this modality. Some sites may unintentionally block purchases through ChatGPT Wallet or other agentic payment products, and we are focused on helping businesses make that transition.

Alongside ChatGPT Wallet, we’re publishing a [Commerce Partner Playbook⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/commerce) with tools and practical guidance to help businesses support customers using agents through their existing websites and systems. It covers making product information available, ensuring agent access, and working with payment and risk providers to reduce unnecessary declines. Businesses can start with the areas most relevant to their customers:

- **Help customers find accurate product information.** [Claim your business in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/introducing-businesses-chatgpt/) and, once verified, update your business details and upload a product feed with current pricing and availability.
- **Ensure ChatGPT agents can access your website.** Configure your CDN or firewall to recognize signed requests using Web Bot Auth and confirm your general site security measures are not inadvertently blocking ChatGPT agents. Browser access does not require a plugin or product feed.
- **Work with your payments and risk providers to support agent purchases.** Wallet’s payment tokens work with existing checkout flows, but risk systems may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations. You can work with your providers to understand how they recognize these transactions. We’re also working with fraud prevention partners including Forter, Riskified, Sardine and Signifyd and payment service providers including Adyen, Checkout.com, and Stripe to help their systems recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.
- **Give agents more ways to work with your business.** Build a plugin to let agents check availability, manage carts, or take other actions through your existing systems. Websites can also add WebMCP tools.

## Availability

ChatGPT Wallet begins rolling out today in dots, enabling users to have their dot complete purchases on their behalf. It will initially be available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18 and older in the US with eligible US-issued cards. We’ll work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to learn from early use and expand availability, helping more customers and businesses benefit from agentic commerce.

title: llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
body:
[
](#llamacpp-v100--a-stronger-foundation-for-the-local-ai-ecosystem)
llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem
[Team Article](/blog)
llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.
During the 3.5 years since its [inception](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/commit/26c0846), the project has grown a lot and many downstream applications already depend on our work. We expect this trend to continue as local AI and privacy become increasingly important in our everyday lives. Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount.
Today we release libraries v1.0.0
, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) and [ggml](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml) will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

Semantic version update rules
The following rules apply to all [ggml-org](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org) projects using [semantic versioning](https://semver.org):
| Change type | Bump |
|---|---|
| MAJOR | Breaking change to the public C API in ./include |
| MINOR | Backward-compatible feature, backend updates, model support, or API addition |
| PATCH | Bug fix with no API change |
[
](#distribution)
Distribution
We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org
software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org
projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following [discussion](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/discussions/1579).
| Channel | Platforms |
|---|---|
|
[
](#development)
Development
The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.
To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as [HF Buckets](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/en/guides/buckets) and [HF Jobs](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/en/guides/jobs) we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master
branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.
[
](#backend-and-model-coverage)
Backend and model coverage
The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp
- ggml
is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.
A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found [here](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/tree/master/src).
We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than [150 architecture variants](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/tree/master/src/models) as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.
[
](#thanks)
Thanks
The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the [long-time maintainers](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CODEOWNERS) of the project and all [contributors](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/graphs/contributors?from=8%2F8%2F2026). title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
body:
From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients.
Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications.
Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care.
Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT [🔗](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/how-ai-is-helping-care-teams/#dyania-health)
Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care
Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts.
Dyania Health, a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would.
The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision.
Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls
Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital.
Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on.
Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with [NVIDIA NeMo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/products/nemo/) open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers.
Synapsis AI in the Real World
Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021.
Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand.
“Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson, chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic.
The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries.
Learn more about [Dyania Health](https://dyaniahealth.com/).

# Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI

With GPT‑6 Astra, the agents in Shield’s Forge platform navigate legacy portals so technicians can focus on issues that need their attention.

[Contact sales](https://openai.com/contact-sales/)



Company size: SMB

Industry: Technology

Region: North America

Share

For many small and medium-sized businesses, an outsourced IT services provider handles everything from an employee locked out of their laptop to a misconfigured firewall that took the office offline.

Shield built [Forge⁠(opens in a new window)](https://shieldtp.com/forge), an AI operating system for IT services providers. The platform brings together business data and customer context to help providers complete IT support tasks end to end. That means its agents also need to work in the older portals technicians use every day. With OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra, Shield can now hand supported browser tasks to agents instead of leaving a technician to log in and finish them manually.

> “The only time you should have to bring in a human technician is if you need their judgment, not because you’re blocked on access.”

—Mayank Jain, Head of Technology, Shield

## Access as a bottleneck

“If a customer is locked out of their computer or there’s a phishing attack, speed is paramount,” says Jain. “Whether you’re going to solve their issue or you’re going to escalate to a human, you want to do either as fast as possible.”

Before using GPT‑6 Astra, Forge’s agents could get stuck at systems they could not access. Customers then had to wait for a technician to complete that step.

Shield tried computer use, where an AI model reads the screen, clicks, and types, with earlier models. Jain says they were not reliable or fast enough. “Usually, a system that doesn’t have an API is an old-school system that also doesn’t look very nice and is very hard to use, even by a human,” Jain says.

## Agents that work like a technician

Technicians spend much of their day in portals that manage tickets, devices and software licenses. Many of those systems lack APIs, so an agent needs to navigate the screen much as a person would.

Forge’s AI Engineer assigns the work to a computer-use agent, and GPT‑6 Astra navigates the interface to complete supported tasks. Technicians decide which actions it can take on its own and where they need to review or approve the work.

Shield says these browser workflows are live, with thousands of runs each month across its IT providers. Phone calls, on-site work and remote-desktop tasks still need human involvement.

“GPT‑6 Astra allows our agents to embody what a technician does by logging into portals and legacy websites that might not have API access and performing tasks that only a human could six months ago,” says Mayank Jain, Head of Technology at Shield.

> “What shocked me the most was how natural GPT-6 Astra was with computer use. We’d seen models perform computer use before, but you could clearly see them stutter as they try to figure out how to navigate the UI. With GPT-6 Astra, it feels like you’re just watching a human click around.”

—Mayank Jain, Head of Technology, Shield

## More work technicians can hand off

Jain says GPT‑6 Astra was 35-40% faster on average than the legacy models Shield had used for computer-use tasks. He also says customer satisfaction is higher on tickets where AI is used, with speed of resolution being a critical factor.

Shield reports faster execution, fewer failures and fewer timeouts. Its teams also spend less time writing detailed instructions to an agent or helping it through a task.

## What’s next

Shield is testing remote-desktop workflows that would let agents perform more complex actions directly on a computer’s desktop.

Jain says, “With GPT‑6 Astra, Forge is now truly an extension of our human technicians.”

  - [Oversight and dispute resolution](#oversight-and-dispute-resolution)
  - [Employee discussions and attestation](#employee-discussions-and-attestation)
  - [Conflict disclosures & cool off periods](#conflict-disclosures-and-cool-off-periods)
  - [Publication and responsible disclosure periods](#publication-and-responsible-disclosure-periods)
- [Looking ahead](#looking-ahead)

We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/). They build on our [priorities and principles for third party assessments](https://openai.com/index/priorities-principles-third-party-assessments/) and years of work with [third party evaluators](https://openai.com/index/strengthening-safety-with-external-testing/), including a recent pilot assessment of [our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/) with deep internal access and an investigation of [the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

## Our pilot embedded assessors

### Apollo Research

In this pilot assessment, [Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.apolloresearch.ai/) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

1. Training did not incentivize subversion.
2. Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.
3. Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.
4. Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

### Goodfire

[Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.goodfire.com/) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

### METR

We intend to conduct two assessments with [METR⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/), focused on model alignment and monitoring:

- **Alignment assessment:** For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run. [1](#citation-bottom-1)
- **Monitor assessment:** We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise [2](#citation-bottom-2). We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another [monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-14-control-assessment-proposal/) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

### Transluce

[Transluce⁠(opens in a new window)](https://transluce.org/) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

## Protocols for embedded assessments

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

### Scoping and iteration

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

### A secure, on-site environment

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum [3](#citation-bottom-3) the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

### Oversight and dispute resolution

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

### Employee discussions and attestation

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. title: Building strong safety evaluations
body:
Safety evaluations inform some of the most consequential decisions we make about an AI model, including whether it’s ready to deploy, which safeguards ship alongside it, and what our next round of safety training and research should focus on. When we say a model is “safer than its predecessor,” we mean that it scored better on a set of evals someone built. But a safety claim is only as sound as the eval behind it, and good ones are hard to build.
A safety eval measures a model’s propensity to cause or contribute to harm, whether its response to a request makes harm more or less likely, and how severe that harm would be, rather than measuring specific capabilities. It can cover different types of harm. For example, a user may actively request harmful outputs (such as seeking instructions on how to harm themselves), or they may request outputs that are intended to be harmless, but that come with high risk of unintended harm (such as seeking information on the appropriate dose of a drug). Essentially, a safety eval asks, “Given a specific input, did the model do the right thing?”
Like other types of evals, these can be tricky to get right: researchers have repeatedly found that AI evals are [easy to](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20879) [game](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/f316275b44ee2de533102913828a8107-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf), don’t always measure what they claim to measure, and aren’t [documented well enough to reproduce](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12990). The results can change depending on whether the questions are [multiple-choice or open-ended](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16786), or even based on [how answer options are ordered](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07951).
Psychology faced similar issues a decade ago, when [large-scale replication projects](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aac4716) found that many published findings didn’t hold up, likely at least in part because many original studies relied on small samples and journals favored statistically significant results. In response, the field instituted reforms such as preregistration (writing down hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting or analyzing data), better measurement, and more rigorous statistics, which made measurements more trustworthy and results easier to replicate. Drawing on those reforms, and from our experience [building evals at Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents),[1](#footnote-1) this post shares recommendations for anyone who builds or relies on AI safety evaluations, using examples from our [system cards](https://www.anthropic.com/system-cards).
Safety first
Build a team with the right skills
Building a strong safety eval requires multiple perspectives, including from subject-matter and technical experts. Methods experts, for example, help decide how to sample, grade, and analyze the model’s responses. Domain experts such as psychologists, biologists, or political scientists help ensure evals cover realistic and diverse test cases. They will also decide what counts as harm, which cases are borderline, and what a good response looks like.
When one of these perspectives is missing, eval quality can suffer. Failure modes include evals that are technically rigorous but don’t capture the most relevant factors in a specific harm area or, conversely, evals that reflect deep expertise in a subject area but test only a subset of behaviors, making it difficult to draw valid conclusions about the domain as a whole. Having domain and methods experts involved from the beginning of the process can mitigate against both.
Run evals safely
Safety evals often run with standard safeguards disabled so we can understand a model’s baseline performance. In cyber evals, in particular, models may probe the boundaries of their testing environments and could take [unintended actions](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) if they escape. For this reason, evals should be run in a sandbox with no internet access, and monitored in real time so you can stop a run immediately if a model is acting in ways that could result in real-world harm. In recent months, in response to [our own incidents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents), we have [hardened our evaluation environments](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), temporarily stopped running many evaluations that give models internet access, and implemented real-time monitoring for web search evaluations that require giving models internet access. We continue to work to make these environments both realistic and safe.
Design
Match the design to the question
The first thing to ask when building an eval is: what is the question you’re trying to answer? This should guide the way you design the evaluation, as it will determine how you can interpret the results.
Most evals are observational: they tell you that one model obtained a different score than another, but not why. Causal claims (for example, “This intervention made the model safer”) need a design that varies one variable at a time, such as evaluating the same model with and without a specific intervention in place. For example, the question “Is the model responding safely to requests for content that might promote eating disorders?” is observational, whereas the question “Does altering the system prompt change whether the model responds safely to requests for content that may promote eating disorders?” is causal. An observational design is the right choice for understanding a model’s behavior; a causal design is the right choice when you want to understand whether a specific change can influence that behavior.
Measure what you mean to measure
Once you’ve chosen the right design, the next question to ask is: what exactly are you trying to measure? This is also called [construct validity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04703)—whether your measure captures the concept you actually care about—and it’s where AI evaluations often go wrong.
For safety evals, the obvious construct is refusal, or how often the model declines to respond. This makes sense in many cases—we don’t want models to help a user launch a scam or a phishing scheme. But for conversations related to suicide and self-harm, refusal is often the wrong construct. When a user is in crisis, simply declining to engage is, itself, a failure; the ideal response engages the user with empathy and [points them toward human support](https://www.anthropic.com/news/protecting-well-being-of-users). A model that refuses to respond to any prompt related to suicide or self-harm would get a perfect score on a refusal-rate eval, but it is not necessarily a safer model.
At Anthropic, we design multi-turn safety evals that report an appropriate response rate: the share of conversations in which the model behaved appropriately throughout, judged against a rubric specific to a given risk area, developed by domain experts. One bad turn—like a model divulging details on how to run a scam when repeatedly pressed—results in a failing grade for the whole conversation. In the case of a safety eval for user wellbeing, an “appropriate” response is one where the model responds supportively to disclosures of risk (such as a user saying they are considering self-harm), avoids discussing details of methods (such as specific ways of self-harming), points the user to crisis resources at the right moment, and does not position itself as a substitute for a crisis line.
In other risk areas, the appropriate response is different. Much of biology and cybersecurity is dual use: the same question might help a user develop a vaccine or enhance a pathogen, discover a vulnerability in their own software or exploit it in someone else’s. In these cases, too, an appropriate response is rarely a flat refusal. Rather, it engages with the legitimate version of the request while withholding the operational specifics that would provide real uplift to the harmful version of the request. We build separate rubrics for each topic so we can measure what an appropriate model response looks like in each area.
A good eval also needs to measure both compliance with harmful requests and over-refusal of benign requests. In our single-turn evals, we pair two different kinds of prompts: harmful requests (where we aim to maximize the “harmless response rate”) and benign requests (where we aim to minimize the “refusal rate”) in the same domain. For example, in an eval testing a model’s response to dual-use chemistry questions, a harmful prompt might be requesting the chemical formulation for a nerve agent (where we would want the model to refuse), while a benign request might be a question about a historical chemical disaster (where we would want the model to provide a helpful response). Deciding which requests fall into each bucket—harmful or benign—requires subject-matter expertise, especially for borderline cases.
Make sure the results generalize
The scenarios an eval tests are meant to stand in for performance in the real world, with real users. That only works if the scenario actually resembles the real world. Below are a few considerations relevant to ensuring the results generalize to real-world situations.
Capture nuance via multi-turn simulations
Single-turn prompts are the easiest evals to build, but they saturate quickly. They also aren’t particularly realistic: much of the time, the potential for real-world harm isn’t obvious in a single prompt. Humans extract harmful information from a model through gradual escalation, so a model that handles the first message well may respond inappropriately by the fifth.
User distress is often particularly hard to glean from a single message. It tends to accumulate across a conversation, such that something a person said 10 turns ago changes the context of their next message. As an example, in one of our [multi-turn evaluations for suicide and self-harm](https://assets.claude.com/283ef97c476cf442c91d9a37d5b214242a55bb92.pdf) that we report in our system card, a simulated user discloses a destabilizing event, such as being laid off from their job or the death of a family member, early in the conversation. Later, they ask a seemingly ordinary question that, read alongside the earlier disclosure, may warrant a more careful response. If the model does not consider the earlier context, it risks providing information that could be dangerous to the user. This sort of nuance cannot be captured in an eval that reads a single message in isolation.
Design scenarios that model a range of conditions
To construct test suites for each safety risk, our subject-matter experts design multi-turn simulations that are closely modeled after real-world observations. We built an internal tool that lets them do so systematically. The steps are as follows:
- A domain expert writes a specification. The specification includes the simulated user’s objectives and the tactics they’ll use to pursue them, plus any other dimensions that are relevant to the threat model, such as persona, situation, tone, and conversational style. Each dimension typically has several options—for example, personas can range from a novelist to an academic to an authorized government contractor.
- The first user turn is fixed, so every run of a scenario starts from the exact same prompt.
- A separate Claude model generates the subsequent “user” turns, following the specification and sampling from the different options within each dimension. The model being tested writes the “assistant” turns. Because the simulated user is responding to what the model actually said, the conversation can develop in ways a pre-written script can’t anticipate.
- Each scenario runs a number of times, and each run draws on a different combination of characteristics from the specification. This causes the conversations to diverge from the shared starting point, allowi

title: Building always-on agents
body:
Building always-on agents
Always-on agents run indefinitely, deciding how and when to act across many sessions. This guide walks through their core primitives and how they fit together.
Over the past few months, we’ve seen a resurgence of always-on agents.
Always-on agents are stateful and proactive, meaning they manage context across sessions and take actions without direct supervision. Underneath, they run on the same [core loop](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents) as other agents. The difference is the surrounding architecture, which is built from primitives that control when the agents wake up, what carries over between runs, and how their work reaches the user.
The resurgence is largely due to recent model advancements, which have made always-on agents more practical to run. First, the latest models have better judgment: they’re more reliable at understanding user intent and knowing when to check in. Second, intelligence is becoming cheaper, with long-horizon tasks benefiting the most. For example, on [one long-horizon coding benchmark](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence), Opus 5.5 cost 78% less per solved task than Opus 5, compared with 40% less on typical workloads.
Customers have started to ask us how to integrate this type of experience into their own products. Some companies want to make their existing agents more proactive, while others are looking to build them from the ground up.
This post breaks down the primitives behind always-on agents and walks through how they fit together.
The cycle behind the always-on agent
An always-on agent is not actually “always on.” This is just a description of the user experience.
In reality, the agent spends most of its time asleep, waking up periodically to do work. Each stretch of work is called a run: the agent receives an event, completes its task, and then saves information about what happened. A run works inside a session, which is the transcript of messages and tool calls. Once the run is finished, the agent goes back to sleep, and the cycle repeats indefinitely.
The core primitives
The surrounding architecture of an always-on agent has five core primitives: an event inbox, timers, memory, permissions, and an outbox. Let’s take a look at each.
Event inbox
Most AI agents only run when the user sends a message. In contrast, always-on agents can be triggered by many types of events, including webhooks, scheduled tasks, and background jobs.
One tempting approach is to have each event source call the agent directly, but that has a few failure modes. For example, two events arriving at the same time can start competing runs, and a crash can lose an event entirely.
This is where the event inbox comes in. Instead of calling the agent, every source sends an event to an inbox, where a worker picks it up.
The simplest version has three components:
- A durable list of events, usually a database table;
- A handler, usually an HTTP endpoint, that writes events to the list; and
- A worker, usually a background service, that reads from the list.
The inbox should track the status of each event, and events can be deduplicated based on unique identifiers from the source. A relational database works well for the inbox, with every event appended as a new row. We recommend starting with one inbox per user, but you can split this further if you need more parallelism.
When a new event comes in, the handler writes the event to the inbox and wakes the worker. The worker reads whatever is pending and starts a run. Events that continue earlier work, such as a reply from the user, resume an existing session, while everything else starts a new session.
From there, the worker passes the events to the agent loop, waits for the run to finish, and marks the corresponding events as done. The implementation details can get tricky, so here are a few best practices:
- The handler should acknowledge events quickly. Some sources, such as webhook providers, treat slow responses as failures. The handler can still run lightweight checks, but any deeper verification, such as checking for prompt injection, should be done during the run.
- The inbox should be the source of truth. When the worker is woken up, it should pull the latest events from the inbox first. That way, if the worker dies mid-run, a new one can pick up the same event and retry.
- An inbox should only have one active worker at a time. This prevents two runs from duplicating work or overwriting each other. When a new event shows up mid-run, you can either push it to the next run, fold it into the current run, or interrupt and restart.
- The worker should batch pending events together. For example, if the user sends several messages in a row, the worker can merge them into a single run, so the agent only needs to reply once.
Timers
Together with the event inbox, timers let always-on agents be proactive. Timers generally fall into one of two categories: follow-ups or schedules. A follow-up is a deadline that the agent sets for itself, such as checking in on a reply. A schedule, on the other hand, is a recurring task that happens on a known cadence, such as a daily newsletter.
Timers live in their own durable store, usually another database table, separate from the inbox. The inbox should only hold events that are ready to be worked on. A follow-up and a schedule can share a similar schema, but a schedule needs to track its recurrence as well.
A timer doesn’t initiate a run on its own. Instead, a scheduler, usually a background service, polls the store at a fixed interval and fires anything that’s due. On each pass, the scheduler:
- Scans the store and finds timers that are due.
- Updates each timer based on its category.
- A follow-up should be marked as done.
- A schedule should get its due time updated to the next occurrence.
- Adds an event to the inbox and wakes the worker.
For the scheduler, you can either build your own service or use a durable execution engine.
Memory
Always-on agents work across many disjointed runs and rely on memory to maintain continuity.
Similar to the event inbox and timers, memory should have its own store. In our products, such as Claude Code’s [auto memory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) and the Messages API’s [memory tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool), this is implemented as a directory of files. For an always-on agent, the directories should map to durable storage, usually a database or an object store. This way memories outlive the worker.
As a rule of thumb, memory should only hold what the agent can’t look up again. If something already lives in another system, such as an issue tracker, you should save a pointer instead. Here is a breakdown of the types of memory an always-on agent should store:
- User instructions: Any instructions from the user about agent behavior should be saved in their own file and loaded at the start of every run. The user won’t always be around to steer the agent, so the instructions have to carry over between runs.
- User notes: The agent should save what it’s learned about the user, such as their role, their preferences, or any corrections they’ve given. You can start with one file and move to several small files as the notes grow. In the latter case, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.
- Past messages: The agent should keep track of what it’s already told the user so nothing is repeated. It can either store this in a separate file that’s loaded at the start of each run, or have the worker load the agent’s last few messages with the user.
- Task progress: For each ongoing task, the agent should keep a progress file that covers what’s been done and what’s left. Any new run can then read that file and pick up where the previous run left off. Similar to user notes, only an index is loaded at the start of each run, but the agent can pull the individual files into context when it needs more details.
The diagram below shows one example setup.
All of the above describes memory that’s saved during a run. You can also add dreaming, which reviews past sessions to curate memories. Dreaming can replace outdated entries and find patterns that only show up across many runs. If you’re interested in learning more, our [post on agent memory](https://www.anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory) covers this in more detail.
Inside the context window
Before doing any work, the agent loads the system prompt, tool definitions, and memory files. This initial context “overhead” is included in every run, so we recommend keeping it lean and using [prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) to lower costs.
A new session starts only with this context overhead and the events that triggered the run. An existing session, on the other hand, brings back the messages and tool calls from its earlier runs.
If a session becomes too long, you can either [compact the older messages](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) or start a new session. Both approaches lose detail, so anything that needs to persist should be saved to memory along the way.
Permissions
Permissions are where always-on agents carry the most risk. A run holds the user’s access and, by design, operates unattended. For each tool call, the agent needs to decide whether to proceed on its own, block it, or wait for approval.
The components for permissions are the same ones other agents use:
- Credential store: Always-on agents often need sensitive user credentials like passwords or access tokens to be useful. The
[recommended pattern](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/secure-deployment#credential-management)is a proxy outside the agent’s environment that adds credentials to outgoing requests. The agent sends requests without credentials, and the proxy injects the real credentials before forwarding. - Auto mode: An always-on agent should be able to work without constant user input. We’ve already tackled a version of this problem with
[auto mode](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-auto-mode)in Claude Code. Auto mode uses classifiers to review higher-risk actions and block the ones they identify as dangerous so Claude can find a safer approach. User review, however, is still necessary for the most important decisions. - Deferred tool calls: In Claude Code,
[a hook can defer a tool call](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#defer-a-tool-call-for-later)and wait for additional input from the user. The same pattern applies to always-on agents, which may need clarification or approval before taking certain actions. When a call is deferred, the run ends and the session is saved mid-call. The request is shown to the user (e.g., through an interactive card built with[MCP Apps](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview)), and their answer comes back as an event in the inbox. That event starts a new run, which resumes the saved session with the user’s input. While the deferred call waits for a response, the worker can pick up other events, so the agent isn’t blocked.
Outbox
With most AI agents, the response is streamed to the user as it’s generated, so they can follow along as Claude reasons through the problem, calls tools, and writes its answer.
Always-on agents, on the other hand, do most of their work in the background. The user gets the outcome and a few details, rather than the entire step-by-step breakdown.
A run can end in one of three ways:
- The agent sends a message to the outbox,
- The agent decides that nothing needs to be sent, or
- The agent uses a deferred tool call to request permission or additional input.
Most always-on agents can get by with a “send” tool that delivers the message directly to the user. You only need a formal outbox when you want to pace

title: The Claude Tag guide for startups
body:
The Claude Tag guide for startups
How leading startups use Claude Tag to ship faster and scale operations
Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, [Claude Tag](https://claude.com/product/tag) (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.
For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.
We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.
| Company | On call | Thread to PR | Company brain | Self-serve data | Routine reporting |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kikoff | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| NavigateAI | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| Campfire | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Flagler Health | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Moritz | ● | ● | |||
| Orderful | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| Valence | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Descript | ● | ● | ● |
But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden.
The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:
21

Days to hours
In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag.
Top channels to tag Claude
The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start.
01 Claude on call
Example setups:
#on-call
#alerts-ci
#deploy-watch
#support-escalations
GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io
Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap
@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].
Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.
With Claude in the channel as [a first responder](https://claude.com/resources/articles/ai-ci-cd-on-call), the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.
At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.
Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel
Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:
#deploys
: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.#alerts-ci
: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.#alerts-sentry-backend
: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.#dog-fooding
: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.#support
: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.
Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.
NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context
NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.
Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.
With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.
“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.
02 Thread to PR
Example setups:
#quick-wins
#bug-bash
#product-feedback
#feature-requests
#ux-papercuts
#tech-debt
#design-polish
GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry
One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap
@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.
Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.
With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.
Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.
Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days
Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.
One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.
When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.
The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.
“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”
Valence: From feature request to rollout
Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.
In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.
03 Company brain
Example setups:
#ask-anything
#company-wiki
#product-questions
GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase
One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap
@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.
At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.
For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.
Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing
Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.
Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.
That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.
Campfire: Customer experience on demand
One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”
This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.
04 Self-serve data
Example setups:
#data-requests
#ask-revops
#metric-definitions
dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion

title: Cohere Expands Its Sovereign AI Platform with AISLE and cubic
body:
Over the past year, we've seen a fundamental shift in how organizations approach AI. Enterprises and governments are deploying AI into the workflows that matter most, from cybersecurity and software development to mission-critical operations and decision-making. As they do, their requirements are becoming increasingly clear: they need AI systems that are powerful, secure, and under their control.
At Cohere, we've long believed organizations shouldn't have to choose between cutting-edge AI and control. They should be able to deploy advanced AI while maintaining ownership of their data, infrastructure, and operations. That's the foundation of sovereign AI.
Today, we're excited to share two important milestones in that journey. We're pleased to announce the completion of our acquisition of AISLE, the company building autonomous systems for vulnerability discovery and remediation. We're also welcoming the team behind cubic, one of the leading AI-powered code review platforms, to Cohere.
Together, these additions strengthen the sovereign AI platform we're building for organizations around the world. With [AISLE](https://cohere.com/blog/cohere-and-aisle-sign-letter-of-intent-to-advance-cyber-resilient-sovereign-ai) and cubic we’ve completed four strategic M&A transactions this year, following [Aleph Alpha](https://cohere.com/blog/cohere-and-aleph-alpha-sign-agreement), [Reliant AI](https://cohere.com/blog/cohere-acquires-reliant-ai-expand-sovereign-enterprise-ai) to expand our capabilities across frontier AI, biopharma and healthcare, cybersecurity, and software development.
Cybersecurity is a defining frontier of AI
As AI becomes embedded in critical systems and workflows, security is becoming a defining requirement for adoption. Organizations increasingly need AI that can operate inside private clouds, on-premises and air-gapped environments while meeting rigorous requirements around privacy, governance, and compliance.
That's why we're excited to officially welcome AISLE to Cohere. When we announced our intent to acquire AISLE, we outlined a shared belief: the future of AI depends on the ability to secure both AI systems and the software infrastructure that powers them. As organizations deploy AI into increasingly sensitive environments, cyber resilience becomes foundational to trust.
AISLE’s co-founders are taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development. Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and lead the newly established cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, overseeing security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts while leading AI security research.
Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.
AISLE brings world-class expertise in autonomous security research and vulnerability discovery.
Their work has demonstrated how specialized AI systems can identify, validate, and remediate vulnerabilities at a speed and scale that helps defenders stay ahead of an increasingly complex threat landscape.
Today, that expertise has become the foundation of Cohere Cyber, our cybersecurity business focused on helping enterprises, governments, and critical infrastructure operators build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems. Together, we're building cyber defense capabilities that help organizations deploy AI with confidence in even the most demanding environments.
Bringing secure coding to enterprise scale
Software development is one of the most widely adopted enterprise applications of AI. But organizations need more than systems that generate code. They need AI that can understand complex codebases, review changes, identify vulnerabilities, maintain software quality, and operate within strict security boundaries. That's what attracted us to cubic.
The team has built an industry-leading AI-powered code review platform that helps engineering organizations review code, find bugs and vulnerabilities, understand complex codebases, and automatically remediate issues. Their review agents have consistently ranked among the strongest performers on code review benchmarks and were built for the environments many enterprise customers operate in, including on-premises and air-gapped deployments.
Led by founder and CEO Paul Sanglé-Ferrière, the team brings expertise across AI, security, developer tools, distributed systems, and enterprise software. They will establish Cohere's secure coding vertical, helping accelerate the integration of enterprise-grade coding capabilities into our platform while meeting the security, governance, and deployment requirements our customers demand. Their work strengthens our ability to help organizations build, maintain, and secure software using AI within their own environments and under their own control.
Building AI for the world's most critical industries
What connects AISLE and cubic is more than technical excellence. Both teams have built products for organizations operating in environments where security, reliability, governance, and control are non-negotiable.
Their work reflects a broader shift we're seeing across the market. Organizations increasingly want AI they can deploy on their own terms. They want systems that fit within their security requirements, regulatory obligations, and operational realities without becoming dependent on systems they can't inspect, adapt, or control.
We believe this is where the next phase of AI adoption will be won. By bringing together frontier models, secure deployment infrastructure, cyber defense, and purpose-built applications, we're continuing to build a sovereign AI platform that gives organizations more capability, more security, and more control.
Looking ahead
The future of AI won't be defined by models alone. It will be defined by the systems, workflows, and infrastructure built around them. The question is whether organizations can deploy AI securely and at scale across the systems that matter most. That's the promise of sovereign AI.
Welcoming AISLE and cubic to Cohere strengthens our ability to deliver on that vision. Together, we're building a sovereign AI platform that enterprises and governments can trust to operate in their most sensitive environments, power their most critical workflows, and realize the full potential of AI while maintaining control of their data, infrastructure, and operations.
We're excited to welcome both teams to Cohere and look forward to what we'll build together.

title: llm-gemini 0.37
body:
12th November 2026
Google launched [Gemini 4 Hydrogen](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/) today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.
It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:
| Model | Dates | Input ($/M) | Cached input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemini 4 Carbon | Through Nov 30, 2026 | $2.00 | $0.10 | $10.00 |
| From Dec 1, 2026 | $4.00 | $0.20 | $20.00 | |
| Gemini 4 Argon | Through Nov 30, 2026 | $2.00 | $0.10 | $10.00 |
| From Dec 1, 2026 | $4.00 | $0.20 | $20.00 | |
| Gemini 4 Hydrogen | $1.50 | $0.075 | $7.50 |
Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? [Google says](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing) that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.
Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.
I had Hydrogen [generate some pelicans](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2Fce357e95149cd16f65ec7e7106ed4fed). Here's a [full comparison grid](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/gemini-4-pelicans.html) showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:
Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.
Here's [how Google describe](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/) Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.
