Amplitude has always helped teams see how people actually use their products. Its proactive product agent Wave helps teams turn those insights into shipped improvements. Amplitude describes Wave as roughly 80% powered by OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna, and GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare. Wave turns product insights into implementation plans teams can ship to coding agents, including Codex, then measures the impact.

Amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month.On Amplitude’s own homepage, Wave helped personalize suggestion cards, driving a 160% lift in card-driven sends.

> “AI can now find useful work we never thought to assign it. OpenAI’s models can investigate a problem, write and run code, and use the results to decide what to try next.”

—Spenser Skates, CEO, Amplitude

## From product data to shipped improvements

Wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. It then tracks outcomes and uses those learnings to inform the next round of improvements.

Behind that workflow, Amplitude uses different OpenAI models for different tasks. GPT‑6.1 Sol supports the opportunity manager and deep investigations into code and data. GPT‑6 Luna handles frequent, lower-cost tasks such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks. GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare generates product mockups using screenshots from session replays as visual references.

When an opportunity is ready to build, teams can send it directly from Wave to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical plan and acceptance criteria to guide implementation.



## How Wave drove a 160% agent engagement lift

“The idea with Wave is you have a unified platform with agents that comb through massive amounts of session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities to improve products,” explains Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager at Amplitude.

Amplitude tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help users start a conversation with an AI agent. Wave discovered that people often bypassed them: in a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion.

Wave proposed personalizing the cards using recent charts, dashboards, or the page a user had come from. It illustrated the change and produced a technical plan, including preserving free typing and showing generic suggestions when personalization context was unavailable. After a brief review, the team handed the work to a coding agent and A/B tested the change.



In the experiment readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards increased 160% relative to control after one day. “It is a great example of how non-groundbreaking things that just get ignored can increase the adoption of features in unexpected ways.” explains Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude.

## Choosing the right OpenAI model for each task

Wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly.

> “OpenAI gave us both strong reasoning models and smaller, faster models, so we could balance quality, latency, and inference cost across the product”

—Spenser Skates, CEO, Amplitude

For Wave’s Opportunity Investigator, Amplitude evaluated whether models corroborated findings, avoided false positives, incorporated evaluator feedback, recovered from tool failures, and kept claims aligned with evidence. GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternative models. It led on all five investigation criteria and had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes.

In a separate evaluation of Wave’s Data Science Agent, GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 67.5 out of 100, compared with 69.3 for another leading model, at a mean model cost of $1.28 versus $2.63 per dispatch. GPT‑6.1 Sol also scored higher on tool-contract compliance, estimation and uncertainty, and evidence grounding.

### GPT‑6.1 Sol data science agent evaluation

For high-volume work such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks, Amplitude uses GPT‑6 Luna to keep latency and cost low. Splitting work across specialist agents lets the team reserve more expensive reasoning for the tasks that need it the most.

For generating wireframes and mockups, OpenAI’s image generation model scored 80.3 out of 100 for solution wireframes, compared with 63.9 for another image generation model. Amplitude’s evaluation covered communication quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, text and UI legibility, and visual coherence across 15 opportunities.

### GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare wireframe evaluation

## Keeping teams in charge of what ships

Customers across industries are already using Wave in beta to identify and ship product improvements. Wave analyzes session and analytics data, then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria.

From there, teams can control the level of automation. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while new features and bigger bets get a human review.

For changes that reach launch, the path from discovery to execution can be short: among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity, half in under four days, and two in three within a week.

*Interpolated from supplied milestones; the curve is illustrative, not individual observations.*

## What’s next

“Our ambition with OpenAI is to make self-improving products the way companies build software,” says Skates. As OpenAI’s models get better at reasoning and coding, teams will be able to delegate more investigation and implementation work to agents, ultimately resulting in better products reaching users faster. Amplitude is already seeing it, as agents find and help deliver improvements in its own product while the team works on other priorities: “I think teams will be surprised by how much they can accomplish when their software is working alongside them to make the product better.”

title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
body:
Text Generation • 4B • Updated • 1.77k • 8
[
](#llmon-an-llm-native-markup-language-now-in-granite-41-3b-and-8b)
LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.
To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.
Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: [granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.1-3b-llmon-preview) and [granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.1-8b-llmon-preview). We are also releasing a [GitHub](https://github.com/generative-computing/llmon) repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.
What it enables:
- Indirect prompt injections, hidden in user data, are mostly ignored by LLMON models due to explicit instruction/data separation. For some benchmarks, attack success rates drop to nearly zero, whereas regular instruction-tuned models get hijacked with high probability. This is achieved while maintaining general capability relative to Granite 4.1 Instruct models.
- Unrelated passages, old chat turns, and tool outputs don’t get pulled into the answer because each instruction is bound to the exact data it applies to.
- Instructions, data, and requirements are clearly marked so that their structure and meanings at the application’s code level can be leveraged by the model. Try it out in
[Mellea](https://github.com/generative-computing/mellea), which has native LLMON support enabled by automatically LLMONizing its LLM calls. - You no longer need to worry about forcing LLMs to observe JSON structure. Use our converters to turn existing JSON into LLMON without loss. You can also define your own structure and associated tags and tune a LoRA on top of the LLMON models to understand it.
[
](#why-not-json)
Why not JSON?
JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.
LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.
Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created [conversion tools](https://github.com/generative-computing/llmon/tree/main/llmon/lang) and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.
[
](#how-is-llmon-related-to-chat-templates)
How is LLMON related to chat templates?
LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.
The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages
list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template
as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec
: True
or False
. A part marked True
is bound into the exec
block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False
is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.
messages = [ { "role": "user",
"instruction": [{ "value": "Write a short paragraph about", "exec": True }],
"data": [{ "value": "IBM Company", "exec": True }],
"requirement": [ {"value": "Use less than 10 words", "exec": True},
{"value": "Do not use commas", "exec": True}]
} ]
Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):
<|open|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|close|>Write a short paragraph about<|open_end|>
<|open|>data<|:|>ä¦<|close|>IBM Company<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>Á¼<|close|>Use less than 10 words<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>¢¬<|close|>Do not use commas<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|:|>ÄÐ<|close|>
<|open|>exec<|.|>instruction<|close|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|.|>input<|close|>data<|:|>ä¦<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>Á¼<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>¢¬<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|.|>output<|close|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|open_end|>
<|open_end|>
<|open|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|close|>
The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.
The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.
[
](#how-llmon-addresses-prompt-injection-attacks)
How LLMON addresses prompt injection attacks
Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.
We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the [OPI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12815) benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.
All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks ([ASB](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.02644) and [StruQ](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.06363)). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.
[
](#general-capability)
General capability
Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.
In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.
[
](#how-we-trained-the-models)
How we trained the models
The models start from [Granite 4.1](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.1-8b-base) base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.
LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.
The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the [LLMON Attention Visualization](https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-granite/LLMON-Attention-Visualization) on Hugging Face Spaces.
[
](#bring-your-own-vocabulary-scienceworld)
Bring your own vocabulary (ScienceWorld)
LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal
, req.planning_policy.r

title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
body:
Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.
While our frontier models, [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/) and [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-4-hydrogen), the Gemini API, [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise), the [Gemini app](http://gemini.google.com/), [Google Search](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/gemini-4-hydrogen-search-upgrade), and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/).
Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing [Orchestrator in Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-hydrogen-in-google-antigravity). Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On [Terminal-Bench 4.0](https://www.tbench.ai/news/terminal-bench-4-0), Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling [Terminal-Bench 4.1](https://www.tbench.ai/) scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:
- Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.
- Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on
[Agent Arena](https://arena.ai/leaderboard/agent), arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on[Vals Tax Agent Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/tax_agent_bench)(52.3%), ties for #1 on the[Vals Legal Research Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research)(55.8%), and leads its class on[AutomationBench-AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/automationbench-aa).
- Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new
[Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA)](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/multimodal-knowledge-agent-benchmark/)benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on[Agents’ Last Exam v1.1](https://agents-last-exam.org/leaderboard)(71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows. - Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.
Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels
We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.
Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search
For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.
In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.
- Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details.
- Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list.
- Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.
Hydrogen is significantly upgrading [Search](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/gemini-4-hydrogen-search-upgrade), delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.
- Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.
- More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search.
- Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered.
Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:
- Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.
Building on our commitment to[reasoning transparency](https://institute.deepmind.com/essays/the-case-for-reasoning-transparency/), Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. - Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.
For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen [model card](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/Model-Cards/Gemini-4-Hydrogen-Model-Card.pdf).
Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today
Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:
- For developers: Build with the Gemini API in
[AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/whats-new-gemini-4-hydrogen)and[Android Studio](https://developer.android.com/studio), try it in[AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-4-hydrogen)and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in[Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/). - For enterprises: Deploy it in
[Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise)via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions. - For everyone: Start using it in the
[Gemini app](http://gemini.google.com/)model drop down[1](#footnote-1)and in[Google Search](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/gemini-4-hydrogen-search-upgrade)for all users, and in Gemini in[Google Sheets](http://sheets.new/)starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

title: To the man with AI, everything looks like a task
body:
Now I’m having fun!
[My Ramp post](https://sessions.bensbites.com/ramp/) was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair).
The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding.
Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’.
But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc.
I want to focus on using AI for fun.
AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using [Droid](https://factory.com/) with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on).
As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week…
Can you guess which company it is?
And yes, these animations are staying. Honestly I love them. I love making them too.
So much so that I set up a sophisticated camera set up to monitor what my days look like and here’s the footage.
Morning voice dump. Kids. Stickmen.
Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio, lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools. You stay in control from first idea to finished result. [Try it today in the Firefly Assistant!](https://www.adobe.com/products/firefly.html)*
Quick bites
Anthropic is building all office software inside Claude. Latest addition:
[whiteboards, sheets and data](https://claude.com/resources/articles/more-ways-to-work-with-claude-sheets-whiteboards-and-interactive-connectors). Meetings soon?[Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/)is out for Ultra subscribers and in the API. Also see:[Gemini Decision 1](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/decisions-api)(Google’s Jev-like model)[Grok Bot](https://x.ai/news/grok-bot-1-0)is now in Slack, Teams and your video calls.You can now
[claim your business in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/introducing-businesses-chatgpt/)and see how often it gets mentioned.Granola now writes a nightly
[Agent Brief](https://x.com/meetgranola/status/2120551910789046391)about you that any agent can read.[Practical Data](https://practicaldata.dev/)colours any table on the web so you can see what’s good and bad at a glance.
I'm on the other side of this. A lot of my week runs through n8n and a Telegram bot, and a real chunk of my evenings goes to fixing those automations. Honestly the fun for me is in building them, not the time they save. How do you decide what's worth handing to an agent and what you'd rather just keep doing yourself?

title: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW
body:
Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/), allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming.
There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet. Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) this week.
Kronus Calls for Reinforcements
[Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2272360/), developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2272360/) Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus.
Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test.
GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2272360/), and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch.
DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming
NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature.
Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle.
In Where Winds Meet, DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game.
Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including [GeForce NOW Ultimate](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs.
Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find [more details](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/hogwarts-legacy-war-thunder-dlss-5-3d-guided-neural-rendering/).
A New Tale for the Arisen
Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon.
Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization.
Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration.
GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice.
In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:

[Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2523740/DreamWorks_Shrek_2_Remastered/), Nov. 10) - Warhammer Survivors (New release on

While running his creative production agency, Fresh Tape Media, Jared Kleinstein noticed a problem: incredible creative work was being made for social media, but the makers weren’t getting proper credit. So he built the [Gondola⁠(opens in a new window)](https://gondola.cc/) platform to help creatives show what they made, prove its impact, and turn their work into their next opportunity.

For Gondola’s small team, one of the biggest constraints was how much product and operational work it could take on. Even small experiments competed with core product priorities for engineering time, and finding information and drafting work required sifting through tools and systems.

Today, the team uses Codex to turn more ideas into software and ChatGPT to simplify daily operations. Monthly engineering output is up 25% across the team and up 50% for its lead engineer. Company revenue has more than doubled year over year. For Jared, this has changed what feels possible for the team.

> “Using OpenAI has increased the ambition of what we think a company our size can build.”

—Jared Kleinstein, Founder and CEO, Gondola

## Enabling business teams to build alongside engineers with Codex

Many of Gondola’s product ideas come directly from customer conversations and operational problems that the business development and leadership team sees firsthand. Before Codex, they would have to define the need and write requirements and then wait for an engineer to have capacity to build the first version.

Now the same team uses Codex Cloud to explore the codebase, prototype an interface or workflow, test assumptions, and often get to a functional first version before an engineer needs to step in. Jared and Gondola’s Creator and Client Partnerships Manager Jojo Hesketh have both merged their first-ever code contributions into the main codebase.

> “A product manager doesn’t need to stop at a written product requirement anymore. They can bring engineering a working prototype.”

—Jared Kleinstein, Founder and CEO, Gondola

One example is Programs, a tool Gondola built to help companies find creatives, review applicants, manage projects, and track budgets, with plans to help coordinate contracts and payments.

Jojo sponsored Programs and used Codex to prototype its workflows before handing them to engineers to refine and release. The team started with GPT‑5.4, did most of the work with GPT‑5.5, and used GPT‑6.1 for later features, optimizations, and bug fixes.

Jared estimates that Codex saved days, if not weeks, of development time and helped the team launch Programs with fewer bugs than if they had coded it by hand. “The Programs feature benefited from our ability to rapidly prototype, throw away things that didn’t work, and keep the things that did,” says Jared.



Gondola’s engineers use Codex through the command-line interface (CLI) and editor tools to accelerate implementation, and in GitHub to review pull requests. The company connects Codex to its repositories, development environments, and Slack, so product context can inform development. Engineers remain responsible for architecture, security, data handling, and production readiness.

## Building faster for a timely customer need

Before Codex, time-sensitive ideas might sit in a backlog awaiting engineering resources while the opportunity passed by. But this summer, Codex enabled Gondola to build and test a World Cup Creator Map while it was still timely.

The team used Codex to rapidly turn data it already held into an experience built for an immediate customer need, creating a map that allowed brands, teams, and agencies to find photographers and videographers in World Cup host cities.

Jojo also sponsored the Creator Map and built a fully working prototype with Codex. Engineers polished it for launch shortly afterward. Jared describes the build as “incredibly quick,” thanks to its small, self-contained scope and hard deadline. He believes both the Creator Map and Programs launched with fewer bugs and more polish than they would have without Codex.

## Running the business with a small team using ChatGPT

Building products is only part of running Gondola. The team also uses ChatGPT to prepare proposals, manage schedules, and find information across company systems, as well as to automate tasks.

Gondola used ChatGPT to build a daily report template that employees can use first thing in the morning to plan their day. It integrates Google Workspace, including Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, and Drive, as well as Asana, Slack, QuickBooks, weather information, and other sources to give them a comprehensive look at the day ahead.

Jared says preparing such a thorough report manually would take “hours and hours of work,” but it comes together quickly in the ChatGPT setup. A person still reviews consequential work before it’s sent externally or used to make a business decision.

## Creating more capacity to help creatives thrive

Since adopting Codex in early 2026, Gondola’s lead engineer has increased monthly shipping output by about 50%, measured in merged changes. Across the team, output is up about 25%, with no change in engineering headcount. The team is also shipping larger changes, while PR review time has held steady.

Gondola reports that company revenue has more than doubled year over year, with no added payroll costs or significant overhead. The company has also helped brands hire 2.5 times as many creators year over year.

> “OpenAI gives product people more ability to build, engineers more time for difficult engineering, and our business team more time to spend with customers, partners, and creatives.”

—Jared Kleinstein, Founder and CEO, Gondola

Looking ahead, Gondola wants AI to help complete more of the work that connects companies and creatives. For Programs, that could mean reducing the coordination involved in finding talent, managing budgets and approvals, handling contracts, and getting people paid.

Gondola aims to keep expanding what its small team can deliver to advance its founding mission: helping creatives get credit for their work and turn it into their next opportunity.

[Holiday Extras⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.holidayextras.com/) helps customers search, book and manage trips. For CEO Matthew Pack, becoming an AI-based travel technology business means changing how the whole organisation works: giving the people who understand customers and operations the ability to improve them directly.

Company-wide ChatGPT Enterprise access established the foundation. Codex extended it into building software, from customer-facing apps to internal systems. Pack builds with Codex himself, using that experience to understand what colleagues need and raise his expectations of what the business can achieve.

> “This isn’t about one or two people anymore. It’s about taking the entire team on the journey.”

—Matthew Pack, CEO, Holiday Extras

## Inside the rollout: rebuilding the app and the way it is made

Holiday Extras had spent years developing its [mobile apps⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.holidayextras.com/our-apps/). Major changes to its main app centred on an annual release. With Codex, it challenged itself to rethink the experience and how it was built.

Within two weeks, the team had a fully working rebuild, achieving development progress that previously would have taken over six months. Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation and formerly Head of Design, worked with engineers to translate his understanding of customers into software. Small, documented packages created reusable foundations, while engineers focused on architecture, APIs, security and development workflows.

The rebuilt app offered a more personal experience informed by customers’ bookings, trips and history. Codex enabled iOS and Android features to be developed together, bringing improvements to both platforms without Android following behind.

> “It’s not a question of can I build it anymore. It’s how I would build it.”

—Liam Thompson, VP of AI Innovation, Holiday Extras

## Results at a glance: better bookings and faster responses

- Higher conversion: open-to-book conversion on the main app increased 32.5% following the rebuild.
- Fewer errors: the main app’s error rate fell from 19% to 9%.
- More frequent improvements: the main app moved from an annual major release to weekly releases in the first month after the rebuild, each containing multiple new features.
- Faster iteration: Countdown moved from adding a feature roughly every six months to multiple additions a week.

*Conversion and error-rate results compare the previous and rebuilt main app across different periods.*

Faster development also gives customers more influence. When a Countdown customer complained about a missing list view, an agent prepared a fix. Liam Thompson approved it, the update was submitted and the customer changed their one-star review to five stars.

The same emphasis on acting on customer insight extends into operations. David Lee, Director of Innovation and Growth, describes an automated system that turns airport-transfer customer chats into actionable tickets, helping the team identify problems across its supplier network. Customer insight becomes work the team can act on.

> “So, you can build things more quickly. You can test them more quickly, and you can learn from them because it can understand the data.”

—Matthew Pack, CEO, Holiday Extras

## Putting business expertise to work

Matthew Pack describes giving everyone permission to try AI, then actively encouraging them to use it. That permission comes with guardrails. Employees have access and encouragement to experiment; engineers build the packages, security controls and workflows that make that experimentation practical.

David Lee sees the effect in an experienced accountant who rebuilt finance systems around his understanding of the business and feedback from colleagues. The opportunity reaches beyond learning to code: people can apply years of operational knowledge directly to the tools they use. Leadership’s role is to make that possible, support experimentation and help successful ideas spread.

## Why OpenAI: a partner in how the business develops

Holiday Extras values Codex’s ability to explore ideas, reason through complex problems, propose a plan and deliver independently. Liam Thompson describes being able to question an approach and receive suggestions throughout the work.

The wider partnership connects building with everyday work. ChatGPT Enterprise supports employees across the business, while OpenAI models power the app’s personalised experience. dots adds coordination and insight: Thompson recalls his dot proactively preparing a performance report after an app launch. David Lee values model quality and efficiency alongside the relationship behind the products.

> “I love how OpenAI thinks differently. I love how you are open to feedback as well. We have a fantastic two-way relationship.”

—David Lee, Director of Innovation and Growth, Holiday Extras

## What’s next: expanding what the business can pursue

Pack’s ambition is for more of Holiday Extras’ systems to be administered through AI, with employees directing the work and shaping the outcomes. The app rebuild demonstrates the potential: better booking performance, fewer errors and capacity to keep improving.

That gives Holiday Extras a new basis for deciding which opportunities to pursue across its products and markets. As more people can act on their expertise, Pack is asking the leadership team to reconsider the scale of its ambitions.

> “Our dreams are not hard enough, clearly. We need to go back and rethink what we’re capable of doing.”

—Matthew Pack, CEO, Holiday Extras

title: Stop Shipping LLM Settings That Only Win on Paper - Rohan Pandey & Balaji Varadarajan, DigitalOcean
body:
Most LLM serving "wins" come from turning up a single setting, and on production hardware that setting often has little to do with what your users actually get. Rohan Pandey and Balaji Varadarajan walk through the optimization agent DigitalOcean runs on its AMD MI355 inference servers: it proposes a vLLM and Kubernetes configuration, rolls it out, measures throughput under real latency targets, and either keeps the winner or safely restores the old setup. They share what four studies revealed, including a +4% "winner" that turned out to be run-to-run noise, and how they're extending the same agent to disaggregated prefill and decode serving.

title: Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
body:
[content type paper](/research/)published November 2026
Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
AuthorsLucas Monteiro Paes*, Natalie Mackraz*, Barry-John Theobald, Federico Danieli
Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
AuthorsLucas Monteiro Paes*, Natalie Mackraz*, Barry-John Theobald, Federico Danieli
Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of- alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. We characterize the information-theoretic limits of KL-regularized alignment by deriving the maximum achievable expected reward gain for a fixed KL-divergence budget. Our first result provides a closed-form expression for the optimal reward improvement, governed by a Jeffreys divergence term rather than the used in prior analyses. We further reformulate this expression as a covariance under the base model, yielding a practical estimator that predicts achievable alignment gains from base model samples alone. We extend our analysis to the proxy reward setting, showing that the gap between ideal and proxy alignment (reward hacking) grows with the magnitude of reward error and when the KL penalty factor decreases. We then prove that reward ensembling mitigates reward hacking, providing a theoretical justification for this technique used in practice. Empirically, we compute the KLâreward Pareto frontier for two tasks for LMs, safety and summarization, and show that best-of- closely approaches the theoretical limit, while PPO and GRPO remain substantially suboptimal. Our theoretical results shed light on several empirically observed phenomena in the alignment literature and suggest that algorithmic improvements are needed to achieve optimal alignment without high inference costs.
- * Equal contribution

title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
body:
Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
A new plugin with 17 skills and four connectors helps manufacturers draft quotes, quality reports, and supplier requests from the systems they already run.
Today we’re launching [Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab)](http://claude.com/solutions/manufacturing), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier.
Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they [enter data (opens in new tab)](https://manufacturingleadershipcouncil.com/survey-october/)manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first.
Skills built for manufacturers
The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include:
- Quoting a new job: An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release.
- Investigating a failed inspection: A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report.
- Diagnosing a breakdown: A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps.
- Sourcing from another supplier: A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back.
- Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion: An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo.
- Reporting on production: A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost.
These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time.
Connectors to manufacturing systems
Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business:
- Autodesk Fusion: Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model.
- Infor: Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor.
- Microsoft 365: Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes.
- Oracle NetSuite: Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote.
Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report.
Making changes in Infor with Claude
Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also [releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/directory/infor). With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude.
For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions.
Manufacturing teams stay in control
Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents.
Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the [Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-hardware-standard-research-preview), a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits.
How to get started
On Team or Enterprise plans, [install the plugin (opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/customize/plugins/id/45112ff2-6233-4954-b8ec-c448ef2d1e59%40anthropic-plugin-directory) and tell Claude, “Set us up.” Claude asks which systems the team uses, tests the connectors, and reports which skills can’t fully run yet.
To see the plugin at work, [register for our technical webinar (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/webinars/claude-for-manufacturing-put-your-plants-know-how-to-work) on November 17 at 11:00 a.m. ET. To talk through a company’s manufacturing systems, [contact our sales team (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/contact-sales).

title: Introducing Claude Meetings
body:
Introducing Claude Meetings
Add Claude to your video call and get the work started while you talk
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.
Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.
Claude also works with you live to build docs, [whiteboards (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.
Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.
What it looks like
Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.
When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.
Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in [claude.ai (opens in new tab)](http://claude.ai).
Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.
We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, Otter, and Plaud, so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.
Security and privacy
Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in [claude.ai (opens in new tab)](http://claude.ai) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.
By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.
Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.
When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.
Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.
Getting started
Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, [whiteboards, (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027.
Setup steps are in the [Help Center](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/18325154).

title: The Claude Tag guide for startups
body:
The Claude Tag guide for startups
How leading startups use Claude Tag to ship faster and scale operations
Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, [Claude Tag](https://claude.com/product/tag) (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.
For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.
We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.
| Company | On call | Thread to PR | Company brain | Self-serve data | Routine reporting |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kikoff | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| NavigateAI | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| Campfire | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Flagler Health | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Moritz | ● | ● | |||
| Orderful | ● | ● | ● | ● | |
| Valence | ● | ● | ● | ||
| Descript | ● | ● | ● |
But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden.
The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:
21
