Days to hours
In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag.
Top channels to tag Claude
The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start.
01 Claude on call
Example setups:
#on-call
#alerts-ci
#deploy-watch
#support-escalations
GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io
Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap
@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].
Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.
With Claude in the channel as [a first responder](https://claude.com/resources/articles/ai-ci-cd-on-call), the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.
At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.
Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel
Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:
#deploys
: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.#alerts-ci
: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.#alerts-sentry-backend
: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.#dog-fooding
: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.#support
: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.
Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.
NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context
NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.
Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.
With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.
“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.
02 Thread to PR
Example setups:
#quick-wins
#bug-bash
#product-feedback
#feature-requests
#ux-papercuts
#tech-debt
#design-polish
GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry
One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap
@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.
Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.
With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.
Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.
Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days
Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.
One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.
When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.
The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.
“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”
Valence: From feature request to rollout
Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.
In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.
03 Company brain
Example setups:
#ask-anything
#company-wiki
#product-questions
GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase
One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap
@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.
At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.
For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.
Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing
Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.
Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.
That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.
Campfire: Customer experience on demand
One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”
This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.
04 Self-serve data
Example setups:
#data-requests
#ask-revops
#metric-definitions
dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion
One question per thread, weekly pre-standup readout, launch and experiment readouts, pipeline failure triage, new question triage
@Claude remember for this channel: answer from our governed models and the definitions in [data skills repo]. If the data isn’t covered there, say it’s unvalidated instead of guessing. Lead with the answer, then give the number, what’s driving it, and any cav

title: J. Crew brings its signature approach to styling to life with Claude
body:
J. Crew brings its signature approach to styling to life with Claude
J.Crew's new Style Advisor uses Claude to offer a more personalized way to shop online, with complete looks instead of individual products.
Online, shopping usually happens one product at a time, so a customer who finds a sweater has to search again for the pants and shoes that go with it. To change that, J.Crew today launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on [JCrew.com (opens in new tab)](https://www.jcrew.com/) that helps customers shop by complete outfit. J.Crew’s team built it with [Claude Code (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) using multiple Claude models, from Fable to Haiku, each matched to the work it does best. It is available now for women’s and men’s styles in the U.S.
For more than 40 years, J.Crew’s own stylists have built complete looks by balancing proportion, color, and layering and by pairing pieces in unexpected ways. Style Advisor brings that expertise online. Customers describe what they need, such as an outfit for a beach wedding or a first job interview, and it answers with complete looks drawn from J.Crew’s own photo shoots. They can keep refining from there, so shopping becomes a visual conversation.
How it's built
J.Crew’s product team used [Claude Fable (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable) 5.1, Anthropic’s model for complex, open-ended work, to plan how Style Advisor should reason like a stylist, then built a working prototype with [Claude Opus (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/opus) 5.5 in Claude Code. J.Crew’s engineers took that prototype to production. In each conversation, [Claude Sonnet (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/sonnet) 5.5 acts as the stylist and decides each step of the response, while [Claude Haiku (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/haiku) 5.5 handles quick, focused tasks so Style Advisor answers quickly. Because every look comes from J.Crew’s stylists, its recommendations stay consistent with J.Crew’s styling point of view.
How customers use Style Advisor
- Shop complete outfits. Every recommendation starts from looks J.Crew stylists created for the brand's catalog shoots, and Style Advisor shows them in photos so customers see the full outfit.
- Build from a single piece. A customer can start with one item and get suggestions for the pieces that complete the look.
- Dress for the occasion. Customers can say where they're going, whether that's a vacation, a holiday party, or a wedding, and get recommendations for it.
- Get J.Crew's point of view. Style Advisor applies the same styling principles a J.Crew stylist would use in a store.
What's next
At launch, Style Advisor helps customers find new outfit ideas and shop with more confidence. Over time, J.Crew plans to make it more personal by tailoring suggestions to each customer's preferences and past purchases, and to bring it to more markets and product lines.
“As consumer expectations evolve and AI opens up new possibilities for retail, J.Crew is challenging the traditional model of online shopping, moving beyond individual product searches toward a more connected and inspiration-led experience,” said Libby Wadle, Chief Executive Officer of J.Crew Group. “For a long time, we’ve been thinking about how customers will want to shop in the future, and how we can lead that evolution rather than react to it. We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience. Through our work with Anthropic, we're bringing decades of J.Crew styling, merchandising and creative expertise together to help shape what’s next for customer behavior.”
“J.Crew has one of the most recognizable points of view in fashion, and its team used Claude to bring that expertise to customers in a new way,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic. “They used a frontier model to build the experience and faster, more efficient models to run it, so customers get quick answers that stay true to the brand’s styling.”
Start building with [Claude Code (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) today.

title: Operate Claude Managed Agents inside your security perimeter
body:
Operate Claude Managed Agents inside your security perimeter
Introducing self-hosted Claude Managed Agents. Now you can run agents in your own environment, whether that’s in your own cloud or on-premise. You host the agents, credentials, and session history, and choose where requests to Claude are sent.
[Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/self-hosted) is now available in private beta. Developers can build agents that work directly in their company's code and internal systems, and run those agents in their own environment.
Self-hosting is a new way to run [Managed Agents](https://claude.com/platform/claude-managed-agents), a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying autonomous agents. Managed Agents provides the agent harness, sandboxes, credential handling, and session history to get long-running agents into production.
Run your agent control plane in your own environment
We first launched Managed Agents as a hosted service on the Claude Platform, where Anthropic runs the infrastructure for you. For teams who needed their code to stay in their own environment, we added [self-hosted sandboxes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/self-hosted-sandboxes).
Since then, agents have become more capable and are taking on more critical work, like fixing broken builds, testing releases, triaging alerts, and working through your bug backlog. They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems. For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.
With self-hosted Managed Agents, every part of the service runs in your own cloud or on-premise, including the harness, sandboxes, credentials, and session history. You operate the Managed Agents server, its database, and the workers where agents run their shell and file tools. Model requests go where you choose, whether that's Anthropic directly, your cloud provider (Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry), or your own gateway. Your developers still build agents with the same core APIs as the hosted Managed Agents service.
Session history is stored in your own database. If your organization has [zero data retention (ZDR)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/api-and-data-retention#zero-data-retention-zdr-scope) in place with Anthropic, it applies to the requests sent to Claude in the same way as any other Messages API call.
Designed for agent security
When an agent runs unattended inside your code and systems, you can't rely on a person checking every step, so the limits have to be built into the system itself. That's why agent security starts with architecture, and why we designed Managed Agents around four principles. These principles apply whether Anthropic hosts everything, you host just the sandbox, or you host the whole service.
The brain and the hands are split
The harness (the brain) calls Claude, and the sandbox (the hands) is where the agent's code runs. They are kept separate by design. The agent's code runs in the sandbox, while the agent loop, session history, and vault secrets stay outside it. [Separating them](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) also means an agent doesn't depend on one sandbox surviving its whole run, sandboxes start only when a tool needs them, and session history lives outside the sandbox as an event log.
Credentials stay out of the sandbox
Vaults are designed to keep credentials out of the sandbox. For MCP tools and supported API calls, [a proxy outside the sandbox adds the credential to the request](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/vaults). With self-hosted Managed Agents, you can also store credentials in your own secrets manager.
Network access can be limited
You can limit each environment to [a list of allowed hosts](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/secure-deployment), and requests to any other host are blocked. For an agent that fixes broken builds, that list might be just your git host and your package registry. When you host the sandbox yourself, you set the same limits in your own firewall.
Every session leaves a full record
Managed Agents keeps a record of every step an agent took, including the tool calls it made and what came back. The record exports over [OpenTelemetry](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/opentelemetry), so you can send it to the monitoring tools you already use and review agent activity alongside the rest of your systems.
Get started
Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Contact your Anthropic account team to request access, or read the [docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/self-hosted) to learn more.

title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
body:
Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
Opus 5.5 is the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. Here's how it compares with our other models, and how to get the most from it for knowledge work.
Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks.
If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which [can then offset much of its higher price per token](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence).
Here's how the current models compare:
| Model | Use it for | Price per million tokens (input / output)* | Relative speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | Quick lookups and high-volume work where speed matters most | $0.10 / $0.50 | Fastest |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Quick, well-scoped tasks, and polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets from a clear brief | $2 / $10 | Fast |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | Most knowledge work: research, analysis, and finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets that need judgment | $4 / $20 | Moderate |
| Claude Fable 5.2 | The most ambitious, open-ended technical work, in fields like coding, finance, and the sciences | $8 / $40 | Moderate |
*Prices are for usage billed by the token ([model comparison](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/opus-5-5/overview)). Haiku 5.5's prices apply to prompts up to 100k tokens, and longer prompts cost $0.50 / $2.50. On Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, higher-priced models use your limits faster. Pro plans and standard seats on Team and seat-based Enterprise plans don’t include Fable 5.2 in their limits outside limited-time launch offers, so it runs on usage credits.
[Haiku 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-haiku-5-5) is our fastest and least expensive model, built for quick lookups and high-volume work like writing summaries and sorting data. This is our first Haiku model with effort controls, so you can ask for a more careful pass before switching to a larger model. It’s best suited to short, narrowly scoped tasks. For longer analysis, switch to Opus 5.5.
[Sonnet 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5) is faster and cheaper than Opus 5.5 for well-scoped tasks that have a clear brief. This could be asking Claude to turn finished notes into a polished document, or to build a deck using a slide template. At higher-effort settings, however, cost per task with Sonnet 5.5 gets close to Opus 5.5, so if you find yourself pushing Sonnet to Extra high or Max effort, consider switching to Opus 5.5.
[Opus 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5) is built for complex work that needs careful judgment, like research, financial analysis, and producing finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets. We share details on why we recommend Opus 5.5 for daily knowledge work later.
[Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) is best for your most demanding reasoning and long-running work, like deep multi-step research or coding that you can hand off to a large team of subagents that run for hours. For most knowledge work, start with Opus 5.5 and move to Fable 5.2 when a project’s scope and complexity calls for it. Fable 5.2 is available on all paid plans, though [how it draws on your usage](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15424964-claude-fable-models-on-your-plan) depends on your plan.
Whichever model you're on, if Claude didn’t do as well as you expected, try a higher effort first before moving up a model. If it had the context, clearly tried, and still got it wrong, move up a model.
Opus 5.5 does its best work on documents, research, finance, and charts
Opus 5.5 follows instructions precisely and stays in scope, so the spreadsheets, slides, and documents it produces often need little editing. It's careful with figures and sources, too. In one internal research test, Opus 5.5 wrote reports on a company's quarterly performance using only a saved snapshot of the web, in which the company’s earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against the pages in that snapshot, under a condition that the report would fail if even a single figure or quote was invented. Across effort settings, 16 of its 18 reports passed.
Its writing is clearer than that of earlier models, too. Opus 5.5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you. That also makes its work easier to check, which we count as a safety benefit as well as a practical one.
John Ruelas, a staff software engineer at Ramp, [said](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5): “It writes like a good colleague, and follows our writing rules. A design spec came out usable with very minimal edits, and when it rewrote one of our prompts I preferred its version to my own.”
Financial analysis is another strength. Opus 5.5 reads dense filings, financial models, and charts accurately and keeps track of context across a whole project or deal. In another internal test, it analyzed a proposed merger between two fictional HR software companies, building a financial model in Excel and then turning it into an executive presentation on whether the deal made sense at its price. It finished in 63 minutes, compared with 93 for Opus 5 on the same task, at half the cost, with a more thorough model, and an easier-to-read presentation.
Frank Corrao, who leads central equity quant research engineering at investment firm Walleye Capital, [said](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5) that at higher effort settings, Opus 5.5 “detected that the minute indexing in our own instructions was off by one and corrected for it, noting that this would cost it points with the grader. It was right, and no model we’ve tested had caught and acted on that before.”
Opus 5.5 is our best Opus model for vision. It reads dense documents, charts, screenshots, and diagrams accurately, which makes it reliable for pulling data out of documents. Even at its lowest effort setting, it read values off dense charts more accurately than Opus 5 did at its highest.
Getting more out of Opus 5.5
Each new model is a reason to retest what you hand to Claude and to drop prompting habits built for older models.
Try these tasks first
- Ask for a finished file. If you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the spreadsheet or document rather than an outline to build from. More often than not, Opus 5.5 can get from your request to the finished file in one pass.
- Have it check long documents. Give it a long plan, report, or deck and ask it to find mistakes and inconsistencies. Opus 5.5 catches details that are easy to miss in long documents, such as a chart in a deck that doesn’t match its source data.
- Hand it a research question. Ask a question without a set answer and have it pull sources together, work through long documents, and write up what it finds as a memo, report, or deck.
- Try visual work. Its vision gains carry over to design, so try it for prototyping an interface, building a website, or illustrating a concept.
Change these prompting habits
- Connect Claude to your work files and systems. This is one of the most useful steps for getting output that fits your work, because when Claude can reach your files and systems through connectors, it can go get what a task needs instead of working only from what you paste in. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner has to turn a connector on before members can use it.
- Say what done looks like in your first message. Instead of prompting Claude with instructions one at a time, describe your goal, the finished output, and when you want it to stop and ask. Opus 5.5 carries long, multipart work through to the end better than Opus 5 did.
- Delete “think hard” and “think carefully.” Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5, and it decides how much to think based on your request and the effort level. In our testing, removing those lines made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.
- Start at Medium effort. Medium is the default for Opus 5.5, and on our coding and knowledge-work evaluations, Opus 5.5 at Medium matched or beat Opus 5 at High. Higher settings think longer and cost more without always producing better work, so move up to High when Medium stalls. To change the setting, click the model name next to the send button and choose Effort.
- Attach the chart instead of retyping it. Share the chart, screenshot, or diagram itself rather than copying its numbers into the prompt. Workarounds built for earlier models, like transcribing a chart's values, may no longer be needed.
- Name the styles you don't want. For design work, a general instruction like “avoid a generic look” tends to swap one default style for another. Naming specific patterns to avoid, such as a cream background or pill-shaped buttons, works better.
- Give it your house style. Paste your brand or writing guidelines into the request, or point Claude to your best existing decks, for example in a Google Drive folder it can reach through a connector, and ask it to match them. Expect a few rounds before it's exactly right.
The effort finding held for early testers, too. Zimu Li, Member of Technical Staff at Factory, [said](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5), “Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model we’d default to at medium effort. In our testing it matched Opus 5 on high effort, while using 20 to 25% fewer output tokens.”
Testing Opus 5.5 on a demo project
Here's what all this looks like on one project we worked through in a demo. At a hypothetical retail company, revenue growth had slowed over the past year, leadership had four theories about why, and an analyst had a folder of material: spreadsheets of sales by store, PDFs from the latest leadership off-site, and other files. With Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, the prompt read, roughly:
Growth slowed a lot this year. Leadership has a couple of theories about why; they're in [my manager's] note. Everything I have is in the uploaded folder. Please test each of the four theories against the data and tell me which ones hold up.
The prompt doesn't tell Claude to think hard, and it doesn't say which file to check for which theory. It states the goal and what the final output looks like, and leaves the approach to Claude.
Claude found that the data didn't support any of the four theories, though one couldn't be fully ruled out. It then proposed an explanation that nobody had raised: new stores had opened too close to existing ones and were drawing sales away from them. The pattern was a little unclear with the stores listed by city, and clear once they were filtered by proximity to a new store. Claude backed the finding with a regression of the sales impact against that distance.
Next, Claude turned the analysis into a document that holds charts and interactive elements alongside text, including a slider showing how sales change with the distance between a new store and an existing one. A teammate reviewed the doc at the same time.
The manager then asked Claude to turn the doc into board slides that opened with the answer. For teammates who don't use Claude, docs export to Word, PDF, or Google Docs, and decks export to PowerPoint, PDF, or Google Slides.
To see the whole project, including the Q&A, [watch the Opus 5.5 for Work session on demand](https://claude.com/resources/webinars/opus-5-5-for-work).
Try Opus 5.5 on your own work
Pick something you'd normally split across several requests, like a research memo, a variance analysis, or a deck built from an existing doc. Giv

title: Welcoming Jaya Baloo as Cohere's First CISO
body:
As AI becomes foundational infrastructure for governments and enterprises, trust is becoming just as important as capability. Organizations aren't simply evaluating model performance, they're asking whether the systems they deploy can be trusted with their most sensitive data, critical operations, and strategic assets.
Today, we're excited to welcome Jaya Baloo, co-founder of AISLE and one of the world's foremost cybersecurity leaders, to Cohere as our first Chief Information Security Officer (CISO). In this role, Jaya will help advance our mission to build the world's most trusted Sovereign AI platform.
Security is the defining challenge of enterprise AI
Organizations around the world are moving AI from pilots into production. As they do, security, governance, and compliance are becoming central requirements for deployment.
The challenge is especially acute for governments, critical infrastructure operators, and highly regulated enterprises. These organizations need AI that can operate within their own environments, meet strict security requirements, and remain under their control.
At Cohere, we've long believed that successful AI deployment requires more than powerful models. It requires a complete platform that combines frontier AI capabilities with enterprise-grade infrastructure, governance, security, and deployment flexibility. That's why we're investing deeply in the people and technologies that help organizations deploy AI with confidence. Bringing Jaya to Cohere is an important step in that journey.
A global leader in cybersecurity
Over the course of her career, Jaya has established herself as one of the most respected voices in cybersecurity. She brings more than two decades of experience protecting critical systems and advising organizations operating in some of the world's most demanding security environments.
She has held senior leadership roles at some of the world's leading technology and telecommunications organizations. Before co-founding AISLE, she served as CISO at Rapid7, Avast, and KPN Telecom. She has also advised organizations including the World Economic Forum and Europol's European Cybercrime Centre (EC3).
Her work spans cyber resilience, critical infrastructure security, vulnerability management, and quantum readiness, fields that are becoming increasingly important as agentic AI systems grow more capable and more deeply integrated into essential services.
Why AISLE
Jaya joins Cohere from AISLE, the AI-native cybersecurity company she co-founded alongside Ondrej Vlcek and Stanislav Fort. AISLE was created to address one of cybersecurity's most persistent challenges: organizations can identify vulnerabilities, but often struggle to remediate them at the speed required to stay ahead of attackers.
To solve this problem, AISLE developed autonomous AI systems capable of discovering, validating, and helping remediate previously unknown vulnerabilities in production software. In its first year out of stealth, the company identified more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities across more than 100 codebases, demonstrating the growing potential of AI-native approaches to cybersecurity.
That work reflects a broader shift taking place across both AI and cybersecurity. As systems become more complex, organizations need intelligent technologies that can help them operate securely at scale.
Building a More Trusted AI Platform
At Cohere, our mission is to help organizations deploy AI on their own terms. That means giving customers the flexibility to run AI wherever their data lives while maintaining the security, governance, and control their operations demand. Jaya's appointment reinforces our commitment to that vision.
"Organizations are entering a new era where AI and cybersecurity are becoming increasingly interconnected," said Jaya Baloo. "As AI becomes part of critical infrastructure, security and trust need to be built in from the start, not added later. I'm excited to join Cohere and help advance a future where organizations can confidently deploy AI while maintaining the control, resilience, and security they require."
As CISO, she will help shape Cohere's security strategy as we continue building a platform that combines frontier AI models, agentic applications, secure deployment infrastructure, and advanced cybersecurity capabilities. Her experience at the forefront of cybersecurity will help ensure trust remains at the core of everything we build.
We're thrilled to welcome Jaya to Cohere and look forward to building the future of trusted, sovereign AI together.

title: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
body:
Updated
[
](#the-definitive-fine-tuning-guide-for-3d-generation-models)
The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/3d-lora-finetuning.md)
TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can
[use our scripts]with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself[with this repository]. If you want to learn more, we go through[how the script works]. Let’s go!
[
](#introduction)
Introduction
3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as [GLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GlTF) and [PLY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLY_(file_format)). There are also [many representations](https://huggingface.co/spaces/suvadityamuk/3d-representations-guide), such as [neural radiance fields (NeRFs)](https://www.matthewtancik.com/nerf) and [3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_splatting). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.
[TRELLIS](https://huggingface.co/papers/2412.01506) introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.
The same team then released [TRELLIS.2](https://huggingface.co/papers/2512.14692), which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.
[
](#what-we-want-to-improve)
What we want to improve
A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.
Our goal is to use the [Google Scanned Objects (GSO)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/hugging-3d/google-scanned-objects) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.
Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.
[
](#what-will-we-use)
What will we use?
[
](#lora)
LoRA
LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our [LoRA guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/package_reference/lora).
[
](#hugging-face-jobs)
Hugging Face Jobs
Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:
- A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain
[from here](https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens/new) - Your Hugging Face account must have
[access to DINOv3](https://huggingface.co/collections/facebook/dinov3), because DINOv3 is a gated model - If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start.
[
](#how-trellis2-works)
How TRELLIS.2 works
Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.
TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.
[
](#encoding-the-input-image)
Encoding the input image
First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.
[
](#sparse-structure-generation-sparse-structure-flow)
Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow)
The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.
[
](#o-voxel-and-structured-latents)
O-Voxel and Structured Latents
O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.
Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.
[
](#geometry-generation-shape-flow)
Geometry Generation (Shape Flow)
The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.
We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.
[
](#material-generation--mesh-creation)
Material Generation + Mesh Creation
In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.
Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.
[
](#planning)
Planning
[
](#which-components-to-fine-tune)
Which components to fine-tune
We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.
Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.
If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.
[
](#why-use-lora)
Why use LoRA
Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.
[
](#what-youll-run)
What you’ll run
A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on [Jobs](https://hf.co/jobs) or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.
To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:
- Give the containers access to your data.
- Set the parameters for your task.
- Run the preprocessing container.
- Run the fine-tuning container.
Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.
[
](#experiment-overview)
Experiment overview
We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:
- Prepare the data. Convert GLB or OBJ meshes into the latent representations TRELLIS.2 uses for training, and render the input images.
- Train the adapters. Run one job for each DiT, with the prepared dataset and a LoRA configuration.
- Explain the code. Examine how the containers load the data, add adapters, and train the models.
We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.
[
](#walkthrough)
Walkthrough
[
](#running-on-hugging-face-jobs)
Running on Hugging Face Jobs
[
](#preprocessing)
Preprocessing
The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the [preprocessing pipeline](https://github.com/microsoft/TRELLIS.2/blob/main/data_toolkit/README.md). See the [footwear dataset here](https://huggingface.co/datasets/suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents) for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in [this companion repository](https://github.com/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning/blob/master/preprocess.py).
export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx
# Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username
hf jobs run -d --flavor a100-large --timeout 6h --secrets HF_TOKEN \
cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-prep:latest \
trellis2-prep \
--meshes your-username/my-meshes \
--push-to your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \
--private --holdout 0.05 \
--views 16 --workers 8
For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:
| flag | meaning |
|---|---|
-d |
Detach: print the job ID and URL, then return. To follow the job, run hf jobs logs -f <id> |
--flavor a100-large |
The hardware. We use a100-large (80 GB). To see all options, run hf jobs hardware |
--timeout 6h |
The job stops after this time. Both commands resume. Preprocessing skips finished objects. Training continues from the newest checkpoint in --push-to |
--secrets HF_TOKEN |
Send your token (from HF_TOKEN or hf auth login) to the job as an encrypted environment variable. The token is not written into the image |
cr.hf.co/...:latest |
The image to run. All text after it is the command that runs in the container |
This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can [find documented over here](https://github.com/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning#1-preprocess-trellis2-prep). The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in [this section](#preprocessing-into-latents) later.
[
](#lora-fine-tuning)
LoRA Fine-tuning
The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.
We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes

title: ChatGPT Ads increases its market presence in 44 countries
body:
Final URL: https://openai.com/ads/blog/chatgpt-ads-increases-its-market-presence/

Markdown Content:
OpenAI

Starting today, brands and agencies in 44 countries can contract, pay and get local support for ChatGTP Ads through Aleph, OpenAI’s exclusive reseller. Aleph offers local advertisers in these countries an additional buying option alongside our existing [global technology partners⁠](https://openai.com/index/new-ways-to-buy-chatgpt-ads/) and our self-service [ChatGPT Ads Manager⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/).

The reseller agreement covers advertisers based in the following 44 markets:

*   Latin America (14): Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico and Uruguay
*   Europe and Central Asia (16): Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine* and Uzbekistan
*   Middle East and Africa (10): Egypt, Kenya, Kuwait, Morocco, Nigeria, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates
*   Asia-Pacific (4): Bangladesh, Cambodia, Hong Kong* and Sri Lanka

Today’s announcement does not impact any advertisers ability to target any of these countries in a campaign. Advertisers globally can continue to create and run campaigns targeting any country where [ChatGPT Ads are available⁠(opens in a new window)](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001245-ads-manager-availability#ads-manager-availability).

Advertisers and agencies in these markets who are interested in buying ChatGPT Ads from a local entity or local salesforce, can [contact Aleph’s local teams⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alephdigital.com/OpenAi) to learn more. Aleph offers local contracting and invoicing in local currency, payment terms, onboarding, campaign support and training.

Advertisers and agencies interested in buying ads directly can continue to buy through Ads Manager. Advertisers and agencies interested in buying through global technology partners in these markets can continue to do so.

Over one hundred thousand marketers have advertised on ChatGPT, and we continue to improve the platform based on what we learn from people and businesses. Today’s announcement represents additional local ways to purchase ChatGPT Ads across these markets.

We’ve made significant progress in ten months, but we are still early in building the full potential of ChatGPT Ads. As we expand into new markets, and develop new formats, optimization tools, and measurement solutions, we’ll remain focused on broadening access to powerful AI, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT, and helping businesses achieve their goals.

## Author

OpenAI

*OpenAI models and ChatGPT are not available to users in mainland China or Hong Kong, so ChatGPT Ads are not available in-market. Businesses based in these markets can advertise to ChatGPT users in markets where Ads are available through authorized advertising partners, subject to applicable eligibility requirements.

# Supporting research on AI and children’s safety

OpenAI pledges $2 million as part of a global effort to better understand AI’s impact on children and support their safety and wellbeing.

Loading…

Share

Earlier this week at the Paris Peace Forum, OpenAI signed the [Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children⁠(opens in a new window)](https://parispeaceforum.org/app/uploads/2026/11/charter-of-engagement-for-safer-ai-for-children.pdf) and committed $2 million to support the scientific research network under the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI.

This builds on [our call for global standards on youth AI safety](https://openai.com/index/advancing-youth-safety-and-opportunity-through-global-leadership/), and sustained collaboration among governments, researchers, civil society and industry to translate shared evidence into practical safeguards.

Our contribution supports shared measurement work: developing tools researchers can use to better understand and measure AI’s risks and opportunities for children, helping inform safer products and better policy.

The charter sets out shared principles for safe, age-appropriate AI, alongside a research programme and safeguards for its independence. Research teams retain control over their conclusions, and findings will be published, including negative or inconclusive results.

This work will help build the evidence needed to support the benefits of AI for young people while addressing risks to their safety and development. It builds on our support for comprehensive youth AI safety legislation that establishes strong, enforceable protections while preserving access to tools for learning, creativity and opportunity. Such frameworks should include age-appropriate safeguards by default, tools for parents, regular risk assessments and mitigation, and meaningful accountability. We look forward to engaging with European policymakers as the EU Kids Act develops, and with partners around the world to advance stronger protections and opportunities for young people.

# Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

[Gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.gtlaw.com.au/) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

## Sam, what is Gilbert + Tobin trying to achieve with AI?

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

> *“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”*

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You describe Gilbert + Tobin’s journey in three phases: experimentation, personal productivity, and organisational productivity. How did the firm get started?

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

## You’ve noticed that adoption is unusually high for your firm, with 87% active usage among enabled ChatGPT users, more than twice the rate Gilbert + Tobin typically sees for other tools. How did leadership shape that culture?

Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

> *“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”*

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You have made ChatGPT central to your own work. What have you learned from what you’ve built?

To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins)using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

## What advice would you give other CEOs beginning this journey?

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.

**Find out more about Gilbert + Tobin’s work with OpenAI through the case study** [**here**](https://openai.com/index/gilbert-tobin/)**.**

title: Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
body:
Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the [Gemini API](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/decisions-api) in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/gemini-decisions-api-playground?fullscreenApplet=true).
The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.
Strong performance and calibration
On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.
Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.
Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass
Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.
You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:
- noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
- choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
- score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.
The input
field uses the same Content
block format as the [Interactions API](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/interactions-overview). Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:
from google import genai
client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"})
result = client.decisions.create(
model="gemini-decision-1",
input=[{
"type": "image",
"uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg",
"mime_type": "image/jpeg",
},
{
"type": "text",
"text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.",
},
],
questions={
"has_spill": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?",
},
"next_action": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?",
"criteria": {
"wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.",
"dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.",
"ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.",
},
},
"severity": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.",
"criteria": [
"Clean and ready.",
"Minor localized spill.",
"Major spill or safety hazard.",
],
},
},
)
How teams are building with the Decisions API
Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:
- Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks.
- Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new
[rapid canvas experiment in Stitch](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/rapid)uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish. - Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency.
- Safety layer for MCP tools in Search: Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope.
Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).
Start building today
Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/gemini-decisions-api-playground?fullscreenApplet=true) for prototyping. Your shared input
is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.
You can start building today by grabbing an API key in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/api-keys), trying our [Doorstep Parcels](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/doorstep-parcels-qa?fullscreenApplet=true), [Speed Sketch](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/speed-sketch?fullscreenApplet=true), and [Find the Zoo Keeper](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/find-the-zoo-keeper?fullscreenApplet=true) demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the [Decisions API documentation](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/decisions-api).
Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/google/gemini-decision-1), [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/providers/google), [Vercel](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/ai-sdk-providers/google), [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/gemini), [Pydantic AI](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/google/), [Pipecat](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/classifiers/google), [LiveKit](https://docs.livekit.io/agents/integrations/google/), and [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/) alongside the google-genai
SDKs, with support [coming soon](https://forms.gle/NFt1W6pL1gCY9FGM8) to Gemini in Google Cloud.

title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
body:
11th November 2026 - Link Blog
[Anthropic's IPO roadshow video](https://ipo.anthropic.com/us/#roadshow-video). Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.
The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's [one that I extracted](https://gist.github.com/simonw/9806757fe8acec6221cb0a5cce4d720d) using MacWhisper. Highlights below:
We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]
As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]
The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.
Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.
We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their [postmortem of three recent issues](https://www.anthropic.com/research/a-postmortem-of-three-recent-issues), where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.
