title: From custom infrastructure to hosted agents
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/from-custom-infrastructure-to-hosted-agents/

Published Time: 2026-11-11T15:07:19+00:00

Markdown Content:
Clinical research rarely ends with the questions defined in a trial protocol. Medical experts also explore the data from new angles: testing a hypothesis, comparing patient populations, visualizing a trend, or identifying a promising direction for further research.

As part of a [forward-deployed engineering](https://commandline.microsoft.com/thinking-about-the-evolution-of-forward-deployed-engineers-over-the-last-24-months/) engagement, a joint Microsoft and [Novo Nordisk](https://www.novonordisk.com/) development team built an agent that helps medical experts perform this kind of secondary analysis of clinical trial data. We described the original project in a [Microsoft customer story](https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/26569-novo-nordisk-as-azure). More recently, we reimplemented the solution as a [hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents).

The move gave us a simpler operating model, stronger session isolation, and a direct path into Foundry’s tracing, evaluation, experimentation, optimization, and governance capabilities. It also taught us practical lessons about infrastructure planning, observability, and preserving the learning loop that already made the agent better over time.

Here’s what changed, what we measured, and what we would recommend to teams making a similar move.

## An agent for questions that don’t have a fixed workflow

Secondary analysis of clinical data is a great task for an agent because the execution path depends heavily on the question. The agent interprets the request, inspects the available data, writes and executes analysis code, examines the result, and often revises its approach before returning a summary and visualization.

> “Rearchitecting the solution helped us focus on what matters: enabling our medical experts to explore clinical data and generate insights that support pharmaceutical development. With managed scaling and isolated analysis sessions, we could deliver a reliable, secure agentic experience to thousands of researchers faster without building and operating all the infrastructure ourselves.”

– Sid Prabhu, Senior Director, Head of FounData AI Application, Novo

This isn’t just attaching a chat interface to a single API. The agent needs a reasoning loop, access to domain-specific skills, and tools for working with data. In our implementation, code execution is the central tool. The agent can generate analysis code and visualizations inside a controlled environment while the surrounding application manages the conversation and presents the result to the user.

Our first production architecture ran the agent in [Azure Container Apps](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/container-apps). We used PostgreSQL for conversation storage and Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions for sandboxed code execution. That architecture gave us explicit control over every component, and it proved the value of the use case.

It also meant that our team owned much of the platform around the agent: container scaling, session lifecycle, conversation persistence, execution isolation, networking, telemetry, and the integration among them. Foundry hosted agents offered a simpler division of responsibility.

## Moving the runtime boundary into Foundry

A hosted agent is our code, packaged as a container, running on infrastructure managed by [Foundry Agent Service](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/ai-foundry/agent-service). We retain control of the orchestration logic, models, tools, and runtime behavior. Foundry manages the endpoint, agent identity, session compute, state persistence, scaling, and lifecycle around it.

At runtime, each session gets its own VM-isolated sandbox. Foundry provisions compute on demand, keeps it active while the session is in use, and de-provisions it after the configured idle period. Session files can persist and be restored when the session resumes. Scaling follows active sessions rather than a replica count that we have to predict and configure.

For Novo’s workload, that model aligned well with the unit of work we were building for: one expert conducting one analysis session. It also changed the architecture in four important ways:

1.   **Scaling became session-native.** We no longer needed to connect application-level session creation to a separately scaled pool of execution environments. The platform owns that lifecycle.
2.   **Isolation became the default unit of execution.** Each session runs in a VM-isolated sandbox rather than sharing a process or general-purpose application container with other sessions. That matters when the workload includes model-generated code operating on sensitive clinical data.
3.   **Network isolation became part of the service architecture.** Foundry Agent Service supports private networking, including virtual network integration and private access to dependent Azure resources. This lets us design controls for both ingress and egress around the agent environment. Those controls are especially important for data that must remain inside an approved network boundary.
4.   **The agent joined a broader development lifecycle.** Traces, evaluations, experiments, monitoring, and optimization can now be connected through the same platform. [Microsoft Agent 365 integration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/agent-365-integration) also provides a path to enterprise inventory, identity, access control, and lifecycle governance.

Using Foundry hosted agents didn’tt remove our responsibility for security or quality. We still had to define access controls, minimize and protect telemetry, test the agent for our use case, and review every system it can call. What changed is that several controls we previously assembled ourselves are now platform capabilities we can configure and operate consistently.

> “For us, agent quality is paramount and must be measurable. We can now connect tracing and evaluation, so we can diagnose failures, measure quality against expert-validated answers, and continuously improve the agent. Data protection is equally fundamental: session isolation and private networking provide key controls. Together, these capabilities give us a more systematic way to keep improving the agent based on our in-house intelligence while leveraging our existing strong data controls.”

– Rasmus S Andersen, Associate Director, Products and AI, FounData, Novo

## Lessons learned

Here are the top lessons we learned during this project—and some practical advice for your own hosted agents projects in Foundry:

### Lesson 1: Treat infrastructure choices as product decisions

Private networking should be an early architecture decision, not a production hardening task left until the end.

Hosted agents consume network capacity according to sessions. The Foundry account, its projects, hosted agents, concurrent sessions, and agent revisions all contribute to IP usage. Because the assigned subnet is an immutable reference at the account level, an undersized range can turn a capacity adjustment into a broader infrastructure migration.

Our advice is to estimate peak concurrent sessions across the account, include headroom for deployments and growth, and involve the network team before creating the Foundry resource. The current [networking guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/networking-options) recommends a /24 subnet for production hosted agent deployments and documents /27 as the supported minimum for smaller deployments.

We used Azure Verified Modules as the foundation for repeatable environments. That gave us a strong starting point, but infrastructure as code doesn’t remove the need to inspect generated dependencies. Throughput for resources like Azure Cosmos DB should reflect expected concurrency and data access patterns. Where a setting requires an operational adjustment, capture it in the deployment process or operator runbook rather than leaving it as unwritten production knowledge.

Subnet sizing, database throughput, private endpoints, DNS, and concurrency aren’t separate infrastructure details. Together, they shape the scale ceiling and reliability of the product.

### Lesson 2: Make traces easy to navigate

Foundry tracing uses OpenTelemetry and stores telemetry in Azure Monitor Application Insights. It can capture user inputs, agent outputs, model calls, tool activity, token usage, and latency. That gives us the raw material to understand both reliability and agent behavior.

During the migration, we sent agent traces to both Application Insights and Langfuse. Keeping the existing telemetry path available gave the team continuity while we connected the agent to Foundry’s observability capabilities.

An engineer needs to move quickly from a reported problem to the relevant interaction: what the user asked, what the agent returned, how many operations the run produced, how long it took, and how many tokens it consumed. Stable user, session, conversation, agent-version, and trace identifiers make those views searchable and connect activity across the frontend, backend, agent, and tools.

Be equally deliberate about what not to record. [Foundry’s tracing guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/observability/concepts/trace-agent-concept) notes that traces can include prompts, outputs, tool arguments, and tool results. For clinical workloads, telemetry needs the same access control, minimization, redaction, and retention discipline as other sensitive production data.

### Lesson 3: Preserve the learning loop during migration

We kept the backend contracts stable, which made the migration significantly easier. Our evaluation framework could call the Foundry-hosted implementation through the same interface it used before, so moving the runtime didn’t require us to rebuild the quality system around it.

We could continue to run the same evaluation set against the agent and apply the same graders to its output. Those graders included comparisons with golden answers supplied by subject matter experts. The resulting scores gave us a baseline for the migration, guarded against regressions, and pointed to areas where changes to instructions, tools, or orchestration improved the system.

This is where the broader Foundry lifecycle becomes especially useful. Traces explain what happened in a run. Evaluations measure the result. Experiments compare alternatives. Optimization turns that evidence into candidate improvements. Bringing those capabilities closer together creates a shorter path from a production observation to a tested change.

**CONTINUOUS LEARNING LOOP**

**01 / TRACE****02 / EVALUATE****03 / EXPERIMENT****04 / OPTIMIZE**

  
Keep contracts stable. Run the same evaluation set and SME-backed graders, compare versions, then turn the evidence into tested improvements.

## The takeaway

Our original architecture gave Novo a working agent for a valuable and demanding research scenario. Moving it to hosted agents let us keep control of the agent logic while transferring more of the undifferentiated runtime work to Foundry. The result is not only a different place to run a container. It’s a cleaner platform boundary: isolated compute per session, managed scaling and identity, private networking, durable state, and an integrated path from tracing to evaluation and optimization.

For teams deciding how to take an agent from prototype to production, that boundary is worth evaluating early. Build the part that makes your agent distinct. Let the platform carry more of what every production agent needs.

title: AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
body:
AlphaGenome 2: Deciphering how cells read DNA to better understand disease
Our next-generation DNA sequence model bridges single-cell biology and human genetics, predicting how genetic variants affect hundreds of human cell types.
Today, we are announcing AlphaGenome 2, our next-generation model that predicts how DNA sequences and their variations impact specific human cell types, giving scientists a powerful new tool to uncover the cellular drivers of disease.
Cells are the building blocks of life. Every cell in our body carries the same DNA blueprint, yet each cell type and stateâlike a heart muscle cell or an immune cell fighting an infectionâswitches different genes on or off to do its job. Global efforts like the Human Cell Atlas are mapping this gene expression for millions of cells, but it is still an unsolved challenge to predict how subtle DNA variations affect this expression in cells, which is a key driver of human traits and disease.
Last year, we launched [AlphaGenome](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-ai-for-better-understanding-the-genome/) to predict how DNA variants affect molecular activity across broad tissues. We expanded its reach with [AlphaGenome Atlas](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-atlas-a-predictive-map-of-every-possible-dna-letter-change-in-the-human-genome/), a platform containing predictions for all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome. These tools help researchers prioritize and interpret variant effects, driving discoveries in rare diseases, complex traits, and fundamental biology.
By zooming in from broad tissue averages to individual cell types and cell states, and redesigning the modelâs architecture, [AlphaGenome 2](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/DeepMind.com/Blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/alphagenome-2.pdf) represents a step-change improvement in variant predictive performance. Importantly, it allows researchers to predict variant effects in disease-relevant cells that would be missed in broad-tissue models, as well as predictions for cell and disease states that the model hasnât seen before.
AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that change gene expression in cells, compared to our previous state-of-the-art model. Trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues, the model turns static cell atlases into a predictive engine for human genetics. AlphaGenome 2 is available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API, and in private preview for commercial research.
Redesigning AlphaGenome for specific cell types
The first AlphaGenome model took a million-letter DNA sequence and predicted properties across thousands of experiments from many tissues all at once. While efficient, this parallel approach spread the modelâs capacity thin and made it hard to capture subtle differences between closely related cell types.
To improve this, we fundamentally redesigned how cell types are treated by the model. Instead of predicting in parallel, AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional model that predicts DNA effects for one condition - defined as a tissue, cell type or state - at a time. Alongside the million-letter DNA sequence, it uses the target biological condition as input at every stage of its architecture. This allows it to learn how the same stretch of DNA is read differently across cell types.
A conditional model also allows cross-modality imputation, enabling AlphaGenome 2 to predict missing experimental data. The model separates a cellâs biological state from its outputs, so if a scientist inputs just one measurement, like single-cell gene activity, AlphaGenome 2 can then predict unmeasured properties, such as chromatin accessibility. This can then help researchers prioritize which experiments to do next.
We trained AlphaGenome 2 on both bulk and single-cell data from human and mouse samples, including over 107 million individual cell profiles. Moving beyond the bulk tissue averages of the original model, AlphaGenome 2 can resolve activity inside specialized cellsâsuch as distinct heart muscle or blood immune cellsâto help uncover crucial DNA variants that act only in specific cell types.
The model predicts the same core experimental readouts of DNA function as AlphaGenome â such as gene expression, histone modifications and chromatin accessibility â but also DNA methylation, a widely requested readout.
State-of-the-art cell-type predictions and variant recall
AlphaGenome 2 is significantly better at predicting gene regulation in specific cells, helping researchers pinpoint disease-relevant variants.
- Improved cell type specificity On genome regions outside its training data, AlphaGenome 2 explains significantly more of how gene expression differs across cell types within a tissueâtracking continuous changes in gene expression, such as when human blood stem cells mature into red blood cells and immune lineages.
- Improved variant effect prediction On the TenK10K dataset, a large single-cell map of 28 primary immune cell types, AlphaGenome 2 reliably identified nearly twice as many causal variants (30% vs. 16%) and directional gene effects (43% vs. 23%) as the original AlphaGenome fine-tuned on single-cell data and other specialized tools. This precision helps researchers find overlooked candidate variants for new discoveries.
- Pinpointing disease-relevant variants A recent
[landmark study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07501-1)showed that a variant in a distant regulatory switch drives IBD by overactivating the ETS2 gene in gut immune cells (macrophages). Making predictions across various immune cell types in the gut, AlphaGenome 2 reproduced this finding computationally. It singled out the causal variant and showed that it selectively boosts the ETS2 gene in gut macrophages, leaving other cell types and genes largely unaffected.
Analyzing new cell types and states without retraining
AlphaGenome 2 can also generalize to entirely new single-cell experiments without needing to be retrained. Scientists can upload a single-cell RNA-seq snapshot of gene activity from just a few dozen cells; this gene activity is then compressed into a cell state representation, before being used to condition the model on unseen states. AlphaGenome 2 can match or outperform models trained or fine-tuned directly on those datasets.
This enables AlphaGenome 2 to predict variant effects and gene regulation for new cell states, such as those that occur from disease or vaccination. For example, given unseen single-cell data from a COVID-19 mRNA vaccine study, AlphaGenome 2 distinguished vaccine-activated immune T cells from resting ones. It also revealed that a variant linked to severe COVID-19 disrupts gene activity more strongly when cells are in this activated state â an effect that would be missed in unactivated cells.
Bridging human genetics and single-cell biology
One way to better understand disease is by linking human genetics to cell biology. An important part of building this link requires connecting the thousands of trait and disease-associated variants found in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to the growing single-cell maps of the human body.
To help researchers make these connections without running large-scale computations themselves, we precomputed AlphaGenome 2 predictions for trait-associated variants across hundreds of human cell and tissue conditions, tackling two major challenges:
- Mapping enhancerâgene links in real human cell types: Many disease-linked variants sit in distant regulatory switches called enhancers, making their effects hard to trace. Because experimental CRISPR screens mostly use stable, lab-grown cell lines, scientists often lack these wiring diagrams for specific cells in the human body. AlphaGenome 2 extends enhancer-gene mapping to primary human cell types â such as brain astrocytes, which support and protect neurons â helping researchers connect regulatory variants to their target genes in the specific cells where disease unfolds.
- Pinpointing causal GWAS variants and the cells where they act: Genome-wide association studies flag broad stretches of DNA linked to disease, but researchers canât always then find the exact causal variant, target gene, and cell type with high confidence. Across a number of complex traits, ranging from height to type 2 diabetes, AlphaGenome 2âs precomputed variant scores help pinpoint the specific variants and cell types most likely to be involved. When confident, the model also accurately predicts whether a variant turns a geneâs activity up or down â a critical clue for understanding how that gene contributes to disease.
Looking ahead with the scientific community
As scientists map more of the human body at the single-cell level, AI models will continue to become more powerful. Through our ongoing collaborations, including with researchers at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, we are working to profile an even wider spectrum of human cell types, developmental lineages, and perturbed cellular states. We look forward to seeing how researchers from across the community use AlphaGenome 2 and its improved cell-type specific predictions to uncover how genetic variants act across cells,Â and what that reveals about basic biology and disease.
AlphaGenome 2, and interactive Colab tutorials for expression conditioning are available today for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API and in private preview for commercial research. And soon, we will release AlphaGenome 2 Skills in Google Antigravity, our agentic development platform. The combination of specialized models, like AlphaGenome 2, with powerful agentic science tools like Gemini 4 in Antigravity, will help scientists accelerate research and make new discoveries.
We are hugely grateful to our community of trusted testers for their feedback on AlphaGenome 2, as well as the many individuals and researchers that helped create the datasets used to train it. We'd love to spotlight interesting AlphaGenome 2 use cases the community can learn from. Get in touch via this [form](https://forms.gle/ftBfHGH7NUrCZEjN6) by 30 November; selected projects may be eligible for additional quota and credits. We also want to be guided by community input to shape our future roadmap, please share your feedback and ideas in our[ community forum.](https://www.alphagenomecommunity.com/)
Please note that AlphaGenome and AlphaGenome 2 are intended for research use only and have not been validated or approved for clinical or diagnostic purposes.
Acknowledgements
The core research work was done thanks to the contributions of Adam Gayoso, Anne Mottram, Alexander Karollus, Guido Novati, Pavol DrotÃ¡r, John Reid, Laetitia Meng-Papaxanthos, Adam Kosiorek, Eirini Arvaniti, Vincent Dutordoir, Soham De, Tom Ward, Lai Hong Wong, Matteo Perino, Kyle Taylor, Jun Cheng, Natasha Latysheva, Joshua Pan, Dhavanthi Hariharan, Clare Bycroft, Lauren Nicolaisen, Demis Hassabis, Pushmeet Kohli and Å½iga Avsec
We wish to thank the following people for their support and feedback including Gabriella Stanton, Charlie Taylor, Raina Thomas, Lucas TenÃ³rio, Antonio GarcÃa, Joseph Powell, Angli Xue, Trygve Bakken, Nelson Johansen, Junyue Cao, Ziyu Lu, Jacob Hepkema, Leopold Parts, Irina Voineagu, Souradeep Basu, Michal Zielinski, Jeff Cao, Ioannis Sarropoulos, Sarah Teichmann, Amanda Stafford, Eliseo Papa.
Finally we wish to thank Evie Gray, Adriana Fernandez Lara, Alex Wilkins, Danielle Breen, Dimple Vijaykumar, Muinat Abdul, Chris Kwaku-Abdullahi, Kathryn Seager, Ryan Smith, Ross West and Gaby Pearl for their expertise in communicating this work.

title: Experience the art and legacy of Dr. Esther Mahlangu
body:
Experience the art and legacy of Dr. Esther Mahlangu
Today we’re sharing the [first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu](https://artsandculture.google.com/project/esther-mahlangu) on Google Arts & Culture, honoring her pioneering spirit on her 91st birthday. More than 45 stories and a rich archive covering her [art](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/_QVhsTxpEWbtnQ), [life](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/TQWRPyjN0Luu_g), and [legacy](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/AQUxh9rtUMe9mQ) are now accessible to a global audience.
For many years, I have worked closely with Esther and her family. It’s a relationship built on years of research and a deep admiration for her as both an artist and a person. It was out of this long-standing connection that the vision for “‘[Then I Knew I Was Good at Painting’: Esther Mahlangu, a Retrospective](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/cAVhFwrQ8k2kag),” was born.
My goal has always been to present a comprehensive exploration of her life and work, contributing to my long-standing research on South African women artists who have made an impact on the arts since the early 20th century.
Through my research, I gathered a rich collection of her work, including [large-scale murals](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/9wWRh4woZhmiOg), [intimate pieces](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/kgVhZwuHYWhn1g), and [rare archival materials](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/9AUB-bLz0QU8DQ). But the archives didn’t include anything from her life before 1980, so crucial pieces of her history were missing. This void challenged us to find new ways to tell her full story.
A collaboration session with Esther Mahlangu, Nontobeko Ntombela, and the Google team.
In collaboration with Google Arts & Culture, we used [AI to visually recreate Esther’s undocumented memories](https://youtu.be/FWhQt-NfIKw). The process brought us closer to her work and prompted further recollections from Esther herself.
This project brought our curatorial and archival work together with the technical expertise of Google DeepMind and Google Arts & Culture Lab, alongside research and design studio Domestic Data Streamers’ synthetic memories initiative. Through a series of [workshops and interviews](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/OwUBQR258WOrrw), we were able to [document a missing period](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/iQUxnW9XyhhFQg) of Mam' Esther's history, from when she started painting at age 10 until her first documented works in 1980. These stories — such as [the moment she discovered her talent for painting as a 10-year-old](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/JwXRghigf-9lOw) using feathers instead of a brush — became the source material for our work. Following the methodology from the [synthetic memories initiative](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/synthetic-memories/ewVh6MMjnKk7Yg) and using archival material, the team generated still images based on Esther’s memories. They then used [Veo](https://deepmind.google/models/veo/) to turn the images into videos that brought Esther's early days to life.
The stories also contribute to the online archive of Esther’s life on Google Arts & Culture. More than [45 exhibitions](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/exhibit?project=esther-mahlangu), curated in collaboration with Art of Contemporary Africa, Iziko Museums of South Africa, the British Museum, the Jean Pigozzi Collection, the National Museum of Women in the Arts, and Serpentine, tell the story of [how she came to be known](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/CwXRnb-h-CMBpA) in the world, through her [artwork](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/asset?project=esther-mahlangu-explore-artworks), archives, [Street View](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/streetview?project=esther-mahlangu), and more.
This project demonstrates a new way to approach the preservation of cultural heritage, with technology that’s guided at every step by a respect for personal memory and historical accuracy.
It is my hope that this retrospective cements Esther’s place as a pivotal voice in global contemporary art, invites audiences to reimagine the possibilities of her archive, and ensures her story and her artistic vision can inspire generations to come.
Explore the exhibition at [goo.gle/esther-mahlangu](https://goo.gle/esther-mahlangu).

## 20,000 veterans are using ChatGPT to build what comes next

In the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of [ChatGPT Plus at no cost](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-veterans/) after being offered free access by OpenAI. As Veterans Day approaches, that milestone gives us a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers and to figure out what comes next for themselves and their families.

The effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and our community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, [with seven more⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/home/events) scheduled before the year ends.

## Preparing for civilian careers

Leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role. Many veterans are turning to ChatGPT to organize their job search, rehearse for interviews, and explore paths they hadn’t considered.

Air Force veteran [Tilak Bhatnagar ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ACoAACLpKeMBgVdc2b2nami8B_Wr_EecZXqRfDY) used his free year to prepare for a dozen interviews, find the right words to describe his military experience to civilian employers, and weigh competing job offers. Along the way, those conversations helped him clarify what he actually wanted from life after active duty.

He ultimately took a role at a tech company. What he valued most was being able to pick up where he left off, returning to the same thread about his background, goals, and constraints. As he put it, “each conversation built on the last.”

[Sadarian Bell ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ACoAAFDy8p8BLQADQImjs514hHT6yRuJ2ym1r6k), also an Air Force veteran, started planning more than a year before he left the service. He used ChatGPT to map out his transition and to turn nearly a decade of military healthcare experience into a civilian résumé.

To prepare for interviews, he practiced out loud using ChatGPT voice mode, working through one question at a time until his answers felt natural. “It has genuinely become my career coach,” Sadarian said, though he also learned to recognize when he’d had enough help and could trust his own judgment.

For Navy veteran [Kelli Ramirez ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kelliann-ramirez-hart-540a475a/), the transition was a chance to chase a long-held dream: becoming a published author. She’d already invested in a book-writing course to sharpen her craft, and ChatGPT filled in the gaps. “ChatGPT helped me organize ideas, ask questions about publishing, and work through the Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing process,” she said.

Kelli has since published two books, which she says “reflect my desire to help women approach technology with confidence and, for those who share my Christian faith, with wisdom grounded in that faith.”

## Learning to use ChatGPT, together

Not everyone arrives confident about using AI tools, which is why OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn alongside people who understand what they’re going through.

OpenAI recently wrapped our first six-event Academy series with [Veterans Forge⁠(opens in a new window)](https://veteransforge.org/), focused on helping veterans and military families use ChatGPT to work toward their goals. That pilot, together with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, is shaping what we offer veterans next.

At one [workshop in Reston, Virginia⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/en/public/events/openai-academy-for-veterans-w8zz8dfrts), nearly [100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) explored ways to put AI to work. Participant [Ryan Kaono-Wedemeyer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryan-kaono-wedemeyer) learned to start by writing out a detailed account of his military experience, then asking AI to help shape it into a civilian résumé.

Instructor [Erin Marie⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) helped participants build custom GPTs to support their transitions, and watched people who walked in skeptical begin finding ways the tools could genuinely help them.

In Louisville, Kentucky, [more than 80 Legionnaires⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/veterans-forge_theamericanlegion-veteransforge-veterans-activity-7499820737151541248-PqzY) attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion’s national convention. For those who can’t make it to an event, our [online veterans collection⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/collections/veterans) and [100 chats for veterans⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/use-cases/veterans) offer examples to try on your own.

## What’s next

We’re continuing this work with partners across the country through the rest of the year:

- November 12: [NPower event in St. Louis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-st-louis-mo-0khw38ivta)
- November 14: [Nashville event with Veterans Forge and Wounded Warrior Project⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-veterans-nashville-tn-dix3h7movo)
- November 17: [30-minute virtual session⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-veterans-explore-your-next-career-move-9ogzt3abfx)
- November 19: [NPower event in Dallas⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-dallas-tx-n6del7j00o)
- November 21: [NPower event in San Antonio⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-san-antonio-tx-x48nh426r8)

Our goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. We’re grateful to [ID.me⁠(opens in a new window)](http://ID.me) for helping servicemembers and veterans access the free-year offer, and to our community partners for making these events possible.

This Veterans Day, OpenAI thanks veterans for their service and for contributing to their communities.

title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
body:
[
](#botpsy-on-device-personal-assistant-with-a-sub-billion-parameter-agentic-language-model)
BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
[Team Article](/blog)
Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.
Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the [Intended Use and Limitations](#intended-use-and-limitations) for more information.
🤗 [Model (safetensors)](https://huggingface.co/qvac/BotPsy-0.8B) | 📦 [GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)](https://huggingface.co/qvac/BotPsy-0.8B-GGUFs)
[
](#copyright-complaints)
Copyright Complaints
We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email [data-apps@tether.io](mailto:data-apps@tether.io) identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.
[
](#key-highlights)
Key Highlights
[
](#benchmark-results)
Benchmark results
- Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets).
- Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus.
- Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5).
[
](#model-capabilities)
Model capabilities
- More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9).
- Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model.
- Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested.
[
](#safety-efficiency-and-deployment)
Safety, efficiency and deployment
- Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%.
- More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device.
- Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp.
[
](#broader-vision)
Broader Vision
Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.
[
](#methodology)
Methodology
BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).
[
](#training-procedure-four-stages-three-types-of-feedback)
Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback
Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.
Learning from demonstrations (SFT)
We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.
Learning from teachers (MOPD)
Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).
Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)
Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.
The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.
[
](#data-composition)
Data composition
Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.
[
](#results)
Results
[
](#tool-use--agents)
Tool use & agents
BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).
| Benchmark | BotPsy-0.8B ours |
Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1× |
Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5× |
LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5× |
MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25× |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BFCL v4¹ | 44.0 | 23.4 | 37.7 | 28.1 | 22.8 |
| ACEBench² | 58.7 | 30.1 | 55.4 | 39.4 | 24.5 |
| τ-bench³ | 51.5 | 23.2 | 46.5 | 6.5 | 28.8 |

title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
body:
[NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/korean-startup-investments-msit/)
As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s [emphasis on zero waste](https://cop.sifiratikvakfi.org/en/news/president-erdogans-cop31-call-zero-waste-movement-is-the-strongest-bridge/) puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, [less than 7%](https://circularity-gap.world/updates-collection/global-circularity-rate-fell-to-6-9---despite-growing-recycling) of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over [2 billion tons](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/global-waste-management-outlook-2024) of trash per year — a figure that could [nearly double by 2050](https://www.weforum.org/stories/nature-and-biodiversity/circular-economy-waste-management-unep).
AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills.
“A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.”
See how four members of the [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation.
Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products.
The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product.
“The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.”
The company uses [NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%.
In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%.
At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items.
EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia.
“Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.”
EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on [NVIDIA data center GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/), optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.
Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries.
Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it.
U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second.
“Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.”
Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six.
Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of [food-grade plastics by 12%](https://www.greyparrot.ai/resources/case-studies/amcor-case-study-a-12-lift-in-food-grade-polypropylene-yield). Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants.
Europe generates [nearly 7 million tons](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/management-of-used-and-waste-textiles-in-europes-circular-economy) of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried.
reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category.
“Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.”
As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with [NVIDIA TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt) software and running on [NVIDIA Jetson](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud.
The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe.
Explore more [NVIDIA-powered sustainability applications](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/case-studies/?filters=%7B%22Industries%22%3A%5B%22Sustainability%22%5D%7D).

title: Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models
body:
Feature Extraction • 0.1B • Updated • 95
[
](#token-pooling-aware-training-for-multi-vector-embedding-models)
Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/token-pooling.md)
Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!
Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.
In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4
, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.
This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's
[Learn to Pool]and[LightOn's pooling regularization study], which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.
Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.
[
](#table-of-contents)
Table of Contents
[Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors](#why-multi-vector-retrieval-needs-so-many-vectors)[Token Pooling](#token-pooling)[Token Pooling-Aware Training](#token-pooling-aware-training)[Using the Trained Model](#using-the-trained-model)[Evaluation Results](#evaluation-results)[Combining Compression Techniques](#combining-compression-techniques)[References](#references)[Code and Models](#code-and-models)
[
](#why-multi-vector-retrieval-needs-so-many-vectors)
Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors
A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. [Multi-vector models](https://huggingface.co/blog/multi-vector-encoder) such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.
For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:
Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by [Fast-PLAID](https://github.com/lightonai/fast-plaid), storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.
The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.
[
](#token-pooling)
Token Pooling
[HierarchicalTokenPooling](https://sbert.net/docs/package_reference/multi_vector_encoder/modules.html#hierarchicaltokenpooling) groups similar token embeddings using [Ward hierarchical clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#hierarchical-clustering). Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.
These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.
You can make compression proportional to document length:
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
With pool_factor=4
, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.
[
](#choosing-a-pooling-budget)
Choosing a Pooling Budget
HierarchicalTokenPooling
offers three alternative controls:
| Setting | What it expresses |
|---|---|
max_tokens=16 |
A maximum of 16 vectors per document, including protected tokens. |
pool_factor=4 |
Approximately one quarter of each document's original vectors. |
distance_threshold=... |
A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry. |
This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4
, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold
, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.
[
](#calibrating-adaptive-pooling)
Calibrating Adaptive Pooling
Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.
Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents
:
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
model = MultiVectorEncoder("lightonai/LateOn")
calibration_embeddings = model.encode_document(calibration_documents)
threshold = HierarchicalTokenPooling.calibrate_distance_threshold(calibration_embeddings, target_tokens=16)
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(distance_threshold=threshold)
# Apply pooling, targeting an average of 16 vectors per document
document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents_to_index, token_pooling=pooling)
Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.
[
](#token-pooling-aware-training)
Token Pooling-Aware Training
Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.
If you've used [Matryoshka embeddings](https://huggingface.co/blog/matryoshka), the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.
For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:
- Retrieval using the original document embeddings.
- Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors.
I average them:
The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.
Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling
uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.
[
](#a-loss-wrapper-in-sentence-transformers)
A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers
[ MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss](https://sbert.net/docs/package_reference/multi_vector_encoder/losses.html#multivectortokenpoolingloss) wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:
from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.losses import (
CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss,
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss,
)
from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling
model = MultiVectorEncoder("answerdotai/ModernBERT-base", similarity_fn_name="maxsim")
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor=4)
base_loss = CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, mini_batch_size=64)
loss = MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss(
model,
base_loss,
token_poolings=[None, pooling],
weights=[0.5, 0.5],
)
CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss
supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity
, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim"
would also use MeanMaxSim during training.
Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss
adds the compression objective. Here, None
means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling
supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.
The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling
implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.
Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.
The complete [training script](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/blob/main/examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py) includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/):
uv run examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py --baseline
uv run examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py
The script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.
You can also train on a cloud GPU with [Hugging Face Jobs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-quickstart). Install the CLI and log in with a token that can run Jobs and upload models:
pip install -U huggingface_hub
hf auth login
hf jobs uv run \
--flavor a10g-small \
--timeout 4h \
--secrets HF_TOKEN \
-- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers/main/examples/multi_vector_encoder/training/token_pooling/training_cached_contrastive.py
This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_

# JioStar’s chief architect on AI discovery at 500M-user scale

A conversation with Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect at JioStar.

[Contact sales](https://openai.com/contact-sales/)



Company size: Enterprise

Region: Asia-Pacific & Oceania

Industry: Media, Entertainment & Sport

Products: API, Codex

Share

What convinced you that AI would fundamentally change how people discover content?

- [What convinced you that AI would fundamentally change how people discover content?](#what-convinced-you-that-ai-would-fundamentally-change-how-people-discover-content)

- [Looking back, what would you do differently?](#looking-back-what-would-you-do-differently)
- [What should executives keep in mind as they move from AI experiments to production systems?](#what-should-executives-keep-in-mind-as-they-move-from-ai-experiments-to-production-systems)

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

JioStar operates entertainment and live-sports platforms used by more than 500 million consumers and has supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers. At that scale, AI has to be fast, reliable, and ready for production.

Using the OpenAI API, JioStar built a conversational video and cricket-stat discovery assistant into JioHotstar. Viewers can speak naturally to find movies and shows, historical highlights, live-match moments, or cricket statistics, with results returned through a visual, conversational experience.

At OpenAI’s Executive Summit in Singapore, Sidharth Sharma, OpenAI’s Head of Go-to-Market for ASEAN, spoke with Vijay Seshadri—Chief Architect, JioStar, about building the experience for more than 15 languages in about eight weeks, and the lessons for leaders taking AI from demo to production.

## What convinced you that AI would fundamentally change how people discover content?

Content discovery has evolved very little in the past 25 years. Recommendations were the last major shift. Much of what followed has been an iteration of the same idea.

But choosing what to watch is deeply personal. A person might say, “I’m feeling sad. Show me something that will cheer me up.” Even that simple request contains a lot of nuance. What kind of sad? What usually cheers that person up? Do they want comedy, comfort viewing or something completely distracting?

A traditional recommendation system may struggle to understand that moment. Conversation gives the viewer a way to explain it. We call this a voice-visual interface.

> “**Content discovery is inherently visual, but combining those visual options with spoken preferences and conversation creates a powerful new paradigm.**”

*—Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect, JioStar*

Listen

## How did you turn that idea into a product in time for a major cricket tournament?

We began working through the concept in October and November, with a major cricket tournament coming in February. We had roughly two months and two very different audiences: entertainment viewers and cricket fans.

An entertainment viewer might say, “It’s Friday evening—surprise me,” or describe a movie without knowing its title. Sports viewers may want a more specific update, like fall of wickets, a series of sixes, or the match in which a player scored a certain number of runs. Cricket experts may want statistics about every ball.

These are very different discovery problems. We worked on bringing entertainment, sports moments and detailed cricket statistics into one experience, across multiple languages, in a very short period.

## At JioStar’s scale, what tradeoffs shaped the technical design?

Very early, we framed the problem as a three-way tradeoff among accuracy, latency, and cost. Every engineering decision had to balance all three at once.

Voice made that especially important. More than 60% of our users use voice rather than text: people prefer to say what they want to watch. The response still has to be relevant, fast, and economically viable at scale.

> “**As much of a cliché as it may sound, the answer is evals, evals, and evals. If you are building an application like this for the first time, you will probably underestimate the importance of evals even if you think you are prepared.**”

*—Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect, JioStar*

Listen

## What does an effective evaluation system look like in production?

I think about it in two parts: an evaluation framework and a validation layer. Before production, the evaluation framework should prompt changes. In production, a feedback loop should turn customer behavior and failures into new eval cases.

That flywheel can become self-amplified, but it is extremely difficult to get right.

Domain experts are essential. For sports-statistics evals, we worked with people such as sports-magazine editors who understood what serious fans might ask. You cannot begin with a prompt alone; you need to seed the system with deep human expertise.

## How did a small team build and launch the experience in about eight weeks?

One thing we got right was the team. We started with a small team of data scientists and engineers around a clear problem statement. OpenAI’s forward-deployed engineers worked alongside us to further identify the few things we absolutely had to get right.

The first was scope. A voice or text interface lets users ask almost anything, so we began by deciding what the system should not answer. Guardrails came first.

For evals, we began with a seed dataset and used models to expand it with more variation. We created what you might now call a maker-checker pattern: one model helped determine how to answer a question, while another acted as a validator—an LLM as judge—with a competing objective.

That raised another question: who tests the judge? Designing the validator was itself an evaluation problem. Codex helped the team accelerate work such as generating eval cases and updating the system, but faster building did not remove the need for judgment and validation.

## Looking back, what would you do differently?

I would invest earlier in production monitoring for model efficacy.

Traditional infrastructure measures such as P99 latency remain important, but they are not enough. You also need to monitor model efficacy in production.

## What should executives keep in mind as they move from AI experiments to production systems?

First, there is a large gap between what technology can do and the reality inside an enterprise. If your company has not matched every frontier-model announcement, you are not alone.

Second, keep focusing on outcomes rather than activity. It is easy to mistake visible motion for meaningful progress, particularly when companies emphasize input metrics. Lines of code generated, for example, do not tell you whether you created meaningful value.

> “**I see AI as a massive simplification hammer for the enterprise. If we do not use it to simplify business processes, workflows, and software-engineering systems, it will be a huge wasted opportunity.**”

*—Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect, JioStar*

Listen

Finally, most enterprises underestimate the human skill and agency required. This cannot be only a generic skilling program. Leaders need people who can apply these tools with judgment. Give a strong engineer a tool like Codex and the impact can multiply; without the judgment to validate production systems, the risk multiplies too.

You have a rocket in your hands. Especially in production systems, you need validation and guardrails, and you need to give the keys to the right people.

title: Your Sub-Agents Are a Distributed System. Treat Them Like One. - Girish Konda, Microsoft
body:
When an orchestrator hands work to sub-agents, you've built a distributed system, and you inherit its classic failures: half-finished work reported as success, guesses read back as facts, rate limits the orchestrator never sees, and retries that run side effects twice. Girish Konda maps each failure to the distributed-systems idea that already explains it, with examples from his open-source MCP Pacemaker and the MCP and A2A specs. He then lays out SAFE hand-offs, the consistency model he uses for sub-agents that touch real systems, including what it costs and where it doesn't fit.

title: Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices
body:
Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices
Gemini Intelligence
[1](#footnote-1)
brings the best of Gemini to Android devices, helping your devices work harder for you. Earlier this year, we [announced Gemini Intelligence](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/android/gemini-intelligence/), and this summer devices started rolling out — from the [Pixel 11](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/pixel/pixel-11-features/) to the [Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Fold8, Z Flip8](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/android/galaxy-unpacked-2026/) and S26 series.
[2](#footnote-2)
Today, we’re introducing new features built for Gemini Intelligence, and expanding capabilities to [more of Android’s most advanced devices](http://android.com/gemini-intelligence/shop-devices).
[3](#footnote-3)
Here’s a look at what’s new.
Gemini Intelligence on more devices, including motorola signature 27 and Pixel 10
Gemini Intelligence is coming to even more devices. Motorola is introducing its first Gemini Intelligence device, [motorola signature 27](https://www.motorola.com/us/en/p/phones/signature/motorola-signature/pmipmka46mo), which is available for pre-order in the U.S. on November 19. And with [today’s Pixel Drop](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/pixel/november-2026-pixel-drop/), Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold get the latest features for Gemini Intelligence.
Alongside this expansion, we’re bringing some of our favorite capabilities to more devices and regions, helping handle the busywork so you can focus on what matters. Rambler
[4](#footnote-4)
— which turns spoken thoughts into clean, organized text in real-time — is now available on Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10, Pro XL and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, as well as the new motorola signature 27. And task automation
[5](#footnote-5)
— which lets you ask Gemini to handle logistics like ordering food, hailing rides, or booking reservations across your favorite apps — is [expanding](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16940971) to the UK, India, and Japan.
Build custom widgets with a prompt
Create My Widget
[6](#footnote-6)
, which is rolling out over the next few weeks, lets you design a personalized widget with a simple description in your own words — no coding required. Whether you want a dashboard for your upcoming trip, a monthly spending tracker, or a race day countdown, [Create My Widget](https://support.google.com/pixelphone/answer/18835879) can pull in information from Gmail, Calendar, and Search to create a custom widget just for you, giving you the information you want at a glance on your homescreen.
Get personalized tech support with Device Assistance
Device Assistance
[7](#footnote-7)
helps you control, change, or fix your device by just asking your phone for help. Ask Gemini to clear up space on your device, check which apps can access your location, or mute distractions while making sure important calls still come through. Gemini deeply understands your device so it can act as your personal device expert.
Experience proactive help across a range of screens
Gemini Intelligence is designed to support you across whatever screen you’re using. Last month we launched [Googlebook](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/googlebook/pre-order-googlebook/), the first laptop designed for Gemini Intelligence.
And if you have a Pixel phone with Gemini Intelligence, it will soon bring proactive suggestions to Android Auto — connecting the dots across your apps to surface helpful, personalized suggestions
[8](#footnote-8)
when you need them. For example, if your friend texts you to ask where you are meeting for a pilates class, Gemini Intelligence on Android Auto can find your confirmation email and instantly suggest sending the address with a single tap.
Plus, in the next few weeks, Create My Widget is coming to Pixel Watch. You’ll be able to design widgets that keep the details that matter to you right on your wrist.
