title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
body:
A year ago, NVIDIA [open sourced its Aerial wireless software](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/open-source-aerial-ai-native-6g/), joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems.
Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world.
Over the past year, global developer adoption of [NVIDIA AI Aerial](https://developer.nvidia.com/topics/telecommunications/ai-aerial?size=n_6_n) and [NVIDIA Sionna](https://github.com/nvlabs/sionna) software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms.
The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents.
Networks That Help Robots React Faster
A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time.
Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses.
At [King’s College London](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15895), researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an [NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/jetson-orin/) running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images.
In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution.
Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better
For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field.
AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area.
[SoftBank](https://www.softbank.jp/en/corp/technology/research/topics/238/?adid=nvblog) demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into [NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aerial-cuda-accelerated-ran) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60%.
Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, [ETH Zurich](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.04004) researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions.
Networks That Learn When to Save Power
As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important.
For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections.
At the [University of Leeds](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/242057/1/Accepted_Network_in_a_box__ICC_2026_Yejing.pdf), researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored.
The team tested their approach using a portable, [NVIDIA DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/)-powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity.
Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built
Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore.
The [Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC)](https://www.cttc.cat/cttc-accelerates-5g-network-simulation-from-hours-to-minutes-with-nvidia/) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow.
In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance.
Faster simulations let researchers compare more designs, investigate more demanding scenarios and refine ideas sooner. As the industry develops 6G, this could shorten the path from a proposed innovation to a thoroughly evaluated network design — helping teams build better connectivity before deploying it in the real world.
At NVIDIA GTC Washington, D.C., attend [6G Developer Sessions](https://www.nvidia.com/gtc/dc/session-catalog/?industries=Telecommunications) where researchers and developers will showcase more innovations shaping the future of wireless networks.
[NVIDIA AI Aerial](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aerial-cuda-accelerated-ran) and [NVIDIA Sionna](https://github.com/nvlabs/sionna) are available on GitHub.

title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
body:
Robotics • Updated • 58 • 2
[
](#toyblocks-a-controlled-world-for-robot-learning-and-evaluation)
ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
💻 [Code](http://allenai.github.io/ToyBlocks) | 📊 [Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/toyblocks-data) | 🤖 [Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/toyblocks) | 📖 [Documentation](https://allenai.github.io/ToyBlocks/docs/user_guide/index.html)
Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.
To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.
Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.
Our first foundation world is [ToyBlocks](https://github.com/allenai/ToyBlocks): an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.
ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.
Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.
[
](#how-toyblocks-works)
How ToyBlocks works
Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including [MolmoAct 2](https://allenai.org/blog/molmoact2), [MolmoBot](https://allenai.org/blog/molmobot-robot-manipulation), and [MolmoSpaces](https://allenai.org/blog/molmospaces), ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.
As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.
Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.
Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.
A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.
ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.
ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.
ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.
To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.
Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.
Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.
ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.
A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.
[
](#research-building-on-toyblocks)
Research building on ToyBlocks
The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."
[
](#low-level-action-models-vla-spatial-generalization)
Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization
Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.
The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.
We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.
We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.
Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on [ManiFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01819), [π0.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054), and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.
[
](#high-level-reasoning-vision-language-models)
High-level reasoning: vision-language models
Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.
We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

title: Your AI Isn't the Advantage. Your Judgment Is - Sid Pednekar
body:
Sid Pednekar, an AI, technology and data executive in asset management, looks at why most companies now have AI but only a few see real results from it. Following two hypothetical firms, he lays out three things the leaders do differently: they pick the right problem and invest deeply in a few high-value workflows instead of scattering pilots, they build shared capabilities by standardizing the core and breaking down silos, and they make every success and failure feed back into the system. Running through all of it is one idea: when intelligence gets cheap, judgment becomes the scarce resource.

title: Your AI Agent Keeps Making the Same Mistakes - Sparsh Jain, CentralAgent AI
body:
Sparsh Jain, Head of AI at CentralAgent AI, argues that giving AI agents more memory isn't the same as helping them learn. After his team worked with the same agent for two years and it still repeated the same mistakes, they rebuilt memory as an experiential system: forming notes from new experiences, updating or deactivating old ones, keeping inactive notes as a record of how a judgment was reached, and forgetting what no longer matters, with a regular cleanup loop that works like a good night's sleep. He shares the rules they learned building it and why agents that learn from every teammate keep compounding over time.

# Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems

Loading…

Share

Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through [Daybreak Red](https://openai.com/index/expanding-daybreak-as-the-cyber-defense-window-narrows/).

As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that [Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint](https://openai.com/index/preparing-our-next-security-sprint-to-harden-openai/). We also [raised our bug bounty rewards](https://openai.com/index/rewarding-defenders-with-bigger-bug-bounties/) to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.

We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their [research⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.hacktron.ai/blog) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work shows what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.

As AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.

> “The future of cybersecurity won’t be defined by who has the largest security team, but by who can best combine human creativity with AI-driven capabilities.  
>   
> OpenAI is setting a strong example by putting frontier cyber models in the hands of security researchers, enabling them to uncover complex vulnerabilities at the boundaries between interconnected systems.  
>   
> We’re excited to deepen our partnership with OpenAI, combining our offensive security expertise with their frontier models to help secure OpenAI and the broader software ecosystem.”

*—Zayne Zhang, CEO, Hacktron*

We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our [Security Bug Bounty program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://bugcrowd.com/engagements/openai).

title: The components of agent memory
body:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. [The hippocampus](https://stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/McCMcNaughtonOReilly95.pdf) plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only [some experiences](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adk8261?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F) are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet [rest](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-06213-1), the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill [those experiences and integrate them](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-019-0467-3) into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed [sleep-time compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13171) as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often [called](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams) [dreaming](https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-for-llms-to-retain-knowledge-in-continual-learning/) (Figure 1).
We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
Memory notes
By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), [in-context learning](https://www.anthropic.com/research/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads) (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and [compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can [mark a memory](https://www.nature.com/articles/385533a0) as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can [write](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool) them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from [Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0](https://continual-learning-bench.com/news/cl-bench-1-0/), a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview). Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a [memory directory](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) that persisted from one session to the next.
Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
Claude has learned to judge salience
We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red, a game that [challenges Claude to navigate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXhYDOvgpuU) complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md
, and earned four badges.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md
file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations
folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay
folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
Steering Claude to write memory
We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).
We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.
In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.
With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.
Dreaming can correct memory
Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
We then tested whether dreaming could help Cla

Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from [Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0](https://continual-learning-bench.com/news/cl-bench-1-0/), a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview). Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a [memory directory](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) that persisted from one session to the next.
Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
Claude has learned to judge salience
We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red, a game that [challenges Claude to navigate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXhYDOvgpuU) complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md
, and earned four badges.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.

Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md
file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations
folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay
folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.

Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.

When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.

title: Teaching AI to build scientific models
body:
[AI for Science]grantees[Jakob Macke],[Daniel Gedon], and[Stefan Wahl]are researchers at the[ELLIS Institute Tübingen]and the University of Tübingen, where they build AI tools for developing scientific models in neuroscience and beyond. In this guest post, they discuss how AI is starting to change scientific modeling.
In 1951, Cambridge University’s computer went out of action for six months. This was inconvenient for physiologist Andrew Huxley, who, alongside his colleague Alan Hodgkin, had just built a set of equations to describe how a particular squid nerve cell fired. The scientists wanted to understand the “action potential” of these nerve cells: the electrical pulses they use to communicate, which underlie everything brains do, from perception to intelligence. The only way to find out whether the equations worked was to solve them and compare the solutions to data.
Huxley had hoped to use the newfangled computer to solve the equations. Instead, he was forced to solve them using a hand-cranked mechanical calculator. It took him over three weeks.
The basic structure of their model was dictated by known facts about the cell. Hodgkin and Huxley modeled its membrane as an electrical circuit. One part of the model, however, was just an educated guess. In order to make the curve fit the data they had measured, they found that they had to raise one variable to the fourth power—that is, to multiply it by itself three times. At the time, they did not know why. They just knew that otherwise the model didn’t predict the observed data as well.
They did offer a hypothesis, however. They cautiously suggested that the variable in question, which governed how particular gates in the cell membrane opened, might require the fourth power because multiple charged particles in the membrane had to move into place before the gate would open.
Decades later, long after both Hodgkin and Huxley had won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1963, another team [found the structure of a related potassium channel protein](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.280.5360.69). And they discovered that, yes, it had four identical pieces arranged [around a central pore](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1116270). The model was fit to the data in 1951. Even then, it predicted how fast the impulse travels relatively accurately. More than that, it turned out to have helped predict the structure of potassium ion channels themselves, which it had never been fit to.
Today, an AI system could plausibly find an equation like Hodgkin and Huxley’s in an afternoon, and perhaps it would fit the experimental data even more closely. But the point of the story is that simply knowing the fourth power did the job was not enough; what mattered was knowing that a simpler version of the model did not work. An AI system that merely hands you the model might give you an answer, but it does not give you understanding. Reproducing the data with a model is insufficient, because any number of models could do the same. What matters is being able to make claims about the real-world system itself, and ideally about other, similar systems. To do so, you need to know which features the model shares with other models that work, and which set it apart from models that don’t. As the mathematician Richard Hamming wrote in 1962, “The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers.”
A three-step program
More than 70 years on, [the Hodgkin-Huxley model](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1392413/) remains the standard description of electrical activity in neurons. The same kinds of equations, with different constants, describe nerve cells across the animal kingdom, from squids to humans, even though our evolutionary lineages separated more than half a billion years ago.
Even more important than its longevity, however, is what the Hodgkin-Huxley model tells us about how models work. Hodgkin and Huxley’s approach can be broken down into three steps, and most scientific modeling involves some version of them.
- The first is building the model. This means deciding what the model is made of and what shape its equations take. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s case, that meant the parts of the electrical circuit—the membrane and the gates—and the form of the equations, such as raising the underlying variable to the fourth power.
- The second is constraining the model—tuning its adjustable parameters to fit real measurements. For Hodgkin and Huxley, that included settings like how often the gates open under different voltages.
- The third is interpreting the model—asking what the model says about the real system, such as suggesting that the fourth power meant the gate had four moving parts.
In practice, scientists [go through these steps repeatedly](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2286841). If the numbers fail to fit the measurements, or if the interpretation makes no sense, they go back and revise.
All three steps were once done by people, but AI systems are increasingly involved in each of them. Machines have arguably made the most progress in constraining models, so we’ll start there.
Splitting the bill, or how to constrain models
When Hodgkin and Huxley constrained their model by eye and intuition, they ended up with a single set of numbers. This told them that the model could match the data. It didn’t tell them whether other numbers would have worked just as well or even better.
Imagine you know that a group dinner added up to $120, but not who ordered what. Many different combinations of orders could have added up to that amount—perhaps everyone ordered a mid-priced burger, or perhaps one person had steak and lobster while everyone else had soup. Models of nerve cells work on the same principle: different combinations of gate parameters can produce near-identical electrical activity. Simply showing one combination that fits well hides all the other plausible parameter settings, and other combinations might have led to different predictions. This is true of almost any phenomenon being modeled. Many different sets of parameters can explain the observed data equally well.
The solution is a statistical method called Bayesian inference. It gives you every set of numbers that works reasonably well, as a probability distribution that takes into account their fit to the data and your prior knowledge about the parameters. The distribution takes the shape of a curve, with the best fits at the peak and the weaker ones at the fringes.
But this method has usually been impractical for complex models, because it involves calculating how likely your measurements would be under every possible set of numbers. In Hodgkin and Huxley’s model, that would still be feasible, but for anything more complicated, it would be computationally impossible. For example, if each of the thousands of ion channels opens and closes at random, you would have to work out every combination. Returning to our restaurant bill analogy: it would be easy to answer, “If person A had the burger and person B had the steak, what would the bill come to?” but much harder to show which combinations could have led to the final bill, especially as the number of people and menu options grows.
A different approach called [simulation-based inference (SBI)](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1912789117) overcomes this reverse-engineering problem with sheer computation. You pick random parameters, run the model, and record the output. You do it again and again—[perhaps 100,000 times for a model like Hodgkin-Huxley](https://elifesciences.org/articles/56261), and millions of times for larger, more complex ones. Then you train a neural network on the results so that, given an output, it can return the range of parameters that could have produced it.
All SBI requires is that you can run the model: put in a set of parameters and get back the kind of data you would expect to see. A model you can run like this—parameters in, data out—is called a simulator, hence the name “simulation-based inference.” You never need to use a formula to calculate how likely your measurements are, which is the step that makes standard Bayesian inference often impractical. These days a simulator is usually a computer program, but it doesn’t have to be: Huxley, cranking through the equations by hand, was running one. Many simulators are easy to run forward but impossible to reverse. Some can’t even be written out as a tidy equation—their assumptions are built into the rules they follow—but they are models nonetheless. For many complex phenomena, from networks of neurons to colliding galaxies, simulators are often the only kind of model we have. SBI lets us constrain those models with data.
Running all those simulations is expensive and can take weeks. But once it is done, a trained network can perform inference on new data in seconds, without requiring further simulations. That speed has changed what’s possible. When [two neutron stars collide](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-08593-z), SBI can work out roughly where in the sky the collision happened, fast enough to point telescopes at it while the signal is still detectable. The same approach has been successfully applied to problems in [cosmology](https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/3sj1-1l9f), [structural biology](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2420158122), [geophysics](https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/241/3/1741/8099925), and many other domains.
And SBI has been applied to [nerve cell models](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04428-3), [including the Hodgkin-Huxley model](https://elifesciences.org/articles/56261). Because it returns a distribution rather than a single fit, we can see which parameters are well constrained by the data, where more than one explanation is plausible, and where more data—and thus another experiment—is most needed.
The bill, one level up, or how to build models
Before you can constrain a model, you need a model to constrain. The equations of the Hodgkin-Huxley model were not derived from first principles. Instead, the fourth power of the underlying variable emerged empirically from the scientists’ biological insight, and from finding that simpler versions didn’t work as well.
For most of the history of science, this is how models have been built. Scientists used their expertise and assumptions to write down a candidate model. Then they tested it, revised it, and tried again. The problem is that the space of possible models is essentially infinite, and a scientist proposing a handful of models from experience will very likely miss models that could have explained the observational data equally well.
AI systems can now help with, or even take over, this step. Given some data and a natural-language description of a system, an LLM-based agent writes code for a candidate model or a set of candidate models. Then it runs the model, constrains its parameters, compares the output to real-world data, and revises it, perhaps by modifying the form of an equation. This loop repeats until the model replicates the data accurately enough. Several such systems have appeared in the past two years.[1](#footnote-1) The details vary, but all use an LLM to design the model itself. Until recently, this was thought to be something only humans could do.
But the fact that a model replicates data doesn’t mean that it provides insight. As with the restaurant bill, or the Hodgkin-Huxley parameters, many different combinations of parameters within a single model can provide the same output. The same is true one level up, for the model itself: many different models, with differently shaped equations, can explain the same data equally well. Run an agent twice on the same data, and it might return two different, and equally good, models. An agent that returns only one of them is hiding the rest, just as a single best-fit set of numbers does.
So it is better to treat building a model the same way we treat constraining one: you ask for t

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
We then tested whether dreaming could help Cla

title: Voice Chat with Agents
body:
Voice Chat with Agents
You can now talk with your agents in a realtime voice call. Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.
Voice chat works in the Agents Window, the IDE, on web, and in Cursor for iOS.
Start a call
When the agent is idle and the chat input is empty, click the waveform button labeled Start voice chat. It sits where Send usually is, next to the microphone button for dictation.
On iOS, you can also say "Hey Siri, call Cursor" to start a call with a new agent, and mute or hang up from the Lock Screen with a Live Activity.
Talk while the agent works
The voice agent listens, replies, and hands coding work to the agent in your chat. While that agent runs, you can keep the conversation going. Ask what changed in a diff, check on a run, search earlier messages and calls with this agent, or switch between workers in a Project that has them.
The coding agent speaks for itself too. It shares short progress notes while it works and a brief answer when it's done, so you usually hear a short update instead of the full written reply.
Powered by Grok Voice
Voice chat runs on Grok Voice. Pick from many voices in Voice settings, including Ara, Eve, Leo, Rex, and Sal. With Privacy Mode on, voice chat runs with zero data retention.
Voice chat and dictation
Voice chat is separate from dictation, which earlier releases called Voice Mode. Dictation still turns your speech into text in the chat input, and Cmd+Shift+Space still toggles it in the IDE. Voice chat is a two-way conversation where the agent answers out loud.
Update Cursor to try voice chat. Learn more in our [docs](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/voice-chat).

# Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science

Introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data across 100 routine wet-lab tasks.

Loading…

Inside BioBasicsBench

- [Inside BioBasicsBench](#inside-biobasicsbench)
- [Results](#results)
- [GPT-6 Astra improvements from GPT-5.6 Sol](#gpt-6-astra-improvements-from-gpt-56-sol)
- [Where models still fall short](#where-models-still-fall-short)
- [Building toward reliable lab assistance](#building-toward-reliable-lab-assistance)

- [Inside BioBasicsBench](#inside-biobasicsbench)
- [Results](#results)
- [GPT-6 Astra improvements from GPT-5.6 Sol](#gpt-6-astra-improvements-from-gpt-56-sol)
- [Where models still fall short](#where-models-still-fall-short)
- [Building toward reliable lab assistance](#building-toward-reliable-lab-assistance)

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.

The benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question.

At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.

## Inside BioBasicsBench

BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.

BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably.

Scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. Each task underwent an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review.

Agents return a structured answer with the requested conclusion, measurement or recommendation and, where required, supporting reasoning. Answers receive credit against individual rubric criteria, allowing the benchmark to distinguish a correct conclusion from a partially correct analysis. Most tasks test several skills together, including biological knowledge, interpretation of images and other data, error detection and protocol understanding.

**“Unique tasks” counts each task once. The skill columns count tasks with each skill tag. These categories overlap: one task can appear in several columns, so the skill counts should not be added to obtain a task total. Color identifies the domain; stronger shading indicates a larger share of that domain’s tasks testing a skill.**

The inputs preserve the forms of evidence scientists work with: gel and blot images, plate photographs, microscopy stacks, sequencing reads, plate-reader exports and videos of bench work. A task can include several kinds of data. Reference sheets, such as ladder charts and plasmid maps, support the interpretation of the experimental evidence.

### What the agent is given

| **Kind of data** | **Tasks** | **What it includes** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gels & blots | 31 | Agarose DNA gels, SDS-PAGE gels, Western blots |
| Protocols, notes & specs | 27 | Protocols and SOPs, lab notebooks and run records, photographed handwritten notes, catalogues, instrument specs, published methods |
| Tables & instrument exports | 20 | CSV and Excel exports, lane layouts and inventories, raw flow cytometry (FCS) files |
| Bench, apparatus & reagent photos | 18 | Benches, gel rigs, reagent and culture tubes, a PCR plate, tube racks, pH strips, a concentrator, a freezer, a liquid-handler deck |
| Microscopy | 14 | Raw brightfield and fluorescence images, multi-channel sets, z-stacks, time-lapse movies |
| Instrument screens & plots | 13 | Photos of flow cytometer, microscope, NanoDrop, plate reader and balance screens; exported standard curves, chromatograms and plots |
| Sequencing files | 12 | Raw long-read FASTQs, FASTA sequences, GenBank maps |
| Protocol videos | 7 | Streaking, inoculation, serial dilution, SDS-PAGE tank and incubator setups, weighing on a balance |
| Agar plates & colonies | 7 | Transformation plates, blue/white screens, antibiotic-disc plates |
| Reference sheets | 21 | Ladder charts, plasmid maps, pH charts (supporting material) |

*Number of tasks that include each kind of data. Categories overlap; reference sheets are supporting material.*

Scientists wrote the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing the experimental evidence with a question and an expert-written grading rubric. Each task went through an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review. Reviewers checked the prompt, experimental evidence, rubric, author notes and a graded model attempt.

Answers are scored against the task’s rubric, which assigns credit to individual criteria. Depending on the task, these criteria assess the conclusion, numerical results, supporting reasoning or recognition that the evidence is insufficient.

## Results

We evaluated seven models on BioBasicsBench: GPT‑5.2, GPT‑5.4, GPT‑5.5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna and GPT‑6 Astra. The evaluation covers 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks per setting, for a total of 18,500 results.

We report **mean reward**: the average task score, expressed as a percentage of the available credit. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals calculated by resampling whole tasks, keeping the five attempts for each task together.

**Mean reward versus average output tokens per task, shown on a logarithmic scale. Each point represents a tested reasoning-effort setting; lines connect those settings in order. The x-axis doubles at each tick. Dashed orange lines show GPT‑5 models, and solid blue lines show GPT‑6 models. Faint whiskers show 95% whole-task bootstrap confidence intervals. Each setting includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Effort settings differ across models.**

GPT‑6 Astra substantially improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol, even at low reasoning effort. These gains suggest that **stronger native multimodal capabilities may be key to improving performance on everyday wet-lab** analysis.

### Performance at xhigh reasoning effort

| **Model** | **Mean reward** | **95% CI** | **Output tokens / task** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **GPT‑6 Astra** | 66.7% | 60.3–73.1% | 4,704 |
| **GPT‑6.1 Sol** | 62.0% | 55.6–68.4% | 5,238 |
| **GPT‑5.6 Sol** | 43.8% | 37.6–50.0% | 9,099 |
| **GPT‑6 Luna** | 38.3% | 32.3–44.5% | 13,120 |
| **GPT‑5.5** | 35.4% | 29.7–41.0% | 11,135 |
| **GPT‑5.4** | 33.2% | 28.3–38.4% | 13,717 |
| **GPT‑5.2** | 31.2% | 26.2–36.3% | 27,620 |

*Xhigh is the highest reasoning-effort setting reported for all seven models. Each row includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Max-effort results, where available, are included in the chart above.*

## GPT‑6 Astra improvements from GPT‑5.6 Sol

### Recognizing what the data can and cannot show

A common trap in science is over-interpreting the data, especially given the nature of bias that occurs when testing a hypothesis. Astra demonstrated a better ability to discern the limit of what the data shows and not draw unwarranted conclusions.

In this example, GPT‑5.6 Sol classified cells as dead based on the signal from a dye used to detect dead cells. But the detector could also pick up light from a second dye, so brightness alone could not justify that conclusion. Astra recognized this ambiguity and called for better controls to separate the signals.

#### The same cells, three detection channels



*Brightfield · transmitted light*



*Channel 2 · SYTOX-labelled · 470–540 nm*



*Channel 3 · FUN-1 green · 525–580 nm*

**The same cell regions in three channels; the detection windows overlap at 525–540 nm. The shared window permits interference; its amount has not been measured. Each channel is displayed with a separate linear intensity scale, fixed across both regions; brightness cannot be compared quantitatively between channels.**

### Better multimodal handling

Scientific research is highly multimodal, requiring constant visual interpretation and decision making. Astra displayed a significant improvement at handling multimodal data which was given in the form of photos and videos, as well as raw outputs from sequencing, plate-reader assays, microscopy and flow cytometry.

At the most basic level, this improvement was noticeable through GPT‑6 Astra’s ability to pick up on finer detail from images taken during experiments and therefore draw more accurate conclusions as shown in this example. This task asked agents to draw conclusions from a DNA cloning experiment, where controls are essential. GPT‑5.6 Sol saw no colonies on the negative control plate and based its conclusions on that observation. GPT‑6 Astra noticed that the plate was labeled with the wrong antibiotic and correctly rejected it as a reliable control.



*Original photograph*



*The label on the rim*

**The original benchmark photograph, with the rim label circled and enlarged. “LB Kan50” identifies kanamycin, a different antibiotic from the ampicillin used in the experiment.**

### Keeping experimental context in mind

Scientists must be able to hold tacit biological knowledge and experimental context in mind whilst analysing data in order to correctly interpret what it shows. Astra demonstrated an improved ability to maintain this context and apply it throughout its analysis.

One task showed cells coming into and out of focus in a series of microscope images. While GPT‑5.6 Sol looked for a biological explanation for the cells’ apparent disappearance, GPT‑6 Astra correctly recognized a z-stack: a series of images taken at different depths.

#### Cha

title: Stop Giving Your AI Agents API Keys - Kim Maida, Keycard & Mason Egger, Temporal
body:
Kim Maida of Keycard and Mason Egger of Temporal show how to build AI agents that are both secure and reliable. Kim replaces shared API keys with OAuth token exchange, so every tool call gets a short-lived token scoped to that one call and tied to both the agent's identity and the user it's acting for, building it live on an expense-approval agent with a full audit trail of who filed and approved what. Mason then uses Temporal's durable execution to kill an agent mid-task and bring it back exactly where it left off, without re-running LLM calls or storing credentials in its history.

title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
body:
AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action.
Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task.
As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power.
What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt.
Why it matters: [NVIDIA Vera](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/) delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity.
The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.
- Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU.
- Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.
Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests:
[Perplexity](https://www.perplexity.ai/en-GB/hub/blog/secure-sandboxes-for-agents): Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system.[DeepInfra](https://deepinfra.com/blog/nvidia-vera-cpu-benchmark): Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested.[ClickHouse](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-performance-on-nvidia-vera): Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard.[DuckLabs](https://duckdb.org/2026/10/16/nvidia-vera-benchmark): Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline.[Daytona](https://www.daytona.io/dotfiles/when-2000-agents-share-one-cpu): Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86.[Modal](https://modal.com/blog/nvidia-vera-sandboxes): Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load.
Learn more about the [NVIDIA Vera CPU](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/vera-cpu/).

title: How Netflix Evaluates AI When There's No Right Answer - Cameron Wolfe, Netflix
body:
Cameron Wolfe, a staff research scientist at Netflix and author of the Deep (Learning) Focus newsletter, lays out a three-part framework for evaluating tasks with no single right answer, like creative writing. Human evaluation with calibrated guidelines is the North Star; LLM judges and rubrics, checked against human "golden" data, scale up offline evals; and A/B tests and production monitoring confirm results in the real world. Along the way he covers fighting noise with power analysis, error bars and resampling, and a Netflix project where an LLM judge's scores were causally linked to viewers abandoning shows.

Cult.fit is one of India’s leading technology-enabled fitness companies, operating 708 fitness centers across 77 cities and serving nearly one million paid members. Its business combines subscription-based access to gyms and trainer-led fitness classes with a growing consumer products portfolio spanning fitness equipment, accessories, workout footwear and activewear.

As the company grew, it wanted to solve more operational and product challenges without adding layers of process and complexity. By standardizing engineering on Codex and then extending it beyond engineering, cult.fit is helping teams across the organization analyze data, build tools, and move ideas into production. Alongside its Codex rollout, it is using the OpenAI API to develop more personalized member experiences, including through its AI Trainer.

For Santhosh Kumar, CTO at cult.fit, AI presented an opportunity to change how the organization works. “We wanted to become more AI-native in the way we run things,” he says. “How can we run our operations or transform our operations to be AI-first? What new customer experiences can we offer? And how can we transform how we run our organization?”

## Standardizing software development with Codex

Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. Different tools meant different conventions for repositories, agent instructions, skills, and development workflows, making it harder to share knowledge and reuse capabilities across teams.

Cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The company chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.

> “Once we standardized on Codex, we could build our software development lifecycle around a single platform.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

The team then extended Codex into more specialized engineering workflows. Its Site Reliability Engineering agent can aggregate information from observability platforms and logs, investigate incidents, and, in many cases, create a pull request with a proposed fix for an engineer to review. Security agents help identify and address vulnerabilities, while other on-call agents investigate recurring production issues.

Cult.fit is also moving toward a more fully spec-driven development model, where a specification can guide work through the software development lifecycle toward a pull request for an engineer to review. This gives teams a more repeatable path from a defined requirement to working code.

One recent example is a social feed for the cult.fit app. Kumar estimates the project would previously have taken more than a year to build. Using the new workflow, the team built and shipped it end to end in two months.

## Giving every team the ability to build

Codex has since expanded beyond engineering. cult.fit made its company data easier for Codex to work with, allowing teams to find answers and perform routine analysis themselves. Previously, even small data requests had to go through a central analyst team, creating a bottleneck.

> “Codex has been our biggest step toward data democratization. Teams can now do the analysis they need themselves.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

Teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. More than 20 internal applications have been built by non-engineering teams in recent months.

That shift is changing how cult.fit thinks about the software it needs to run its business. When the cost of its internal dashboard software increased sharply, one engineer rebuilt the functionality with Codex over a weekend. Cult.fit now runs the capability on its own application, avoiding more than $100,000 in annual software costs.

Making this shift required more than giving employees access to Codex. A large hackathon gave employees an early view of what was possible. The company then brought its management team together for a one-day session where leaders across functions built something relevant to their own work with Codex.

Engineering also runs twice-weekly office hours to help employees move projects from an idea to production, while engineers are embedded in selected functions to provide technical and domain support.

> “Software has been democratized. With OpenAI’s solutions, our people are able to build their own applications around whatever their teams need.”

—Santhosh Kumar, CTO, cult.fit

## Enriching the member experience with AI

Cult.fit is also using the OpenAI API to extend AI into the member experience through its AI Trainer. With over 45% of cult.fit members being first time gym goers, guidance is a key access for helping them build a fitness habit. The company first built the AI Trainer several years ago to give members a guided personalized workout experience without a personal trainer.

Around 20% of Cult.fit’s gym users currently utilize the AI Trainer product. With advances in language models, cult.fit saw an opportunity to make the experience more interactive and conversational.

The latest version is designed around a voice-first workout experience. Using GPT Realtime through an OpenAI API integration, the trainer can provide coaching cues and support workout logging through two-way voice interaction.

## Making AI part of the operating model

Cult.fit is also applying AI to customer support workflows that previously required human agents to assess each case. One example is requests to waive penalties for missed group fitness classes.

When a member says they missed a class for a valid reason, an AI agent can assess the request by checking signals such as local weather and attendance patterns for that class before deciding whether the penalty should be waived.

Cult.fit built these agents into its existing Sprinklr support platform and connected them to its backend systems, moving customer support from a predominantly human-led chat model toward an AI-first workflow.

## Results at a glance

- 20+ internal applications built by non-engineering teams in recent months
- $100,000+ annual software savings by rebuilding an internal capability with Codex
- 50%+ reduction in customer support costs

## What’s next
